SEVEN SABOTAGE MUTATIONS plus one CONTROL: buyer gate removed, confirmUpgrade made a constant, the preview stops simulating the swap, the consent artifact dropped, the page fires the mutation instead of the dialog, the dialog mounted as the wrong product, the disclosed amount blanked - each reddened its own named test; the control changed nothing and nothing went red. ALSO: prd.json had accumulated one passes:true story (US-2433) and the US-2366 archive guard was failing the web suite - archived it (120 active, 2325 archived, nextId unchanged).

userStories.title: No advance renewal reminder exists anywhere — annual plans are charged silently
userStories.description: Confirmed absence, verified three ways: invoice.upcoming is NOT in the Stripe webhook switch (services/edge-functions/src/routes/webhooks.ts:244-281, falls through to a default log-and-drop at :281); no cron in jobs-cron-fleet.ts sends one; and the only upcoming_invoice reference is a read-only pull for the billing page (payments.ts:1142). The first notice a user receives about a renewal is sendSubscriptionRenewalReceiptEmail (email.ts:1183), sent AFTER the money is taken. Yearly price IDs exist for all five paid tiers (src/lib/constants.ts:1344-1366) and flow through the identical path — interval only changes a display string — so an annual subscriber is charged a full year's fee with no prior contact whatsoever.
acceptanceCriteria: Handle invoice.upcoming and send a transactional advance renewal notice stating the amount, the date of the charge, the plan, and how to cancel before it.
Configure the Stripe lead time explicitly rather than relying on the default, and set a longer lead for annual plans than monthly.
Send via deliverEmail as a TRANSACTIONAL category — it must not be routed through the drip/marketing engine where opt-out, suppression or frequency caps can silently drop it.
Also handle customer.subscription.trial_will_end.
Test that an annual subscription produces a reminder before renewal and that a marketing opt-out does not suppress it.

OPERATOR: two Stripe-side steps, and neither is code. (a) AC2 - set the renewal-reminder lead time explicitly in the Stripe Dashboard under Settings -> Billing -> Upcoming renewal reminders, with a LONGER lead for annual than monthly. The 3-day default is thin notice for a full year of charge and is the reason this story exists. (b) AC5 live half - confirm a real annual subscription actually produces the reminder before renewal, which needs a Stripe run and cannot be asserted from a checkout. Everything else shipped: invoice.upcoming and customer.subscription.trial_will_end are handled, the notice goes out as TRANSACTIONAL so a marketing opt-out cannot suppress it, and there is a test for that.
userStories.notes: [P1][Compliance/Comms] Found 2026-07-18 by the subscription-compliance deep-dive audit. LEGAL CONTEXT (verified 2026-07-18, not legal advice): the FTC's 2024 'Click-to-Cancel' Negative Option Rule was VACATED by the Eighth Circuit on 2025-07-08 and is not in force. The FTC restarted rulemaking with an ANPRM on 2026-03-11 (comments closed 2026-04-13), so a successor rule is in flux. The binding obligations today are (a) ROSCA 15 U.S.C. 8403 and FTC Act Section 5, both actively enforced, and (b) STATE automatic-renewal laws — most importantly California's ARL as amended by AB 2863, effective 2025-07-01, which is stricter than what we do today and expressly covers free trials. Design to the California standard: it is the binding one, and it closely tracks the vacated federal rule, so building to it also front-runs the successor. Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). Advance notice before a long-term renewal is a common state-ARL requirement and we have annual plans in production. Cheapest structural fix in the batch: one webhook case reusing existing email infrastructure. | 2026-07-19 AC1 + AC3 + AC4 + AC5 DONE (mechanism, not copy — the fourth compliance story that did not need counsel). invoice.upcoming is now HANDLED and sends sendRenewalReminderEmail, a NEW template deliberately separate from sendSubscriptionRenewalReceiptEmail: a receipt confirms something that happened, this warns about something that has not, and the only action that matters — cancel before the date — is meaningless on a receipt. It states the plan, the amount, the exact charge date and how to cancel. AC3: category subscription_renewal_reminder is registered in TRANSACTIONAL_CATEGORIES, so resolveIsMarketing force-classifies it transactional even if marketing:true is explicitly requested — pinned by a test, because if that ever flips, an opt-out silently drops the only advance warning of a charge and the exact defect returns. AC4 customer.subscription.trial_will_end is handled too, and THE DISJOINTNESS IS THE INTERESTING PART: our signup trial has NO Stripe subscription (handle_new_user grants it directly), and US-2120's cron filters flipdesk_subscription_id IS NULL. This event fires only for a STRIPE-managed trial — someone who started a PAID subscription with a trial period — which is exactly the user that cron skips. The two populations cannot overlap, so neither path double-sends. A test asserts the cron keeps that filter, since removing it would make both fire for the same person. It reuses sendTrialExpiringEmail rather than minting a second trial template, because two near-identical trial emails drift. DECLINES TO SEND WITHOUT A DATE: if Stripe supplies neither next_payment_attempt nor period_end the handler returns. A notice that cannot say WHEN is not a notice, and 'you will be charged at some point' is worse than silence. Same reasoning as US-2117's refusal to write a partial agreement. TWO OF MY OWN EARLIER ARTEFACTS CAUGHT THIS CHANGE, which is the guards working: (1) the US-2128 test asserting invoice.upcoming and trial_will_end were on the known-ignored list went RED, correctly — they had graduated to real handlers, and a handled event must never ALSO be listed as ignored or the list is lying. Rewritten to assert the list stays annotated rather than naming those two specifically. (2) Removing them left an ORPHANED group header ('Covered by their own stories / other handlers.') heading an empty group — deleted. STILL OPEN: AC2 only — configure the Stripe lead time explicitly (and longer for annual than monthly). That is a Stripe dashboard/API setting, not code: Stripe decides when invoice.upcoming fires, and the default is 3 days. Worth doing since a 3-day warning on a full YEAR's charge is thin, but it cannot be set from here. Verified: edge 4306 passed, deno check + lint clean. | 2026-07-19 VERIFIED ALREADY DONE (US-2089-style stale box). This story's premise — 'invoice.upcoming is NOT in the Stripe webhook switch' — is no longer true: webhooks.ts dispatches invoice.upcoming to handleInvoiceUpcoming (:284) AND customer.subscription.trial_will_end to handleTrialWillEnd (:294), both carrying US-2119 attribution comments. Closed by that work; the story was simply never flipped. Found while triaging the P1 Compliance/Comms cluster for US-2122. NOT marking passes:true from here, because I did not verify AC2 (the explicit Stripe lead-time configuration, which is a dashboard setting) or AC5's live test — someone with Stripe access should confirm those two before closing. | 2026-07-22 ADDED THE MISSING AC3/AC5 GUARD (agent loop), passes:false held on the external ACs. The prior note flagged that it "did not verify AC5"; the transactional half of AC5 (and AC3) had NO test at all — sendRenewalReminderEmail uses category subscription_renewal_reminder (email.ts:2936) which IS in TRANSACTIONAL_CATEGORIES (email-transport.ts:49), so resolveIsMarketing force-classifies it transactional and a marketing opt-out cannot suppress it — but nothing pinned that. If someone reclassified it, the renewal reminder would silently become marketing-suppressible and an annual subscriber could be charged with no warning (the exact US-2120 bug class). New services/edge-functions/src/tests/renewal-reminder_test.ts (2 tests, mirrors trial-notice_test.ts): asserts the category is transactional + resolveIsMarketing===false, and structurally that webhooks.ts dispatches invoice.upcoming to sendRenewalReminderEmail (not the drip). Verified: deno check+lint clean, 2 tests pass. STILL passes:false: AC2 (the explicit Stripe lead-time is a Dashboard billing setting — Settings->Billing->Upcoming renewal reminders — not code) and AC5's live half (an annual sub actually producing a reminder before renewal needs a Stripe run). AC1/AC3/AC4 are done (handleInvoiceUpcoming + handleTrialWillEnd wired, transactional category, now guarded). | 2026-08-10 THE BUYER HALF EXISTED NOWHERE, and that is a bigger gap than the one this story last recorded as open. handleInvoiceUpcoming opened with `if (invoiceIsBuyer(invoice)) return;`. That line is copied from three sibling handlers where it is CORRECT - handleInvoicePaymentSucceeded, handleInvoicePaymentFailed and handleInvoicePaymentActionRequired all do seller cycle resets or dunning transitions whose buyer equivalent arrives on customer.subscription.updated. This handler does none of that. It only SENDS A NOTICE, and it is the only place one is sent (verified: sendRenewalReminderEmail has exactly one non-test call site). So a buyer on an ANNUAL plan was charged a full year with no prior contact whatsoever - the literal words of this story's own title, still live on the other product, while the story read as 'AC1 done'. Same shape as US-2118, hours earlier: a compliance control built for FlipDesk and never wired to the buyer product, with a guard that named one route. FIXED: handleInvoiceUpcoming now branches instead of returning. A lapsed buyer (buyer_plan 'free') is still skipped - naming 'Free' in a charge notice is worse than silence. recordEvent keeps from_plan/to_plan as the user's real flipdesk_plan because those columns are typed public.flipdesk_plan and a buyer tier raises 22P02 there; the buyer detail goes in the jsonb payload. Same enum trap US-2118 hit. THE EMAIL WAS SELLER-SHAPED IN TWO PLACES, not one. It hardcoded 'FlipDesk' in the subject AND the body, and linked to /dashboard/billing. A buyer notice with the seller's billing link is arguably worse than no notice: it names the correct charge and then sends the reader to a page that cannot cancel it, at the one moment the whole email exists to enable action. Both values now come from NEW lib/renewal-notice-copy.ts - a pure module rather than an inline ternary, so the values can be ASSERTED rather than regex-matched. `product` on RenewalReminderData is REQUIRED with no default, deliberately: the default would have been 'flipdesk' and every buyer would have silently gotten the wrong one. GUARD: a new census case walks every `if (invoiceIsBuyer(invoice)) return;` in webhooks.ts and requires the comment above it to name where the buyer path IS served ('subscription.updated'). A skip is not wrong; an UNEXPLAINED skip is - and the next person to copy that line now has to answer the question that was skipped here. It also asserts handleInvoiceUpcoming has none, and that the EMAIL argument (not merely the handler) carries the product. THAT LAST SCOPING WAS FOUND BY SABOTAGE, and it is the third time this session the same mistake shape has appeared. My first assertion checked the whole handler body for `product: isBuyer ? ...`, which ALSO appears in the recordEvent payload a few lines above - so pinning the email argument to a constant left the test green while buyers got FlipDesk copy. Checking the use and not the specific site is how a guard passes over the thing it guards. NEW STORY FILED, not scope creep: US-2451. The renewal RECEIPT is inside handleInvoicePaymentSucceeded, behind the same buyer skip, and applyBuyerSubscriptionChange sends none - so a buyer is charged and hears nothing afterwards either. Its skip is legitimately protecting seller cycle resets, so the fix is to split the send out of the skipped body rather than widen it. Out of scope here because this story is about the ADVANCE notice. STILL passes:false on the same two ACs as before, both external: AC2 (the explicit Stripe lead time - a Dashboard setting under Settings -> Billing -> Upcoming renewal reminders, and note Stripe's 3-day default is thin for a full YEAR's charge) and AC5's live half (an annual subscription actually producing a reminder before renewal, which needs a Stripe run). Neither is code and neither moved. VERIFIED: deno check clean on webhooks.ts, email.ts and the new module; deno lint clean across 1482 files; renewal-reminder_test.ts 5 passed (up 3); full edge suite 6434 passed / 0 failed / 176 ignored (up 3). SEVEN SABOTAGE MUTATIONS, each reddening its own named test: the buyer skip restored on the notice handler, a NEW unexplained skip added to another handler, the email argument pinned to a constant product, the buyer manage URL pointed at the seller page, the buyer product name left as FlipDesk, the trailing-slash guard removed, and the template re-hardcoded. | 2026-08-10 (second pass) AC4 WAS HANDLED BUT NOT PRODUCT-AWARE, which is the INVERSE of the five buyer omissions closed alongside it today: not silence, but confidently wrong. handleTrialWillEnd had no subscriptionIsBuyer check. A BUYER subscription with a Stripe-managed trial would have been sent sendTrialExpiringEmail - copy that names a '14-day FlipDesk Pro trial', offers to keep 'your Pro features', and links to the seller billing page. Every sentence of it false for the recipient, on a notice whose only job is to prompt a payment method before access lapses. SKIPPED RATHER THAN GIVEN NEW COPY, and the reason is a product fact rather than caution: A BUYER STRIPE TRIAL IS NOT A PRODUCT STATE. POST /buyer/subscribe builds its Checkout session with no trial_period_days and no subscription_data.trial_end, so one can only exist if someone configures a trial on a price in the Stripe dashboard. Writing a notice for a flow that does not exist means guessing what it should say, and this story's own AC1 reasoning applies - a notice that cannot state the real terms is worse than none. Same call as US-2453's buyer pause/resume decision. THE PREMISE IS GUARDED, NOT ASSUMED, and that is what separates this from the omissions it sits beside. A second test reads /buyer/subscribe and fails if it ever sets trial_period_days or trial_end - so the day a buyer trial ships, the skip fails loudly and names itself, instead of quietly outliving its reason the way the five did. The warn log names the story too, so an operator seeing the event in production has a thread to pull. THREE SABOTAGE MUTATIONS, each reddening its own named test: the skip removed (a buyer gets the seller's trial email), the skip moved after the send, and a trial_period_days added to /buyer/subscribe. AC4 IS NOW GENUINELY DONE - the event is handled and handled correctly for both products. AC1/AC3/AC5's transactional half remain done. STILL passes:false on the SAME two external ACs as before, neither of which moved: AC2 (the explicit Stripe lead time, a Dashboard setting under Settings -> Billing -> Upcoming renewal reminders, where the 3-day default is thin for a full year's charge) and AC5's live half (an annual subscription actually producing a reminder before renewal, which needs a Stripe run). VERIFIED: deno check clean on webhooks.ts; deno lint clean across 1486 files; buyer-lifecycle-emails_test.ts 11 passed (2 new); full edge suite 6461 passed / 0 failed / 176 ignored (up 2).

userStories.title: Substantiation review of every public authenticity claim and its framing
userStories.description: Authenticity verdicts (likely_authentic / inconclusive / red_flags) are shown on public certificates and returned from an unauthenticated public endpoint, currently with no accuracy gate behind them. Separately, the seeded brand KB was written to REFUSE authentication — 00398_coach_brand_knowledge.sql:14 reads 'NEVER auto-authenticate... A creed/serial proves NOTHING about authenticity on its own' — so our own knowledge base contradicts the product's public posture. That contradiction needs resolving deliberately, not by drift.
acceptanceCriteria: Review every user-facing authenticity string against what the evidence can actually support, with counsel — fold into the US-2114 review gate rather than running a separate process.

Decide and document the claim posture: assessment/opinion with stated limitations vs verification. The pipeline is built for the former (confidence ceilinged at 0.9, hard-capped to 0.5 on contradiction, limitations set from a constant the model cannot override) — keep that discipline in the copy.
Reconcile the brand-KB 'never auto-authenticate' guidance with the shipped product posture.

Check eBay policy exposure: grade-badge.ts is already dead because eBay bans grade overlays on listing imagery, and eBay runs its own Authenticity Guarantee — determine what may be stated on a listing before building listing-facing surfaces.
Confirm the unauthenticated public endpoint should expose verdicts at all.

OPERATOR: review every public authenticity claim WITH COUNSEL. AC1 requires it, and the story's own instruction is 'do not let an agent draft the claim language' - so this is not work to hand back to an agent under any framing. Declared because a story that says NOT AGENT WORK only in a note reads, to anyone scanning the backlog, exactly like a story nobody has got to yet.
userStories.notes: [P1][Authenticity/Legal][EPIC: Visual Authenticity] Found 2026-07-19 by the authenticity deep-dive audit. STRATEGY CONTEXT: Certilogo was the starting reference, but its model does not transfer — it verifies a brand-issued CLG code / QR on a security label sewn in at manufacture (its AI image recognition authenticates the TAG and detects cloned codes, not the garment's construction). GradeThread inspects garments it never manufactured, with no token. The transferable play is visual authentication of the garment itself, anchored on evidence we can actually capture. Note the scaffolding is ~80% built (ai-authenticity.ts is live in production) while the evidence base is ~5% — this epic closes that gap in order: contain what is already live, then raise evidence quality, then productize the claim. Pairs with the FTC Section 5 batch (US-2114..2128) — same substantiation problem, different claim. Do not let an agent draft the claim language. ACCURACY GATE 2026-07-19 (decided: adopt the conservative posture ahead of counsel): the public /tools/authenticity-check endpoint now requires a PASSING eval run in addition to PUBLIC_AUTHENTICITY_CHECK_ENABLED. CORRECTION to an earlier characterisation of the exposure: that endpoint was ALREADY fail-closed behind the env flag (default off) and documented as awaiting legal review of the limitations copy — so the risk was lower than described. What was missing is that the env flag is the LEGAL gate (a human read the copy) and says nothing about whether the model is any good; enabling it after a legal review should not be sufficient to publish verdicts from a prompt version that has never cleared the golden set. The two gates are now separate and both required. Authenticated surfaces (paid add-on, buyer check) deliberately still run ungated — they carry the limitations disclaimer and a named account, a different posture from an anonymous public claim. Returns 503 + Retry-After rather than 404 so a crawler does not deindex the tool page behind it. 4431 edge tests pass. | 2026-08-09 AC3 NOW OWNS A REQUIREMENT THAT WAS DUPLICATED, and inherits the evidence. US-2139 AC6 asked for the same reconciliation ('see US-2133' in its own text) and has been closed as a duplicate, so this AC is the single home for it. WHAT THE CONTRADICTION ACTUALLY IS, measured rather than described, so the work starts from facts: 37 seeded brand packs carry prose such as 'NEVER label a Coach item authentic — flag anything inconsistent in condition notes only' (00398_coach_brand_knowledge.sql) and 'LUXURY — never auto-authenticate' (00399_louis_vuitton_brand_knowledge.sql), while the shipped pipeline's deriveVerdict (lib/ai-authenticity.ts) emits 'likely_authentic' as one of three possible verdicts on a PAID add-on. TWO THINGS THAT MAKE THIS SMALLER THAN IT LOOKS. (1) The gap may be one of WORDING rather than of posture: the shipped verdict is confidence-capped (AUTHENTICITY_VERDICT_CONFIDENCE_CEILING 0.9, harder caps for contradictions, no-macro evidence, thin reference coverage and — as of today — unverified brand tells) and carries a mandatory disclosure, so a capped-and-disclosed 'likely authentic' is arguably not the act the KB prose forbids. Settling that is AC2's job and this AC's answer follows from it. (2) THE FIX CANNOT BE AN EDIT TO THE SEEDS. That prose lives in applied migrations, which are immutable — the reconciliation has to land in the vault (vault/20-domain/brands/ already owns the KB's governing rules) with the seeds left alone, exactly as US-2059 requires for any knowledge stranded in a migration header. ⚠ NOT AGENT WORK, restating this story's own instruction because it is the thing most likely to be overlooked by whoever picks it up: 'Do not let an agent draft the claim language', and AC1 requires review WITH COUNSEL. What an agent CAN safely do here is exactly what this note does — locate both sides, quote them, and stop. | 2026-08-10 THE INVENTORY AC1 NEEDS NOW EXISTS, and nothing here drafts a claim. This story's own note says what an agent may safely do - locate both sides, quote them, and stop - and the 2026-08-09 pass did that for ONE example (the brand-KB contradiction). This does it exhaustively, which is the difference between an anecdote and an inventory. NEW vault/20-domain/authenticity-claim-register.md. The three verdicts and the exact strings a user reads; what the pipeline actually supports for them; what the evidence base actually is; and the KB contradiction, carried over rather than restated. THE ONE OBSERVATION WORTH THE WHOLE PAGE: the rendered labels are deliberately WEAKER than the enum names. likely_authentic renders as 'Looks consistent with genuine' - an observation about photographs - where the enum name would read as a judgement about the item. That single string IS the product's legal posture, and nothing was pinning it. A copy edit to 'Authentic' would be a posture change that nobody would file a bug about. It is pinned now. WHAT BACKS THE CLAIMS, gathered so a reviewer is not doing archaeology: AUTHENTICITY_LIMITATIONS is a fixed constant the model cannot author and states in the output that this is 'not a definitive authentication, legal opinion, or guarantee' and 'one trust signal, not proof'; AUTHENTICITY_NO_MACRO_LIMITATION is appended when no close-up backed the read; confidence is ceilinged and capped harder on contradiction, missing macro evidence, thin coverage and unverified tells, composing by minimum and never raising; and the public endpoint has TWO independent gates because the env flag is the LEGAL gate and says nothing about whether the model is any good. AND THE UNCOMFORTABLE NUMBER, because the review needs it more than any of the above: all 179 seeded authentication_tells payloads use the LEGACY {tell, detail} shape and ZERO use the structured one, so coerceTell maps them to category 'other' with no redFlag - they are prose the prompt reads and the verdict cannot use. CANONICAL_TELLS holds 7 structured tells across 3 brands, every one sourced 'unverified - review in admin'. The distinction that matters is between HAVING tells and having USABLE tells (US-2219 measured this; the register carries it forward rather than making the reviewer find it). GUARD: NEW services/edge-functions/src/tests/authenticity-claim-register_test.ts. Reads the verdict union from the TYPE and the labels from the page's map, and fails when either is unregistered - so a fourth verdict or a reworded label cannot ship unseen. It also fails a label containing Authentic / Verified / Confirmed genuine / Genuine item / Guaranteed, requires the positive verdict to stay an observation ('consistent'), and fails if AUTHENTICITY_LIMITATIONS stops saying the two things the register cites it for. Plus the same honesty rule as the subscription register: no line may claim substantiation without a dated record. FIVE SABOTAGE MUTATIONS, each reddening its own case: the positive verdict reworded to 'Authentic', a label reworded without updating the register, a fourth verdict added, the limitations constant losing 'not proof', and the register claiming substantiation. STILL passes:false and nothing here changes that. AC1 is the review itself, AC2 the posture decision, AC3 the KB reconciliation, AC4 the eBay policy question, AC5 whether the unauthenticated endpoint should expose verdicts at all - all counsel or owner work. What changed is that the review has a complete list with its evidence attached, and the one string carrying the posture can no longer move by accident while it waits. VERIFIED: authenticity-claim-register_test.ts 5 passed (new); deno lint clean across 1490 files; full edge suite 6481 passed / 0 failed / 176 ignored; vault:lint --strict clean at 168 notes.

userStories.title: iOS silently omits the entire paid consumer grading path, including the 14-day dispute flow
userStories.description: As a consumer grading on iOS, I want the same journey the web offers. There are TWO independent grading pipelines in the edge: the consumer/certified path (routes/grade.ts:209 /submit, :751 /pay/:id, :837 /status/:id, :1117 /dispute) and the FlipDesk/reseller path (/api/flipdesk/grading/{validate,submit,submissions/:id}). Web implements BOTH (new-submission.tsx:647, bulk-submission.tsx:332, submission-detail.tsx:244). iOS implements ONLY the FlipDesk path — Grading/GradingService.swift:6,55 documents and calls validate -> submit -> GET /submissions/:id — and grepping iOS for grade/pay, grade/status and grade/dispute returns NOTHING. So iOS has no consumer certified-grading submission, no per-grade payment flow, and NO GRADE DISPUTE FLOW at all.
acceptanceCriteria: Decide explicitly whether the consumer grading path belongs on iOS. Nothing in IOS_PARITY_AUDIT.md or the Android plan mentions this omission either way, which is weak evidence it is accidental rather than a product decision — settle it in writing.
If it belongs: implement submit / pay / status / dispute on iOS against routes/grade.ts.

If it does not: document why, and confirm the dispute obligation is discharged some other way — a 14-day dispute window that only one client can exercise is a support and chargeback liability regardless of intent.
Any parity matrix must stop treating 'grading submission' as ONE row; scoring it that way marks iOS complete while the entire paid consumer path is missing.

OPERATOR: decide where the consumer grading path is entered from on iOS, then it can be wired. The flow itself is BUILT and TESTED - ConsumerGradeFlow.swift implements submit, pay, poll and result with the money-first ordering, PhotoGradeSubmit posts to the endpoint, dispute ships - and NOTHING CONSTRUCTS IT. Measured 2026-08-22: ConsumerGradeFlow is referenced only by its own file and its test; PhotoGradeSubmit has no caller outside its own file. A seller cannot reach any of it. ⚠ AND THE PARITY GUARD READS GREEN OVER THIS. grading-pipeline-parity.test.ts asserts iOS has every endpoint of both pipelines, and it does - as strings in two files nothing opens. The guard answers whether the source contains the call, not whether a user can get to it, so it will keep passing until someone looks. The decision is the entry point: a tab, a row on an existing screen, or a route from a push. Once that is chosen the wiring is small.
userStories.notes:
[P1][iOS/Parity] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. Two implementations of the core revenue journey is the highest-value drift surface in the repo, and the mobile client omits the paid half. The dispute gap is the sharpest edge: US-1340 tracks a 14-day dispute window as a real obligation, and a user who graded on iOS has no in-app route to exercise it. | ⚠ 2026-08-17 THE PREMISE IS PARTLY STALE, re-verified against the tree rather than re-read from the story.  This story says "grepping iOS for grade/pay, grade/status and grade/dispute returns NOTHING" and "NO GRADE DISPUTE FLOW at all". The dispute half is WRONG NOW: ios/GradeThread/Grading/ carries DisputeSheet.swift, DisputeReason.swift (with GradeDisputeWindow), DisputeStatusDisplay.swift, and CertifiedGradeSection.swift wires the affordance behind GradeDisputeWindow.isOpen plus an already-disputed check. It shipped with US-1340. So the sharpest edge this story named - "a user who graded on iOS has no in-app route to exercise the 14-day dispute" - is closed.  TWO CORRECTIONS THAT COME WITH IT. First, the window is SEVEN days, not fourteen: US-1340 title said 14, its own AC-DEVIATION note recorded the real rule as 7, and routes/grade.ts:1705 now enforces DISPUTE_WINDOW_DAYS = 7 server-side. Anything in this story reasoning from 14 is reasoning from a number that was never implemented. Second, iOS was filing by INSERTING into the disputes table directly rather than calling the route - fixed in this pass, and the RLS hole it exposed is filed as US-2670.  STILL TRUE AND UNTOUCHED: the paid consumer path. grep of ios/ for grade/submit, grade/pay and grade/status returns nothing; the only /api/grade call is Snap. So AC1 (decide whether the consumer submit/pay path belongs on iOS) is still the open question, and AC3 second half is now ANSWERED for disputes - the obligation is discharged in-app, and it was already discharged before this pass. | 2026-08-17 A REAL PARITY GAP SURFACED WHILE ROUTING iOS DISPUTES THROUGH THE EDGE, and it belongs to this story rather than to the fix.  iOS FILES A DISPUTE WITH NO EVIDENCE PHOTOS. The edge route accepts an `images` array, validates each one (magic-byte sniff), strips EXIF and stores it under the owner folder (US-276); Android sends up to MAX_EVIDENCE = 8 and web posts base64 evidence from submission-detail.tsx. The iOS sheet collects a reason and free text only. For a CONDITION dispute that is the weak half - the seller argument is a photograph of the garment, and the one client built around a camera is the one that cannot attach one.  NOT FIXED IN THAT PASS, deliberately: the routing fix was a correctness change with a guard behind it, and adding a photo picker is a UI feature that cannot be compiled or exercised on this host. Filed here so the parity matrix AC4 asks for has the real row - "grade dispute" is not one row either, it is file-a-dispute (all three clients) and attach-evidence (two of three). | 2026-08-19 THE EVIDENCE-PHOTO ROW THIS STORY FILED IS NOW CLOSED, and the same pass found the dispute path was broken outright. The 2026-08-17 note recorded a real parity gap and deliberately did not fix it: iOS filed a dispute with no evidence photos, while web posts base64 evidence and Android sends up to MAX_EVIDENCE = 8, and 'the one client built around a camera is the one that cannot attach one'. DisputeSheet now sends up to 8, downscaled on device, through the `images` array the route already validated and EXIF-stripped. So AC4's parity matrix row - file-a-dispute versus attach-evidence - reads three of three on both halves now.  AND THE FILING ITSELF WAS FAILING, which nobody had noticed and which this story's own subject made likely to be blamed on the missing feature rather than on the route. DisputeSheet's request struct used a plain gradeReportId property and EdgeAPI encodes with .convertToSnakeCase, so the phone sent grade_report_id against a route that reads body.gradeReportId with no fallback: 400 on every attempt since 2026-08-17. Filed and fixed as US-2688.  WHAT REMAINS ON THIS STORY IS UNCHANGED AND IS AC1, a product decision rather than a build: does the consumer certified-grading path (submit / pay / status) belong on iOS at all? grep of ios/ for grade/submit, grade/pay and grade/status still returns nothing, and the only /api/grade call is Snap plus, now, dispute. AC3's second half is answered and has been since US-1340: the dispute obligation is discharged in-app, and with this pass it is discharged with the same evidence every other client can attach. | 2026-08-22 THE NOTE ABOVE IS STALE AND THE STORY IS IN A STRANGER STATE THAN EITHER READING. It says 'grep of ios/ for grade/submit, grade/pay and grade/status still returns nothing'. All three are present. AC1 was answered by BUILDING it: ios/GradeThread/Grading/ConsumerGradeFlow.swift is headed 'US-2016 - the consumer grade journey as a state machine' and implements submit -> pay -> poll -> result, with PhotoGradeSubmit.swift posting to api/grade/submit and dispute shipping under US-2670/US-2688.  ⚠ AND NO USER CAN REACH ANY OF IT. ConsumerGradeFlow is referenced by exactly two places in the whole repo: its own file and ConsumerGradeFlowTests.swift. Nothing constructs it - no view, no router, no sheet. PhotoGradeSubmit has no caller outside its own file either. The paid consumer path on iOS is fully implemented, fully unit-tested, and unreachable.  THE PARITY GUARD SAYS OTHERWISE, AND IT IS NOT WRONG - IT IS ANSWERING A DIFFERENT QUESTION. src/test/grading-pipeline-parity.test.ts case 'iOS has EVERY endpoint of both, which it did not before US-2016' passes. It walks each client's source files, strips comments, and looks for the endpoint strings. Those strings ARE in ios/GradeThread, in two files nothing reaches. So the guard answers 'does this client's source contain a call to this endpoint', which is not 'can a seller get to it'.  That guard's own header already warns it was once decorative - three sabotages passed until comments were stripped. This is a SECOND way for it to be decorative, and comment-stripping does not touch it: unreachable code is not a comment.  SO AC2 IS HALF DONE IN A WAY THAT READS AS FINISHED. The endpoints, the state machine, the money-first ordering (abstain and credits-prompt are both no-charge states and both get mistaken for failures) and the tests are all real work and all correct. What is missing is a view that constructs ConsumerGradeFlow and a way to open it.  NOT BUILT HERE. That is UI - a screen, a presentation path, and a decision about where the entry point lives in a tab bar that currently has none. I cannot see or run it, and a screen written blind is where an agent ships something that compiles and looks wrong. | COMPILATION SETTLED 2026-08-28. This note corrects one stale claim and changes nothing else about the story.

The notes above say some version of 'never been compiled' / 'iOS CI is the gate and it has not seen this' / 'cannot be verified from a Windows box'. That was true when written and is not true now. Every commit carrying this story's iOS code is an ancestor of iOS CI run 33139420556 on main (2026-08-28T03:37Z, head 1c6067106), conclusion SUCCESS - checked with git merge-base --is-ancestor, all commits in, none outside.

The run was checked for substance rather than for a green tick: both jobs succeeded, and the Build + test job's 'Generate Xcode project', 'Build + test' and 'Build app-extension targets' steps all executed. A green run whose build step never ran proves nothing.

ONE DISTINCTION MAKES THIS READABLE, and without it the evidence points the other way: many of these commits' OWN CI runs FAILED. 33 of the last 100 iOS CI runs on main were non-success, in one unbroken stretch from 2026-08-18 to 2026-08-27. iOS reports one error and stops, so a commit is not guilty of the failure it happens to sit on. 'Did its own run pass' has no useful answer; 'is it in a green build' does.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO: it does not close the story. Compilation was never the only thing outstanding here - what remains is whatever the notes above say it is, and it is now the ONLY thing outstanding, which is the point of writing this down. A story parked behind two blockers where one has quietly cleared reads as further away than it is.

THE CHECK IS TWO COMMANDS AND WORKS FROM WINDOWS: gh run list --workflow='iOS CI' --branch main to find the newest green run, then git merge-base --is-ancestor <commit> <that run's head>. Any story blocked on 'iOS CI has not seen this' can be settled the same way once its commits are on main. macOS-only COMPILATION is not macOS-only KNOWLEDGE.

userStories.title: No price-change notice or consent path on any platform
userStories.description: No code path notifies a user of a price increase before it takes effect. Stripe's price.updated and customer.subscription.updated-with-price-delta are not inspected (webhooks.ts:244-281). On Apple, the ASSN router (lib/appstore/notifications.ts:18-32) does not handle PRICE_INCREASE or DID_CHANGE_RENEWAL_PREF — Apple collects price-increase consent natively so this is not a rejection risk, but the server never learns a price change occurred, and an unconsented lapse arrives only as a generic EXPIRED. On Google Play, PRICE_CHANGE_CONFIRMED is explicitly a no-op (lib/google-play/rtdn.ts:11,107).
acceptanceCriteria: Notify subscribers in advance of any price increase, stating the old price, new price, effective date and how to cancel first.
Handle Apple PRICE_INCREASE and DID_CHANGE_RENEWAL_PREF so server state reflects platform-side changes.
Decide and document whether a price increase requires fresh affirmative consent on the web (it commonly does under state ARLs) and implement accordingly.
Do not implement a price change of any kind until this exists.

OPERATOR: AC3 is a legal determination and belongs with US-2114's counsel review - whether a price increase requires FRESH affirmative consent on the web, which it commonly does under state automatic-renewal laws. Batch it into that same conversation rather than asking twice. AC4 is a standing instruction rather than a task: do not implement a price change of any kind until the notice path exists. Worth keeping visible, because it is the criterion someone will step over when a pricing decision feels urgent.
userStories.notes: [P2][Compliance/Billing] Found 2026-07-18 by the subscription-compliance deep-dive audit. LEGAL CONTEXT (verified 2026-07-18, not legal advice): the FTC's 2024 'Click-to-Cancel' Negative Option Rule was VACATED by the Eighth Circuit on 2025-07-08 and is not in force. The FTC restarted rulemaking with an ANPRM on 2026-03-11 (comments closed 2026-04-13), so a successor rule is in flux. The binding obligations today are (a) ROSCA 15 U.S.C. 8403 and FTC Act Section 5, both actively enforced, and (b) STATE automatic-renewal laws — most importantly California's ARL as amended by AB 2863, effective 2025-07-01, which is stricter than what we do today and expressly covers free trials. Design to the California standard: it is the binding one, and it closely tracks the vacated federal rule, so building to it also front-runs the successor. Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). Currently latent — no price change has been attempted. It becomes a live exposure the moment pricing moves, which makes it cheap to fix now and expensive to fix under deadline. | 2026-07-19 AC2 DONE (mechanism — no counsel). Apple PRICE_INCREASE and DID_CHANGE_RENEWAL_PREF now reach server state. routeNotification gained a THIRD kind of verdict, record_only, distinct from both an entitlement action and 'ignore'. THAT DISTINCTION IS THE WHOLE POINT: Apple owns price-increase consent natively, so ACTING on these would be wrong — if the customer refuses, Apple lapses the subscription and we hear EXPIRED. But ignoring them meant that later EXPIRED was uninterpretable: indistinguishable from an ordinary cancellation, with no way to tell that a price change preceded it. Recording without acting is exactly the right posture, and it is the same 'known-ignored vs unexamined' distinction I built for the Stripe switch in US-2128 — the two surfaces had the identical defect. REUSED recordAppstoreEvent rather than hand-rolling the insert: it already namespaces stripe_event_id as appstore:<id> and swallows 23505, so an Apple retry cannot double-record. (My first attempt DID hand-roll it — the helper was 180 lines above and I had not looked. Worth noting because writing the second copy is always easier than finding the first.) 4 tests, including the two that matter: record_only must NOT be an entitlement action (not sub_active, not sub_expired, not revoke), and an unknown type must STILL fail closed to ignore — widening a router is exactly when a permissive default sneaks in. REMAINING, and correctly split: AC1 (notify subscribers in advance of an increase) needs the COPY, which is US-2114's gate — but note the DETECTION half is now free: US-2117's migration 00486 added pricing_plan_revisions, an append-only price history written BY TRIGGER, so 'a price changed' is already a queryable fact rather than something needing new plumbing. AC3 is explicitly a decision ('decide and document whether a price increase requires fresh affirmative consent on the web') and belongs to counsel. AC4 is a CONSTRAINT rather than work — do not ship a price change until AC1/AC3 exist — and is worth keeping visible: the pricing_plans trigger will now record any change, so an accidental one leaves evidence. Google Play PRICE_CHANGE_CONFIRMED is still a no-op (rtdn.ts) and is the same shape as the Apple fix if someone wants symmetry. Verified: edge 4310 passed, deno check + lint clean. | 2026-07-19 (cont.) AC2 EXTENDED TO GOOGLE PLAY — the symmetry I flagged last pass, and it turned out to be the SHARPER of the two platforms. Apple's PRICE_INCREASE is a notification that a price WILL change; Google's PRICE_CHANGE_CONFIRMED is the user ACCEPTING one. That makes it a consent artifact — exactly what subscription_agreements (US-2117) exists to hold — and dropping it meant the only server-side evidence of the acceptance was the eventual renewal amount, which is an INFERENCE rather than a record. classifyRtdn now returns record_only for type 8, and the reconciler writes an audit row via the existing recordEvent dep (idempotent on the event id) while touching no entitlement: Google owns the consent UI, so acting would pre-empt it, and the next renewal RTDN settles the amount. ADDED A DISTINCT OUTCOME VALUE rather than reusing 'ignored': both leave entitlement untouched, but one wrote an audit row and the other did not. Collapsing them would leave the RTDN log unable to answer 'did we ever learn the user accepted a price change?' — which is the entire point of the branch. TWO THINGS THE TYPE SYSTEM AND AN EXISTING TEST CAUGHT, both of them the system working: (1) adding the union variant broke the route glue's narrowing at `action.productType`, which is TypeScript correctly refusing to let a new action fall through unhandled; (2) an existing test asserted type 8 → ignore and went RED, correctly — it was encoding the old behaviour, and it was right to fail rather than let the change pass silently. Updated it to state WHY 8 left that group, so the next reader sees the reasoning rather than an unexplained gap in [9,10,11]. PROCESS NOTE: this took four attempts because bash ate template literals and regex escapes in inline node -e scripts (the fifth such incident today). Anything containing backticks or regex now goes through the Edit tool, not a shell string. Verified: edge 4312 passed, deno check + lint clean.

userStories.title: Two divergent cancellation paths — the stale portal route bypasses the reviewed flow
userStories.description: The primary cancellation flow is good and should be preserved: self-serve, ~4 clicks / 2 screens, no email or phone required, period-end timing stated on every screen (cancel-subscription-dialog.tsx:106,178,219), a required acknowledgement checkbox, clearly-labelled escape buttons, and an 'Undo cancel' banner afterwards (billing.tsx:373-395). It has one retention interstitial with two off-ramps ('Pause instead' / 'Switch to cheaper plan'), which is defensible but is the part most worth a second look. The defect is a SECOND path: selecting the Free tile in the plan picker routes to the Stripe billing portal instead (flipdesk-plan-picker-dialog.tsx:393-406), with a stale comment 'until US-216's cancel flow ships' — US-216 has shipped. That path bypasses the reviewed dialog and shows different, portal-native copy.
acceptanceCriteria: Route the Free-tile selection through the reviewed cancellation dialog; remove the stale portal path and its comment.
Audit for any other route to cancellation and ensure all converge on one reviewed flow.
Have the review gate assess the retention interstitial against 'simple mechanism' expectations — in particular whether two deflection off-ramps before the confirm step is defensible.
Confirm cancellation is available in the same medium as signup for every purchase path (web-purchased cancels on web; IAP correctly defers to the platform via .manageSubscriptionsSheet).

OPERATOR: in the Stripe Dashboard, check whether 'Cancel subscription' is enabled on the ACCOUNT DEFAULT customer portal configuration, and report on/off. billingPortal.sessions.create is called with no `configuration`, so the account default is what applies, and this checkout cannot observe it. If it is on - Stripe enables it by default in most setups - the portal is a second cancellation path reachable from the seller billing page, the plan picker and the buyer page, bypassing the reviewed dialog entirely: no period-end statement, no acknowledgement checkbox, no reason capture, no undo banner. That is the bigger half of AC2 and it cannot be closed from code.
userStories.notes: [P2][Compliance/Web] Found 2026-07-18 by the subscription-compliance deep-dive audit. LEGAL CONTEXT (verified 2026-07-18, not legal advice): the FTC's 2024 'Click-to-Cancel' Negative Option Rule was VACATED by the Eighth Circuit on 2025-07-08 and is not in force. The FTC restarted rulemaking with an ANPRM on 2026-03-11 (comments closed 2026-04-13), so a successor rule is in flux. The binding obligations today are (a) ROSCA 15 U.S.C. 8403 and FTC Act Section 5, both actively enforced, and (b) STATE automatic-renewal laws — most importantly California's ARL as amended by AB 2863, effective 2025-07-01, which is stricter than what we do today and expressly covers free trials. Design to the California standard: it is the binding one, and it closely tracks the vacated federal rule, so building to it also front-runs the successor. Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). California AB 2863 requires cancellation through the same medium used for the original transaction. Web is fine; the divergent path is the risk, not the flow itself. | 2026-07-19 AC1 + AC2 DONE (no counsel needed — this half is a code defect, not copy). AC1: selecting the Free tile in the plan picker now routes to the REVIEWED cancellation dialog instead of opening the Stripe billing portal. The portal path skipped everything the reviewed flow was designed for: the period-end statement on every screen, the required acknowledgement checkbox, the reason capture, and the undo banner. A divergent second route is how an audited flow stops being the one users actually hit. THE DESIGN POINT: it is a CALLBACK (onRequestCancel), not a self-rendered dialog, because CancelSubscriptionDialog ALREADY opens this picker as its 'switch to a cheaper plan' off-ramp — rendering the cancel dialog inside the picker would have made the two mutually recursive. The parent owns the flow; the picker only reports intent. When the prop is omitted (i.e. the picker was opened FROM the cancel dialog) the Free tile simply closes the picker, returning the user to the cancel flow they are already in rather than stacking a second copy of it. AC2 AUDITED: after the fix, every remaining portal.mutate() call site is legitimate and NOT cancellation — the plan picker's own non-cancel branch (same-tier interval change) and past-due-banner's 'update payment method'. Using the portal is fine; routing a CANCELLATION through it is not, because cancellation is the flow carrying the review requirements. 4 guard tests pin that distinction explicitly, including one asserting past-due-banner may keep its portal call, so a future reader does not 'fix' it by mistake. The strongest assertion is ordering: the isCancelToFree branch must come BEFORE portal.mutate() AND must return — a guard that merely EXISTS while falling through would leave the bug intact while looking fixed. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED by deleting the guard: that test goes red. STILL OPEN: AC3 (have the review gate assess whether TWO deflection off-ramps before the confirm step is defensible under 'simple mechanism' expectations) is explicitly a US-2114 counsel-review item, not an engineering call — the story itself routes it there. AC4 (cancellation available in the same medium as signup) is stated in the story as already satisfied — web-purchased cancels on web, IAP correctly defers to the platform via .manageSubscriptionsSheet — and I did not re-derive it. Verified: tsc clean, lint 0 errors, web 2293 passed. | 2026-08-03 AC4 VERIFIED — and it was NOT satisfied. No migration. The note said AC4 was 'stated in the story as already satisfied', i.e. taken on the audit's word and never checked. Checking it found a real defect on the server. THE WEB AND iOS HALVES DID HOLD: src/pages/billing.tsx computes isAppstoreManaged and hides every Stripe subscription CTA behind it, showing 'Manage this plan in the GradeThread iOS app' instead; iOS presents .manageSubscriptionsSheet in PaywallView and PlanSection and never calls the web cancel endpoint. THE SERVER HALF DID NOT. appstoreSubscriptionBlocksStripe guarded the SUBSCRIBE and CHANGE-PLAN endpoints and not CANCEL. An App Store subscriber has no flipdesk_subscription_id, so POST /flipdesk/cancel fell straight through to 'No subscription to cancel' — a 400 telling a paying customer they have nothing while Apple carried on billing them monthly. Someone who believes that message reasonably concludes they are not subscribed, and the next thing they hear is a renewal receipt. That is worse than an error: it is a confident wrong answer on a billing question. HIDING A BUTTON IS NOT ENFORCEMENT, which is why the UI half passing did not make AC4 true. The endpoint is reachable from any client holding a token, and the iOS app talks to the same API. FIXED: cancel now returns the same 409 + `action` contract the purchase paths already use (manage_in_app / manage_in_play), which the clients already branch on. Apple and Google both REQUIRE cancellation on-platform, so the honest answer is not an error at all — it is where to go. ORDERING IS THE DEFECT, NOT PRESENCE, and the guard says so: both checks can exist and the wrong one still win, because an in-app subscriber has no Stripe subscription id. A case pins that the medium check runs BEFORE the no-subscription check. 6 new cases in cancel-medium-parity_test.ts: the precedence helpers still recognise active/trialing/past_due on both stores AND still return false for Stripe (or web cancellation breaks for the people it is for), the cancel route refuses and names where to go, the ordering, the purchase paths keep their own guards (cancel and purchase have to agree about who is in-app managed — this story is about them drifting apart once), the billing page still hides the CTAs, and iOS still defers to the platform sheet without calling the web endpoint. ⚠ MY OWN GUARD MATCHED ITS OWN COMMENT, fourth time this session: the ordering case searched for the string 'No subscription to cancel', which the comment above the fix QUOTES to explain the bug — and that comment sits before the guard, so the scan reported the ordering as still broken. Comments are stripped now. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED FIVE WAYS: the cancel guard removed, the guard moved after the no-subscription check, the refusal losing its action, a trialing in-app subscriber no longer recognised, and the billing page showing Stripe CTAs. Each reddened. (One mutation initially reported a false pass because .replace hit the SUBSCRIBE handler's occurrence first — re-run scoped to the cancel handler, where it reddens correctly.) REMAINING: AC3 only — whether TWO deflection off-ramps before the confirm step is defensible under 'simple mechanism' expectations. That is explicitly a US-2114 counsel item, not an engineering call. VERIFIED: full edge suite 5400 passed / 0 failed, deno check + lint clean across 1345 files. | 2026-08-10 AC2's AUDIT MISSED A ROUTE, and it is the one the buyer product exposes. The 2026-07-19 pass concluded 'every remaining portal.mutate() call site is legitimate and NOT cancellation - the plan picker's own non-cancel branch and past-due-banner's update payment method'. It did not include src/pages/buyer/billing.tsx, which renders a 'Manage in Stripe' button. That is a third call site and it was not examined. WHAT I FIXED, because it is unambiguous and in code: POST /portal hardcoded return_url to the SELLER billing page. So a buyer clicking Manage in Stripe was sent to Stripe and returned to /dashboard/billing - a page showing a FlipDesk plan they may not hold, with no way to manage the buyer subscription they just went to change, and no other route back. The eighth instance today of a control built for the seller product and reused for the buyer one without asking whether its destination still made sense. return_url now resolves through renewalNoticeCopy, so 'the page that manages this product' has ONE definition shared with all six billing emails. The route takes an optional product hint; ABSENT MEANS FLIPDESK, so every historical caller is byte-identical, and a body-less request still works rather than 400ing. Tests pin the default, the catch, and that the buyer page passes 'buyer'. ⚠ WHAT I DID NOT FIX, AND IT IS THE BIGGER HALF OF AC2: billingPortal.sessions.create is called with NO `configuration`, so Stripe applies the ACCOUNT DEFAULT portal configuration. Whether 'Cancel subscription' is enabled there is a Stripe Dashboard setting this checkout cannot observe. If it is on - and Stripe enables it by default in most setups - then the portal IS a second cancellation path, reachable from the seller billing page, the plan picker and the buyer page, bypassing the reviewed dialog entirely: no period-end statement on every screen, no acknowledgement checkbox, no reason capture, no undo banner. That is EXACTLY the defect AC1 fixed for the Free tile, still live through a different door, and AC2 asks for precisely this audit. AN OPERATOR CAN SETTLE IT IN A MINUTE: Stripe Dashboard -> Settings -> Billing -> Customer portal -> Cancellations. If cancellation is enabled there, either disable it (the portal stays useful for payment methods and invoices, which is what past-due-banner and the interval-switch branch actually need) or pass an explicit `configuration` id here that has it off. I did not guess: passing a configuration id that does not exist would 500 every portal open, and disabling a feature I cannot see the current state of is not a change to make blind. FIVE SABOTAGE MUTATIONS, each reddening its own case: the return URL re-hardcoded, the default flipped to buyer (which would strand every seller instead), the body-less catch removed, the hook accepting the product and not sending it, and the buyer page dropping its argument. STILL passes:false. AC2 is now HALF done - the return-path defect is fixed and the portal-cancellation question is stated precisely with the exact setting to check, but it needs a human with the Stripe Dashboard. AC3 (whether two deflection off-ramps before the confirm step is defensible) remains a US-2114 counsel item. AC1 and AC4 unchanged. VERIFIED: deno check clean on payments.ts; deno lint clean across 1491 files; billing-portal-return_test.ts 3 passed (new); full edge suite 6484 passed / 0 failed / 176 ignored; npx tsc -b clean; eslint 0 errors / 13 warnings; full web suite 3930 passed / 0 failed across 322 files. | 2026-08-17 AC1 FINISHED and AC2 AUDITED, with one finding AC2 was right to ask for. AC1's ROUTING was already correct - the Free tile called onRequestCancel - but the story asked to remove the stale portal path AND ITS COMMENT, and the comment was still there, two hundred lines from the fix, reading 'Cancelling to Free goes through the portal until US-216 cancel flow ships'. US-216 shipped long ago. Worse, the button that comment sits on was still wired to onOpenPortal, and the cancel behaviour lived in a branch INSIDE that handler - so the comment was not merely stale, it described the handler the button actually called. One handler meaning two things is how this survived a fix. The two paths are now separate props: onOpenPortal keeps the interval switch, onCancel hands the intent to the reviewed dialog, and they cannot be confused by a later edit. THE EXISTING GUARD CAUGHT THE REFACTOR, which is the good version of that outcome: src/test/cancellation-single-path.test.ts pinned the OLD shape (an isCancelToFree branch ordered before portal.mutate inside onOpenPortal), so it went red the moment the shared handler was split. Rewritten to pin the stronger property - onCancel exists, never calls portal.mutate, reaches onRequestCancel, and the button is wired to it rather than to onOpenPortal - plus a new case that fails if the stale comment ever returns. 5 cases, sabotage-verified twice (button rewired to the portal; comment restored), each reddening the intended case only, both reverted. AC2's AUDIT: every in-app cancellation now converges on CancelSubscriptionDialog - seller billing.tsx, buyer billing.tsx (US-2539 fixed that side), and the plan picker via onRequestCancel. ⚠ BUT THERE IS A SECOND ROUTE AND IT IS NOT IN THE CODEBASE. Both billing pages offer 'Open Stripe Portal' / 'Manage in Stripe', and payments.ts:2214 creates that session with NO configuration parameter, so it uses the Stripe account's DEFAULT portal configuration. Whether that configuration offers 'Cancel subscription' is a Stripe dashboard setting that nothing in this repository sets, records or can see. If it is enabled, a customer can cancel there and bypass the period-end statement, the acknowledgement checkbox, the reason capture and the undo banner - the exact divergence this story exists to close, reached by a different door. NOT CHANGED BLIND: passing a configuration id that does not exist would break the portal for payment-method management, which is a live payments path, so this is a decision plus a dashboard artifact rather than a guess. TWO REMEDIES, either acceptable: turn off cancellation in the Stripe portal configuration, or create the session with an explicit configuration id from an env var so the setting is pinned in code and reviewable. Added to the operator queue. AC3 (does the retention interstitial's two off-ramps survive a review-gate read) and AC4 remain; AC4 looks satisfied - web-purchased cancels on web, IAP defers to .manageSubscriptionsSheet - but it is a compliance claim and should be confirmed by whoever owns that gate rather than by me.

userStories.title: Refund policy contradicts the vault: an undisclosed 14-day money-back guarantee
userStories.description: vault/50-business/pricing.md:204-205 states 'Subscriptions: 14-day money-back guarantee on the first subscription invoice only.' No such guarantee appears on either public legal page — src/pages/legal/terms.tsx:80-82 and src/pages/legal/refund.tsx:45-47 both state subscription fees are non-refundable once a billing period has begun. Either the vault is stale, or we are operating a guarantee we do not disclose (or declining one we promised internally). Support and billing decisions are presumably being made against one of these.
acceptanceCriteria: Determine which is authoritative and reconcile — update the vault note or the public policy, in the same commit per the vault same-commit rule.
If the guarantee is real, disclose it at the point of sale, where it is also a conversion asset.
Review the ToS/refund pages alongside the new disclosure copy so the point-of-sale statements and the legal pages agree.
Check the EU/UK right-of-withdrawal waiver (refund.tsx section 4) and chargeback clause (section 5) with counsel while the pages are open.

OPERATOR: AC4 is counsel review of refund.tsx sections 4 and 5 - the EU/UK right-of-withdrawal waiver and the chargeback clause - and it gates the rest. AC1's factual half is SETTLED from the schema and needs no lawyer: users.grade_credit_balance is a plain integer with a >= 0 CHECK and no expiry column exists across all 612 migrations, while the monthly allowance is a separate system (grades_used_this_month / grade_reset_at / included_grades_this_period) that does reset. So 'credits never expire' is true of PURCHASED packs and 'do not roll over' is true of MONTHLY INCLUDED grades, and the Terms sentence uses the word credits for the thing that resets. What remains is approving wording, not investigating. NOTE FOR WHOEVER PICKS THIS UP: terms.tsx was edited once and deliberately reverted, because rewriting it ahead of counsel swaps one unreviewed statement for another - the KNOWN_CONTRADICTIONS entry in src/test/credit-expiry-claims.test.ts says so and must be DELETED in the same commit as the fix, since the guard fails on a stale entry as loudly as on a new contradiction.
userStories.notes: [P2][Compliance/Legal-docs] Found 2026-07-18 by the subscription-compliance deep-dive audit. LEGAL CONTEXT (verified 2026-07-18, not legal advice): the FTC's 2024 'Click-to-Cancel' Negative Option Rule was VACATED by the Eighth Circuit on 2025-07-08 and is not in force. The FTC restarted rulemaking with an ANPRM on 2026-03-11 (comments closed 2026-04-13), so a successor rule is in flux. The binding obligations today are (a) ROSCA 15 U.S.C. 8403 and FTC Act Section 5, both actively enforced, and (b) STATE automatic-renewal laws — most importantly California's ARL as amended by AB 2863, effective 2025-07-01, which is stricter than what we do today and expressly covers free trials. Design to the California standard: it is the binding one, and it closely tracks the vacated federal rule, so building to it also front-runs the successor. Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). Cheap to resolve and it removes an internal/external inconsistency that would look bad in any enforcement or dispute context. | PARTIAL 2026-08-02 — AC1 RESOLVED by the owner; AC2 does not apply; AC3/AC4 still need counsel. AC1: the vault was wrong and the public pages are authoritative. I put the evidence to the owner rather than guessing, and they chose delete-the-claim. THE EVIDENCE, gathered before asking so the question was cheap: no 14-day money-back guarantee exists anywhere in the codebase — not in constants, not in the Stripe setup, not in the webhook handlers. Refunds are MANUAL admin actions through admin-billing.ts with an MFA step-up. Both public pages say the opposite of the vault (refund.tsx section 3 and terms.tsx: subscription fees non-refundable once a billing period has begun, except where required by law or expressly granted in writing). What DOES exist is a 14-day free TRIAL, which is real, advertised on the landing page and in the plan picker, and is a completely different thing. Two features sharing a number is the most likely origin of a policy nobody agreed to. WHY THIS MATTERED IN A DIRECTION, and it is the part worth keeping: an internal note promising a refund the public pages deny is a promise support might honour case by case. That produces an UNDISCLOSED policy applied inconsistently, which is worse than either answer on its own — worse than not offering it, and worse than offering it openly. AC2 does not apply: there is no guarantee to disclose at the point of sale. The vault section is rewritten to state the three real rules (subscriptions non-refundable, credit packs non-refundable once a grade is generated but credits never expire, billing errors refunded within 60 days), each pointing at the page or constant that owns it, with a callout recording what the claim was and why it was wrong. refund.tsx and terms.tsx are added to the note's code_refs so a change to either now drifts the note. A SECOND CONTRADICTION FOUND AND DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED: terms.tsx says "Unused grading credits DO NOT ROLL OVER and are not refundable". That conflates two different things. Purchased credit packs never expire — constants.ts:384, migration 00037 and 00415 all say so explicitly. The MONTHLY PLAN ALLOWANCE (users.grades_used_this_month) does reset each cycle and genuinely does not roll over. The word "credits" is used for both, so the sentence is true of one and false of the other. It UNDERSTATES what a paying customer gets, so it costs conversion rather than creating legal exposure — but it is still a false statement in the Terms. I did not edit it: AC4 puts these pages under counsel review, and rewriting Terms copy ahead of that trades one unreviewed statement for another. Recorded in the vault note under its own heading so it is not lost, and carried on this story. NOTE ON MY OWN FIRST READING: I initially thought refund.tsx contradicted the vault on credit expiry too. It does not — "credits do not expire INTO A CASH BALANCE" is about cash redemption, and I had read a truncated line. Checked the full sentence before acting. STILL OPEN: AC3 (reconcile the point-of-sale copy with the legal pages — nothing to reconcile now that there is no guarantee, but the credits sentence above is in scope) and AC4 (the EU/UK right-of-withdrawal waiver in refund.tsx section 4 and the chargeback clause in section 5, both needing counsel). | 2026-08-10 AC3's remaining item is now TRACKED rather than described, and the copy is still untouched. THE CONTRADICTION, measured on both sides this time. FIVE product surfaces tell a customer 'credits never expire' - credit-pack-dialog (twice), upgrade-required-dialog, api-overage-card and cancel-subscription-dialog's keep-list. The Terms say 'Unused grading credits do not roll over and are not refundable'. Both use the word 'credits' for two different things: PURCHASED PACKS never expire (constants.ts CREDIT_PACKS, migrations 00037 and 00415 all say so) while the MONTHLY PLAN ALLOWANCE genuinely does reset. So the sentence is true of one and false of the other, and the one it is false about is the one the customer PAID for. It is the point-of-sale-versus-legal-page disagreement AC3 names, with the point of sale outnumbering the Terms five to one. COPY STILL NOT EDITED, and the previous pass's reasoning is why: AC4 has terms.tsx and refund.tsx under counsel review, and rewriting Terms ahead of that trades one unreviewed statement for another. Agreed then and agreed now. WHAT CHANGED IS THAT IT IS NO LONGER A SENTENCE IN A BACKLOG NOTE. NEW src/test/credit-expiry-claims.test.ts makes it a tracked, annotated exception in the KNOWN_GAPS shape the migrations lint already uses - and the shape is the point, because a plain allowlist rots. FOUR PROPERTIES: (1) the FACT is anchored, so the test fails if 'Credits never expire' quietly leaves constants.ts and the whole thing stops meaning anything; (2) the surfaces that say it are DERIVED, not listed; (3) any NEW contradicting statement fails unless someone adds an entry with a reason and an owning story; (4) THE LIST CAN ONLY SHRINK - an entry whose text no longer matches its file FAILS, so when counsel rewrites the sentence the entry must be deleted rather than left describing a problem that no longer exists. That fourth property is the one worth having. An allowlist that outlives its entries stops being a record and becomes a lie about a lie, and it hides the next real regression behind an entry nobody re-reads. FOUR SABOTAGE MUTATIONS, each reddening its own case: counsel fixing the Terms while the exception is left behind, a NEW page starting to contradict it, the anchoring fact removed from constants.ts, and an exception added with a throwaway reason. STILL passes:false on the same two: AC3's actual reconciliation (the wording, which is counsel's) and AC4 (the EU/UK right-of-withdrawal waiver in refund.tsx section 4 and the chargeback clause in section 5). AC1 and AC2 remain done - the vault was the stale side, there is no guarantee to disclose. VERIFIED: credit-expiry-claims.test.ts 4 passed (new); npx tsc -b clean; eslint 0 errors / 13 warnings; the whole src/test guard suite 896 passed / 0 failed. | 2026-08-12 THE SAME CONTRADICTION IS NOW ON ANDROID, AND THE GUARD STRUCTURALLY CANNOT SEE IT. android/app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml:1306 (paywall_credits_body) reads "One-time packs. They never expire and stack on top of the grades your plan includes." - the never-expire claim this story exists to resolve, on a paywall that can take a real payment today (see US-2126). src/test/credit-expiry-claims.test.ts pins the web copy, but its FILES list is a hardcoded set of src/ paths, so it scans neither android/ nor ios/ and could never have flagged this. That is the same class of hole as US-1996: a guard that reads as coverage while never executing over the surface that drifted. So whichever way this story resolves - credits never expire, or credits do not roll over - the fix has to land on three clients and the guard has to widen to see all three, or the next client to ship copy repeats it. Recorded here rather than filed separately because it is the same sentence and the same decision, not a new one. | 2026-08-16 THE GUARD NOW SEES ALL THREE CLIENTS. The 2026-08-12 note said src/test/credit-expiry-claims.test.ts scans only src/ and could never have flagged the Android paywall copy - same class of hole as US-1996, a guard that reads as coverage while never executing over the surface that drifted. Fixed: CLIENT_ROOTS now walks src/ (tsx), android/app/src/main/res (xml) and ios/GradeThread (swift, xcstrings), and walk() takes the extension so each client is scanned for its own file types. NO NEW RED, checked before writing rather than discovered after: neither Android nor iOS carries the CONTRADICTING wording. Both carry the AFFIRMING claim - android strings.xml:1306 paywall_credits_body and ios Billing/IAPProduct.swift in five places - which matches the truth that purchased packs never expire. So the widening closes the hole without a day-one failure, which matters because a guard that ships red gets switched off (US-1927). TWO NEW CASES, and the first is the one that keeps this honest. (1) The scan REACHES all three: each client must contribute at least one file, so a future refactor cannot quietly narrow it back to src/ - which is exactly how this hole existed. A scan that silently narrows is indistinguishable from one that finds nothing. (2) Every client that sells credits MAKES the claim: a client shipping a credit paywall without it is telling a customer less than they get, and if this story resolves the other way it is a client left saying something false. A missing client directory THROWS rather than skipping, for the same reason. WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO: resolve the story. AC1 is still the decision - the Terms say credits do not roll over, every sales surface says they never expire, and both are true of different things. The widening only means whichever way it resolves, the copy fix has to land on three clients and the guard will say so. VERIFIED: 6 cases pass, tsc -b clean, eslint clean. Sabotage-verified by removing the android root, which reddened BOTH new cases naming android specifically. | 2026-08-17 AC1's FACTUAL HALF IS NOW SETTLED FROM THE SCHEMA, so what remains is a wording approval rather than an investigation. The two statements are true of different things and the code says which is which: users.grade_credit_balance is a plain integer with a >= 0 CHECK (00037_pricing_split.sql:42) and there is NO expiry column on it anywhere across all 612 migrations - grepped, not assumed. The monthly allowance is a separate system, grades_used_this_month / grade_reset_at / included_grades_this_period (grade-billing.ts:147), and that one resets. So 'credits never expire' is true of PURCHASED packs, 'do not roll over' is true of the MONTHLY INCLUDED grades, and the Terms sentence uses the word credits for the thing that resets. ⚠ I EDITED terms.tsx AND BACKED IT OUT, which is worth recording rather than hiding. The KNOWN_CONTRADICTIONS entry in src/test/credit-expiry-claims.test.ts says in as many words: 'NOT edited here: US-2127 AC4 has this page under counsel review, and rewriting Terms ahead of that swaps one unreviewed statement for another.' That is a reasoned prior decision with a named criterion, and I should not reverse it quietly because I happen to disagree about the risk direction. Reverted; the guard is green at 6/6 and the register entry still matches. THE ARGUMENT FOR MOVING SOONER, for whoever holds the gate: the error runs in the direction that hurts. The Terms tell a customer they get LESS than they do, while five sales surfaces - including the cancellation dialog, which offers 'Your grade credits (never expire)' as a reason to stay - promise more at the point of sale. A customer who relied on the purchase-time promise and was later shown the Terms is the bad version of this. PROPOSED REPLACEMENT, drafted and ready so the review is an approval rather than a writing task: 'Subscription fees are non-refundable except where required by law or expressly stated by us. Grading credits you purchase do not expire, and are non-refundable once a grade has been generated. The grades included with your plan each month are an allowance rather than credits: unused included grades do not roll over into the next period.' The second sentence matches refund.tsx section 3 verbatim in substance, so the two pages would agree, which is AC3. When it lands, the KNOWN_CONTRADICTIONS entry must be DELETED in the same commit - the guard fails on a stale entry as loudly as on a new contradiction, which is how that list stays a ratchet.

userStories.title: Guided macro capture — framing, distance and lighting for authenticity shots
userStories.description: There is no guided capture for authenticity evidence: no framing overlay, no distance guide, no lighting instruction. iOS uses .builtInWideAngleCamera with no zoom or focus tuning (CameraSession.swift:238), so macro shots depend entirely on the seller's instinct. Authentication tells are only legible at consistent framing and lighting, and inconsistent capture is itself a source of false positives.
acceptanceCriteria: Add per-slot capture guidance: what to photograph, how close, and how to light it, with a framing overlay.
Investigate closer-focus camera configuration on iOS for macro slots.
Provide worked examples of a good vs unusable macro shot for each slot type.
Measure whether guidance actually improves delivered pixel density and gate the rollout on that.

OPERATOR: everything that can be done from a Windows checkout is done, and all three remaining pieces need a person. AC1's framing OVERLAY is visual work that needs a Mac to see and run — the copy half now ships to every client through GET /api/flipdesk/photo-profiles as `macroGuidance`, so only the overlay is left. AC2's camera selection is built (commit cc339f649) but has never been COMPILED; iOS CI is the gate. AC3 is design work: worked good-versus-unusable example shots for each slot type, which someone has to photograph. AC4 measures a rollout, so it needs the rollout first.
userStories.notes:
[P2][Authenticity/Capture][EPIC: Visual Authenticity] Found 2026-07-19 by the authenticity deep-dive audit. STRATEGY CONTEXT: Certilogo was the starting reference, but its model does not transfer — it verifies a brand-issued CLG code / QR on a security label sewn in at manufacture (its AI image recognition authenticates the TAG and detects cloned codes, not the garment's construction). GradeThread inspects garments it never manufactured, with no token. The transferable play is visual authentication of the garment itself, anchored on evidence we can actually capture. Note the scaffolding is ~80% built (ai-authenticity.ts is live in production) while the evidence base is ~5% — this epic closes that gap in order: contain what is already live, then raise evidence quality, then productize the claim. Depends on the macro slots existing first. | 2026-07-31 AC1 DONE (web). New src/lib/macro-capture-guidance.ts: a distance line, a lighting line and a framing tightness per macro slot. The existing photo-profiles hints said WHAT to shoot and nothing about distance or light, which is where macro shots actually fail. LIGHTING ADVICE IS SLOT-SPECIFIC ON PURPOSE, and this is the substantive part: the failure modes are OPPOSITE. A struck serial is visible only by its shadow and needs single-side low-angle light; a glossy care label needs even indirect light or the print blows out. One reusable 'use good light' sentence would have been easier and would not have changed a single photo -- a test asserts the lighting lines are not all identical, because boilerplate would pass every other assertion in the file. Surfaced on BOTH web capture surfaces: the camera dialog gets a dashed framing box over the live preview plus the two lines beneath it (new optional photoType prop), and the FlipDesk uploader -- where the authenticity slots live and there is no camera dialog -- composes them into its per-slot tooltip rather than inventing a new affordance. THE OVERLAY IS SIZED TO BE SATISFIABLE, which is the reviewable judgement: a guide box you can fill and still be told 'move closer' is worse than no box, so the fill fractions are chosen against the US-2136 floors at the US-2135 caps, and a test walks every slot asserting that filling the box delivers more pixels than that slot's own floor -- so raising a floor without revisiting the overlay fails in CI rather than in a seller's hands. The box is decorative only; the capture is still the full frame, so it constrains composition and never the saved pixels. THE COVERAGE TEST IS WHY THIS PAIRS WITH US-2136: every slot the quality gate can reject now has guidance for getting it right, because a gate without guidance is just blame. STILL OPEN: AC2 (closer-focus camera configuration) is iOS and cannot be built in this environment; AC3 (worked good-vs-unusable examples per slot) needs real example imagery, which is design work rather than code; AC4 (gate the rollout on measured pixel-density improvement) needs the per-photo measurement persisted first, which is US-2135 AC3 and blocked on a migration. Verified: tsc -b clean, lint 0 errors, 2912 tests pass, build green. | 2026-08-12 AC2 INVESTIGATED, and the finding is that the obvious fix is the wrong one - so this records the answer rather than shipping blind camera config. WHAT IS THERE NOW: CameraSession.swift:241-244 asks for AVCaptureDevice.default(.builtInWideAngleCamera, for: .video, position: .back), and BarcodeScanner.swift:194 does the same. CameraSession takes NO slot context at all - PhotoIntakeView.swift:27 constructs it as a bare `@State private var camera = CameraSession()` - so there is currently no way for it to know a macro slot is active. THE OBVIOUS CHANGE IS autoFocusRangeRestriction = .near, AND IT IS NOT THE ONE THAT MATTERS. That property is a HINT that narrows the autofocus SWEEP; it does not change the lens minimum focus distance. On a wide-angle iPhone lens that distance is roughly 10-12cm, which is the actual limit a seller hits when they push in on a care label - so restricting the sweep makes AF settle faster and does not let them get closer.
