So selectAuthenticityImages now ranks detail:hardware / hem / collar / print / fabric above a bare detail, using fractional ranks so a role can never displace serial or marking (US-2134 ordering stands). MACRO_EVIDENCE_TYPES was left alone on purpose: it gates a confidence cap, and widening it would RAISE authenticity confidence on existing submissions. WHAT IS LEFT is an operator action: apply 00589 to prod, then run the golden-set eval with GRADING_PHOTO_ROLES on and take it through a canary slice before flipping it in prod. Both need real vision calls, so neither CI nor an agent can do them. | 2026-08-12 STALE HELD-MIGRATION CLAIM IN THIS STORY, CORRECTED BY MEASUREMENT. Every migration named above is on origin/main AND applied to prod. Evidence, not inference: GET https://functions.gradethread.com/health/ready returns {"schema":{"expected":"00589","applied":"00589","status":"match"}} - that is the running edge reading applied_migrations through the service-role client, i.e. the database own answer, and 00589 is the highest migration on origin/main. So nothing here is blocked on a frozen branch and nobody should hold a push on this story account. The ONLY genuinely held migration today is 00590 (US-2497), which is committed locally and unpushed. THE DISTINCTION THAT KEEPS GETTING BLURRED, and it is why this warning recurs: PUSHED is not APPLIED, and a note written while a migration was held stays true-sounding forever after it lands. Check the endpoint before writing HELD or APPLIED anywhere - the answer is one unauthenticated GET and several passes have reasoned from commit history instead.

userStories.title: EPIC: marketplace coverage + honest automation — close the gap on Crosslist/Vendoo without copying Nifty
userStories.description: As the GradeThread team, we want every marketplace we advertise to actually publish, delist and sync, and we want any engagement automation to run only in the seller's own browser with the terms-of-service risk stated on screen, so that we close the coverage gap on Crosslist and Vendoo while keeping the trust position that Nifty's server-side credential model gives up.
acceptanceCriteria: Umbrella only: children are US-2473..US-2482; this story closes when every child passes

Standing constraint recorded in the ADR (US-2474) and enforced by review: GradeThread servers never hold a marketplace session cookie or password for Poshmark/Mercari/Grailed/Vinted/Facebook, and no GradeThread code solves CAPTCHAs
At close, MARKETPLACE_TIER in src/lib/constants.ts has zero api_pending entries and at least Poshmark+Mercari+Grailed on tier 'extension' with a working publish flow

src/lib/__tests__/marketplace-mechanism.test.ts still passes: every LIVE_CROSS_LISTING_PLATFORMS member is MARKETPLACE_TIER==='api', and every advertised channel has a delist path in cross-listing-sale.ts API_DELIST or DelistMethod 'extension'
No story in this epic ships a feature whose only disclosure is in a README — each seller-visible automation has an on-screen risk statement

OPERATOR: nothing in this epic needs code, and the remaining work is carried by its children rather than here. Four are open and all four already declare their own operator step: US-2473 (Depop partner approval), US-2474 (Etsy app keystring), US-2479 (one live Vinted listing re-run through the popup selector check), US-2480 (Facebook Marketplace enable). Two partner approvals and two sessions with a browser open. This criterion exists so the epic appears in `npm run prd:operator` instead of reading as buildable and costing another session the four reads it takes to discover otherwise.
userStories.notes: 2026-08-22 STATUS, measured rather than read: THE CODE FOR THIS EPIC IS DONE. Six of ten children are closed, and all four still open are waiting on a person, not on a keyboard. Nothing here will advance without the owner.  US-2475 (risk disclosure), US-2476 (ADR + vault note), US-2477 (Mercari), US-2478 (Grailed), US-2481 (queue from mobile, drain on desktop) and US-2482 (Poshmark engagement) are all closed and archived.  THE FOUR OPEN ONES AND WHAT EACH ACTUALLY NEEDS. US-2473: Depop partner approval, then set DEPOP env. US-2474: the Etsy app keystring, then set ETSY env. US-2479: the Vinted DELIST probe - the LIST flow went live 2026-08-11 against www.vinted.com/items/new, so what is left is opening one of your own live Vinted listings and running the popup selector check on the delete path. US-2480: the Facebook Marketplace enable - the content script, ARIA-anchored selectors, manifest hosts, disclosure copy and the tier/mechanism move all shipped, and it deliberately stops at Next rather than publishing, because auto-publishing with a guessed category gets a listing pulled and an account flagged. Each of these is declared as an OPERATOR criterion, so prd-operator.mjs lists all four.  AC3 IS HALF MET AND THE MISSING HALF IS EXACTLY THOSE TWO APPROVALS. MARKETPLACE_TIER has poshmark, mercari, grailed, vinted and facebook on 'extension' - the criterion asked for Poshmark+Mercari+Grailed and got five. It still carries TWO api_pending entries, depop and etsy, which are US-2473 and US-2474 by another name. So AC3 closes the moment those two approvals land, with no code change.  AC4 CONFIRMED GREEN: src/lib/__tests__/marketplace-mechanism.test.ts, 31 passed / 0 failed. That is the test holding LIVE_CROSS_LISTING_PLATFORMS to MARKETPLACE_TIER === 'api' and every advertised channel to a real delist path, and it also parses extension-unified/lister/selectors.js so MARKETPLACE_EXTENSION_FLOW cannot claim a channel is live while its selectors sit at enabled:false. Facebook is 'verifying' there, which matches its disabled selectors - the badge and the code agree.  WHAT I WOULD TELL THE NEXT READER: do not open this epic looking for something to build. The remaining distance is two partner approvals and two sessions with a browser open, and reading the four children to discover that costs more than this note does.

userStories.title: iOS ships English-only while Android ships Spanish, and the localization guard reads as though a migration is under way
userStories.description: As a Spanish-speaking seller, I want the iOS app in my language, or I want the team to have decided on purpose that it will not be - because today Android speaks Spanish, iOS does not, and no one chose that.
acceptanceCriteria: DECIDE FIRST whether iOS is meant to be localized at all. Android has values-es/ and its CI fails on MissingTranslation, so the two clients already disagree about whether a non-English seller is a customer. That is a product call, not a cleanup

If iOS IS meant to be localized: Localizable.xcstrings currently has ZERO entries, so decide whether the catalog is committed (translations live in git and can be reviewed) or generated at build time (translations live nowhere). Today it is the second, which is why nothing is translated

If iOS is NOT meant to be localized: say so in ios/Scripts/no-bare-strings.py, because its docstring describes a migration that is widening and that sentence is what makes the BASELINE read as temporary
Either way the guard must stop being a step that only fails AFTER the simulator build. It caught US-1866 five days late because it runs at ios-ci.yml:128, behind the slowest job in the lane
Reconcile the scope: SCOPE_DIRS covers Prospect/Vision/Speech/Settings and the docstring says the other ~670 app-wide strings are deliberately unscoped. Confirm that is still the intent

OPERATOR: answer one product question - is a non-English-speaking seller a customer on iOS? Android already answers yes: it ships values-es plus a CI lane that fails the build on MissingTranslation, so a new English string cannot land without its Spanish counterpart. iOS answers no by omission, which is what makes this a DECISION rather than a cleanup - nobody chose English-only, it is just what happened. The cost of each answer differs sharply and is worth knowing before choosing: yes means localising the whole iOS string catalogue and adding the same CI gate, which is real ongoing work on every string thereafter; no means saying so on purpose, and it is a defensible answer for a US-first product. What is not defensible is the current state, where the two clients disagree and neither says why. AC4 was always independent of this and is unaffected.
userStories.notes: [P3][iOS/Localization] Filed 2026-08-12 while fixing a red iOS CI lane. THE MEASUREMENT THAT PROMPTED IT: ios/GradeThread/Localizable.xcstrings parses as valid JSON with sourceLanguage en and strings: {} - zero entries. So not one iOS string has ever been translated, including every string in the US-1224 and US-1155 BASELINE sets that the guard describes as migrated. SWIFT_EMIT_LOC_STRINGS=YES populates the catalog at build time on the Mac and the result is not committed, so the artifact the guard validates is permanently empty by construction. THE CONSEQUENCE FOR THE GUARD, which is why this is worth a story rather than a shrug: no-bare-strings.py tells you to localize via a string key OR update BASELINE, and in this repo those are the same action - a SwiftUI Text("...") IS a LocalizedStringKey, so a bare literal is already as localized as anything gets here. What the guard actually buys is a human acknowledging new UI copy, which is worth having, but the docstring sells it as a migration checkpoint and that framing is what makes each BASELINE addition feel like debt rather than a decision. THE CROSS-PLATFORM HALF: Android does the opposite. values-es/strings.xml is real, lintDebug treats MissingTranslation as an ERROR, and US-2492 (Sourcing Radar on Android, in flight as this was filed) is required to ship Spanish for the SAME feature whose iOS strings are English-only. Two clients, one product, opposite answers about whether a Spanish-speaking seller is a customer - and nobody chose that. | 2026-08-12 AC4 DONE. The localization guard now runs as the fourth of four Python lints, ahead of brew, xcodegen and the simulator build. It needed no toolchain and no generated project, so there was never a reason for it to wait behind them - and waiting is why US-1866 failure surfaced at the slowest point in the lane and sat red on main for five days. Verified by parsing the YAML and asserting the step index is before both xcodegen and the build, plus exactly one run line so the step MOVED rather than duplicated. REMAINING: AC1 is the product call (is iOS meant to be localized at all), AC2 follows from it (commit the catalog or accept that it is generated and empty), AC3 is the docstring rewrite that depends on AC1, and AC5 is the SCOPE_DIRS confirmation. | 2026-08-17 AC4 IS NOW FULLY DONE, and the half that was left was not the half the AC names.  THE AC SAID: the guard "must stop being a step that only fails AFTER the simulator build". That part was already fixed - ios-ci.yml carries a comment saying so, and no-bare-strings.py now runs ahead of xcodegen and the build, with the US-1866 five-days-red story recorded beside it.  WHAT WAS STILL TRUE: the whole workflow it moved within is macOS-only. All six iOS guards are pure Python TEXT SCANS - no Xcode, no simulator, no generated project - and they were waiting on a macOS runner, the slowest to schedule and the most expensive minute in the fleet. Being first inside the slow job is better than being last, and it is not the same as being fast.  THE CHANGE: ci.yml (ubuntu, the job that was starting anyway) now runs `node scripts/verify.mjs --ios` right after npm ci, before the vault lint and the long lanes. The macOS copy STAYS - this is a second, earlier reader, not a replacement - and src/test/ios-guard-lane.test.ts already fails if the two lists ever diverge, so there is no new drift surface.  ONE THING THAT WOULD HAVE MADE IT A GUARD THAT DOES NOT GUARD, caught before committing rather than after: the ios lane SKIPS instead of failing when no Python is on PATH. That is right for a dev box (verify.mjs is used on machines without one) and wrong for CI, where a skip is a green tick for a check that never executed. The step runs `python3 --version` first, so if the runner image ever drops it the step goes red instead of quietly passing.  VERIFIED: the YAML parses (23 steps in the build job, the new one registered), the step sits after npm ci and before the vault lint, `node scripts/verify.mjs --ios` is 6/6 green locally, and ios-guard-lane parity is green.  STILL OPEN: AC1, AC2, AC3 and AC5 - every one of them the same product decision. Is a non-English seller a customer on iOS? Android already answers yes (values-es plus a CI lane that fails on MissingTranslation) and iOS answers no by omission, which is what makes this a decision rather than a cleanup. Nothing in this pass touched that, and AC4 was always independent of it.

userStories.title: Walk-around video grading is web-only, on the platform without the camera
userStories.description: As a seller grading on my phone, I want to record one walk-around clip instead of staging four photos, so that I can grade an item in one pass.
acceptanceCriteria: src/pages/new-submission.tsx:217 offers captureMode 'photos' | 'video' and POSTs video plus video_grading=true to /api/grade/submit. A grep of ios/**/*.swift for AVCaptureMovie, videoURL, walkaround or video_grading returns zero matches.
iOS capture offers a walk-around video mode that posts the same multipart fields the web path sends (video, video_grading, video_slot_marks, video_capture_source).
A clip that yields no usable required view lands the submission in needs_photos and is not charged, matching the web behaviour at new-submission.tsx:877-892.
Upload progress is shown for the clip; a 60 MB upload with no feedback is indistinguishable from a hang.

OPERATOR: needs a macOS toolchain. AC2's actual recorder (the AVCapture walk-around mode) and AC4's upload progress are both Swift, and neither can be built or verified from the Windows checkout - the iOS CI lane on macOS runners is the compile gate. AC4 is worth doing rather than deferring: a 60MB upload with no feedback is indistinguishable from a hang, which is the failure a seller reports as 'the app froze'. The edge half is done and verified here (deno check on the route and the isolation suite, deno lint clean, 6 iOS source guards green, full web lane 14/14).
userStories.notes:
SLICE 1 of N SHIPPED - the story is NOT done and is deliberately left open.  AC3's PREMISE IS UNDERSOLD, and that is the most useful thing found here. It describes the no-charge behaviour as matching the web behaviour at new-submission.tsx:877-892, but the guarantee is the SERVER's, not the page's: failVideoGrading in routes/grade.ts returns BEFORE payment precedence runs, refunds a buyer meter debit taken at the gate, sets needs_photos with video_graded false, and answers payment paid:false charged:false. Any client posting the contract inherits that. So AC3 needs NO iOS work at all - and iOS must not implement a client-side do-not-charge, because that is not a guarantee.  SHIPPED: src/lib/video-grading-contract.ts pins the multipart field names (video, video_grading, video_slot_marks, video_capture_source), the exact opt-in string, the two capture sources, and the abstain response shape with an isVideoAbstain helper. new-submission.tsx now APPENDS from those constants instead of spelling the strings inline.  WHY THIS IS THE RIGHT FIRST SLICE. AC2 asks iOS to post the same multipart fields the web path sends. Those names were a private handshake between two files - spelled in new-submission.tsx, read in routes/grade.ts - which is fine with one client and a trap with two: a native client would have to reverse-engineer them out of page code, and a rename on either side would silently break whichever client nobody was looking at. Now there is a spec to implement.  The opt-in is worth calling out: the server compares against the literal string true, so a native client sending 1, TRUE or a JSON boolean would ATTACH a clip and then be graded from photos it never sent. The contract records that and the guard asserts the server still compares exactly.  STILL OPEN, blocked on a macOS toolchain: AC2's actual recorder (AVCapture walk-around mode) and AC4's upload progress - a 60MB upload with no feedback is indistinguishable from a hang. Both are Swift that cannot be compiled or run from this Windows checkout.  AC1's premise re-verified: a grep of ios for AVCaptureMovie, videoURL, walkaround and video_grading still returns zero matches.  Guard: src/test/video-grading-contract.test.ts, 11 cases, but only 1 proven red - and that is honest, not weak. Most of these assertions PIN behaviour that already existed (the edge field reads, the abstain path, the refund) so a second client can rely on it and a refactor cannot quietly move the charge earlier. Only the web-side wiring to the constants is new. The file asserts NOTHING about an iOS recorder existing. | SLICE 2 SHIPPED 2026-08-14, story STILL OPEN. AC2's recorder and AC4's progress UI are Swift and need macOS.  AC4's WEB half turns out to be already done and correct - new-submission.tsx routes the video POST through XMLHttpRequest precisely because fetch has no upload-progress event, with the 60 MB reads-as-a-hang reasoning already in the comment. So nothing to fix there. What slice 1 had NOT recorded is the set of rules a recorder has to be BUILT to, and getting those wrong produces clips the server refuses after the entire upload has gone up a phone connection.  THE SHARPEST FIND: THE LIMITS THAT APPLY ARE THE ROUTE'S, AND THEY ARE NOT THE VALIDATION LIBRARY'S. lib/video-validation.ts defaults to 100 MB and 60 seconds. routes/grade.ts passes its own MAX_VIDEO_BYTES of 60 MB and MAX_VIDEO_DURATION_SECONDS of 45. A Swift author reading the validator - the obvious place to look for what a video upload may be - would build a recorder producing 100 MB, 60-second clips that are rejected every time. Both numbers are now in the contract and the guard reads them back out of the ROUTE, and also asserts the library's really are looser, since that gap is the trap.  SECOND: PHOTOS AND A CLIP ARE MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE, and this is the rule a second client is most likely to break, because the natural iOS flow is additive - stage photos, then also record a walk-around, which feels like sending more evidence. videoPhotoConflict refuses it with a 400. Two reasons worth keeping: the pipeline makes one Vision call per image, so accepting both stacks the 14-slot photo cap on top of the frame cap for one grade's revenue with nothing bounding the request; and it voids the claim the feature is sold on, that every graded view came from one continuous take. So the client must make it a MODE, not an addition.  THIRD, for AC4 one step later: 100 percent uploaded is not 100 percent done. Frame extraction and grading run after the last byte and the server sends no progress for that phase. The web holds the bar at 100 and lets the copy carry the rest. A client that dismisses the sheet at 100 tells the seller their grade is ready while the server has not started.  Also added videoSubmitRejection so a client can refuse a clip BEFORE spending the upload, mirroring the server's order - the photo conflict is reported first, because it is the one thing the seller can fix without re-recording. An UNREADABLE duration deliberately passes through to the server rather than being guessed at locally: null means the client could not read it, which is not the same as knowing it is bad, and guessing would block clips the server would have taken.  A VERIFICATION FLAW FOUND AND FIXED, and it affected this whole loop. I had been running npx tsc -b piped to tail followed by echo TSC-OK. A shell pipeline reports the exit status of the LAST command, so that printed TSC-OK unconditionally - and this iteration it printed TSC-OK directly underneath a real TS2532. Earlier runs were genuinely clean (they printed no errors above the marker) but the check was unsound throughout. Now running the command bare and reading its exit code.  STILL OPEN, blocked on macOS: AC2's AVCapture walk-around recorder and AC4's iOS progress UI. Guard: src/test/video-grading-contract.test.ts, now 25 cases (14 new), verified to bite - drifted the caps to the library defaults and dropped the photo conflict, 3 cases went red naming each. Verified: tsc -b exit 0, lint exit 0, ui:check exit 0, 4109 web tests, deno check exit 0, vault:lint green. No migration. | 2026-08-18 THE BLOCKER IS GONE. The previous segment ends "STILL OPEN, blocked on macOS: AC2’s AVCapture walk-around recorder and AC4’s iOS progress UI." iOS CI answers in about seven minutes on a push and six Swift stories went through that loop yesterday. This slice takes AC2’s recorder; the submit path and AC4’s progress UI are next.  THE CONTRACT IS MIRRORED INTO SWIFT AND THE MIRROR IS TESTED. src/lib/video-grading-contract.ts was written so a native client would have a spec rather than a page to reverse-engineer - and a spec kept in step by hand is the same private handshake one level along. src/test/video-grading-ios-parity.test.ts imports the real TypeScript contract, parses VideoGradingContract.swift, and compares field names, both caps, the container list, the abstain status, the capture-source vocabulary and every rejection sentence. 7 cases, about a second, on this machine.  THE CAP TEST EVALUATES THE EXPRESSION rather than comparing text, because `60 * 1024 * 1024` compared as a string would also pass against `60 * 1024`. SABOTAGE-VERIFIED with the exact drift the guard exists for - a recorder built to the VALIDATOR’s 100 MB instead of the ROUTE’s 60 - which reddens naming both numbers.  THE RECORDER: AVCaptureSession + AVCaptureMovieFileOutput. Four decisions worth keeping.  (1) NO AUDIO INPUT. A walk-around needs none, the frame pipeline discards it, and adding one would mean requesting the microphone permission and shipping an NSMicrophoneUsageDescription for a feature that never listens. Recording a seller’s room because it was the default is the kind of thing only noticed from outside.  (2) 1080p, NOT the highest available preset. A 4K walk-around blows the 60 MB cap in well under the 45 seconds the SAME contract allows, so the two limits would contradict each other and the seller would meet the byte one with no warning.  (3) THE HARD STOP BELONGS TO THE OUTPUT, not to a timer. maxRecordedDuration and maxRecordedFileSize are both set. A timer that fires late produces a clip the server refuses after the whole upload; AVFoundation stops at the boundary itself. The consequence is the fourth decision.  (4) A CAP-REACHED STOP REPORTS AN ERROR AND STILL WRITES A USABLE FILE. AVError.maximumDurationReached and .maximumFileSizeReached arrive through the failure path of the delegate callback, so treating every error as a failure would throw away exactly the clip the caps were set to produce. Both are salvaged by code; everything else deletes the file and fails.  AND THE ONE THE PORT COULD EASILY GET WRONG: an unreadable duration is passed to the server as nil rather than resolved locally. nil means the CLIENT could not read it, which is not the same as knowing it is bad - guessing would block clips the server would have taken, or claim a length the frame planner cannot then find. A duration we DID read and that is zero is a different fact and is refused. Both directions are tested, including that a missing file reports nil rather than 0.  VERIFIED HERE: 6 iOS source guards 6/6, tsc -b exit 0 (read as an exit code, not a piped marker - the flaw the previous segment recorded), 32 web cases across both video suites, plus the sabotage run. 11 new XCTest cases. iOS CI is the compile gate.  STILL OPEN: the submit path (multipart POST to /api/grade/submit with the four fields, choosing video CLEARING staged photos rather than adding to them) and AC4’s progress UI, whose honest shape the contract already specifies - determinate to 100 on upload, then INDETERMINATE while the server extracts frames and grades, because 100 percent uploaded is not 100 percent done. | 2026-08-18 SLICE: the submit path and the progress model (AC3 client half, AC4). The recorder landed in the previous slice; what remains is the screen that puts the two together.  THE SESSION IS ITS OWN, AND THE REASON IS ALREADY WRITTEN IN EdgeNetwork ONE LEVEL UP. EdgeNetwork.shared caps a resource at 60 seconds, which a 60 MB clip on cellular can exceed on the upload alone. Worse, once the last byte lands the connection sits legitimately IDLE while the server extracts frames and grades - which is exactly the shape EdgeNetwork.aiSession exists for, after a 20-second idle timeout killed a 38-second AI extract that had already SUCCEEDED server-side and showed the seller a failure for a result that was on its way. A video grade is that trap with a large upload in front of it, so both ceilings are raised rather than one.  THE BODY IS WRITTEN TO A FILE, not held in Data, and streamed in 1 MB chunks. A 60 MB clip plus its multipart copy is 120 MB resident on a phone that is under memory pressure from the camera that just produced the clip.  AC4 IS A PHASE, NOT A NUMBER. .uploading(fraction) then .grading, and .grading deliberately carries NO number because there is none to carry - the server sends nothing during extraction and grading. A client that finished at 100 percent would tell the seller their grade is ready before the server had started. Tests observe this MID-FLIGHT through a box holding the uploader, because by the time submit returns the phase has moved on; asserting only the final phase would have passed against a client that never entered .grading at all. Progress is also clamped monotonic: a retried body segment can report a lower cumulative count, and a bar that jumps backwards reads as a failure.  AC3 IS RECOGNISED, NOT REIMPLEMENTED. The abstain case is read from the SERVER’S markers - status needs_photos AND payment.charged false, both required. A needs_photos that WAS charged is not the abstain guarantee and must not be reported as one, because that tells a seller they were not billed when they were. The refund itself is failVideoGrading’s, and a client-side "do not charge" would not be a guarantee at all.  A FABRICATED JUSTIFICATION I WROTE AND THEN CHECKED. A test comment said the route "has been seen to answer with either" submissionId or submission_id. It has not: grade.ts sends camelCase on every path - the abstain reply, both paid replies and the free-tier reply. The tolerance is fine and costs nothing; the REASON was invented. Corrected to say it is a defensive fallback rather than an observed variance, because a tolerance that reads like an observation makes the next person believe the route is inconsistent when it is not.  AND CHECKING IT FOUND A REAL WEAKNESS BEHIND IT: `id` defaulted to the empty string when neither key was present, so a malformed response produced a .graded outcome pointing at nothing - the seller told their grade worked with nothing to open. It is optional now and the decode fails loudly. Two cases pin it.  VERIFIED HERE: 6 iOS source guards 6/6. 14 new XCTest cases. iOS CI is the compile gate.  STILL OPEN: the screen. Recorder preview and shutter, then a review step, then the progress sheet - and the entry point has to make video a MODE that CLEARS staged photos, which is the rule the contract says a second client is most likely to break. | 2026-08-18 SLICE: the screen. Record, review, send, watch. AC2 and AC4 are now built end to end; what is left is the ENTRY POINT, which is the part with the rule attached to it.  THREE STEPS, AND THE MIDDLE ONE IS NOT DECORATION. A review step between recording and uploading exists because every refusal in this contract otherwise arrives AFTER a 40 MB upload. It shows length and size, and its footer NAMES the refusal when there is one - too large, unreadable length, photos staged - so the seller meets it before spending the upload rather than after. Four tests pin those four footers.  AND WHEN THE CLIP LOOKS FINE the footer promises the thing that makes trying it safe: "If the clip doesn’t show a required view, we’ll say so and you won’t be charged." That is the SERVER’S guarantee (failVideoGrading refunds before payment precedence runs), which is the only reason it can be promised at all.  THE ABSTAIN RESULT SAYS THE MONEY PART FIRST. "You weren’t charged for this" above the reason, because "we couldn’t grade that clip" reads like a wasted purchase until you know it was not one.  THE TIMER COUNTS DOWN. "18s left", not "27s elapsed". The number that changes what a seller does with their hands is the one that is running out; elapsed time is a fact about the past. The idle hint states the 45-second cap before they start, and the live hint tells them to turn the garment slowly - two different jobs, so two different sentences.  AN UNREADABLE DURATION STILL OFFERS THE UPLOAD, which is the subtle half of the review step. nil means the CLIENT could not read it, and the server has its own rule; refusing locally would block clips the server would have taken. A duration we DID read and that is zero is a different fact and is refused. Both are tested.  reset() REFUSES WHILE BYTES ARE IN FLIGHT. A "back" that abandoned a request mid-upload would leave the server holding a submission the client has forgotten about and the seller with no way to reach it. Tested mid-flight through the same observer box the phase tests use.  PRE-EMPTIVE ON THE ISOLATION TRAP THAT COST A ROUND TWO SLICES AGO: the view’s copy helpers are marked nonisolated. A View conformance can infer @MainActor onto the type, which is exactly what made the recorder’s "pure helpers, testable without a camera" uncallable from a test. One word, versus another seven-minute round trip to find out.  VERIFIED HERE: 6 iOS source guards 6/6. 8 new XCTest cases. iOS CI is the compile gate.  STILL OPEN, and it carries the rule the contract flags as most likely to be broken by a second client: the ENTRY POINT. Choosing video has to CLEAR staged photos rather than add to them - the screen already takes stagedPhotoCount and refuses when it is non-zero, but nothing routes to the screen yet, so nothing has had to make that choice. | 2026-08-18 WIRING THE ENTRY POINT TURNED UP A GAP THAT IS NOT MINE TO GUESS AT, and a misleading parameter I had already written. The parameter is fixed; the gap is a question for the owner and is recorded below.  FIRST, THE PARAMETER. I threaded `stagedPhotoCount` through the screen and the uploader, described as "how many photos are staged for this item". That is NOT what the server counts. grade.ts calls videoPhotoConflict(imageFiles.length) - the image parts IN THE SAME multipart request - and VideoGradeUploadService builds none, so the value is structurally 0 on this client. Passing an item’s photo count would have BLOCKED a submission the server would have accepted, on a screen whose whole point is refusing before the upload. Renamed to photoPartCount with the distinction written down, defaulted to 0, and kept as a parameter rather than hard-coded so a future flow that does attach photos inherits the refusal instead of rediscovering it after an upload.  NOW THE GAP. THE VIDEO ROUTE CANNOT ATTACH A GRADE TO AN INVENTORY ITEM. The story reads "as a seller grading on my phone... so that I can grade an item in one pass", but /api/grade/submit has NO inventory_item_id anywhere - the only linking field on the video path is closet_item_id, which is the BUYER’s portfolio. The FlipDesk path that does link (/api/flipdesk/grading/submit, inventory_item_id) grades from photos ALREADY ATTACHED to the item and takes no clip.  So a walk-around grade posted from iOS today produces a real grade and a real certificate that are NOT connected to the seller’s item. The screen works; where its result lands is the open question, and the two answers are materially different work: (a) STANDALONE - a "grade from a video" entry not tied to an item, matching the shape of the web page the story cites. Ships as built; the seller links the certificate to the listing themselves. (b) ITEM-LINKED - the video path learns an inventory_item_id, or FlipDesk grading learns to take a clip. That is an edge change plus the write-back, and it is the reading the story’s own sentence supports.  Not guessed at, because wiring it to the wrong one is wasted work in both directions: (a) built as (b) is a route change nobody asked for, and (b) shipped as (a) leaves sellers with orphan certificates.  VERIFIED HERE: 6 iOS source guards 6/6. No behaviour change beyond the rename. | 2026-08-18 OWNER CHOSE ITEM-LINKED, and it is built. The video path now accepts inventory_item_id, so a walk-around grade lands on the seller’s item the way a photo grade does.  THE FIELD IS THE CLOSET FIELD’S TWIN, deliberately. Read from the same form data, verified with the same .eq("id", body).eq("user_id", ownerId) lookup, and an UNOWNED id is IGNORED rather than refused - refusing would leak whether the id exists in another tenant, which is the choice closet_item_id and regrade_of already make. So the failure mode is an unlinked grade, never a lost one.  PLACEMENT IS THE PART WORTH READING. The link runs at ONE point: past every abstain and every frame-storage failure (which return earlier), and before payment. Linking sooner would leave an item marked "grading" against a submission that abstained, and a bridge row pointing at a submission the failure paths delete.  TWO WRITES, BOTH ALREADY READ BY THE PIPELINE, so no new mechanism was invented: flipdesk_grading_submissions is what the in-app status poll reads and what grading-pipeline.ts flips to completed / pending_review; inventory_items.submission_id is what the pipeline’s item sync keys on to write grade_value / grade_label / grade_report_id back. Mirrors steps 4 and 5 of the FlipDesk path exactly, so one grade cannot reach an item by two different routes.  THE LINK CANNOT FAIL THE GRADE. A failed bridge write is caught and logged, because throwing there would lose a grade the seller has already paid for - and an unlinked certificate is something they can still attach by hand.  TENANT ISOLATION: no new case, because there is no new vector - the id is owner-scoped at lookup and the inventory_items patch repeats .eq("user_id", ownerId), so a link that somehow survived would still update zero rows. The "buyer routes with NO cross-tenant id/path vector" accounting in tenant-isolation_test.ts was extended in the same commit to say so, alongside the closet_item_id entry it mirrors.  THE CONTRACT GAINED THE FIELD ON BOTH SIDES and the parity guard covers it, so the Swift and TypeScript spellings cannot drift.  VERIFIED HERE: deno check on the route and the isolation suite, deno lint clean, 6 iOS source guards 6/6, and the FULL web lane 14/14 (eslint, tsc -b, 4100+ vitest with coverage, production build with prerender, ui:check, bundle budget, npm audit). iOS CI is the compile gate for the Swift half. | 2026-08-22 AC1'S PREMISE IS DEAD AND THE STORY IS ONE STEP FROM DONE, NOT SIX. AC1 reads 'A grep of ios/**/*.swift for AVCaptureMovie, videoURL, walkaround or video_grading returns zero matches.' Run today it returns 46, across WalkAroundRecorder.swift, VideoGradeUploader.swift, VideoGradingContract.swift, WalkAroundGradeView.swift and three test files. The four slices below this note built every one of them. Anyone reading AC1 first, as the acceptance criteria invite, would start by rebuilding a recorder that has been here since 2026-08-18.  AND THE SCREEN IS UNREACHABLE, which is the part no slice claimed and no test catches. WalkAroundGradeView is mentioned in exactly two places in the repo: its own file and WalkAroundGradeViewTests.swift. Nothing constructs it - no view, no router, no sheet. The last slice ends 'STILL OPEN ... the ENTRY POINT', and that is exactly right; what is new here is that the gap is now MEASURED rather than remembered, and it is the whole of what remains on the iOS side.  THIS IS THE SECOND STORY IN THE SAME STATE AND THE SHAPE IS WORTH THE NAME. US-2016's consumer grade path is the other: ConsumerGradeFlow implements submit -> pay -> poll -> result, is unit-tested, and is constructed by nobody. Two revenue features, fully built, fully tested, zero entry points. Both stopped at the same step for the same honest reason - a screen written blind is where an agent ships something that compiles and looks wrong - so the work queued behind that decision is now two features deep.  A GUARD EXISTS FOR IT NOW: scripts/check-ios-orphans.mjs, in the ios verify lane. It flags a top-level type the app declares and never mentions again anywhere, which is the strictest rule that still finds these three and flags nothing else. Tests deliberately do not count as a caller - two of the three findings HAD unit tests, and counting them would have hidden precisely the cases worth finding. WalkAroundGradeView is allowlisted against this story, so closing it must delete that entry; a stale allowlist entry fails the check.  WHY THE EXISTING GUARDS ALL READ GREEN. video-grading-ios-parity.test.ts compares the Swift contract against the TypeScript one and passes, correctly - the contract IS mirrored. It asserts nothing about anyone opening the screen. Same flaw as grading-pipeline-parity.test.ts on US-2016: source-scanning answers 'does this client contain the call', never 'can a seller get to it'.  NOT BUILT HERE, unchanged: the entry point is a screen plus a decision about where it lives, and it carries the rule the contract flags as most likely to be broken - choosing video must CLEAR staged photos rather than add to them. WalkAroundGradeView already refuses a non-zero photoPartCount, so the refusal is built; nothing has yet had to make the choice. | 2026-08-22 THE GUARD I ADDED FOR THIS STORY PUT CI RED, and the cause is a trap CLAUDE.md already records. Fixed, plus the two real findings it had been hiding from this machine.  check-ios-orphans.mjs strips comments so a name in PROSE does not count as a reference. Its stripper split on \n and then ran //.*$ per line — and in JS a `.` never matches `\r`, so on a CRLF checkout the pattern cannot reach the end of the line and the replace is a NO-OP. The ios/ tree is CRLF. So on this machine the guard has been running with comment-awareness switched off since I wrote it, and every doc-comment mention counted as a real reference.  GREEN HERE, RED ON LINUX, which is the only reason it surfaced. CI checks out LF, the stripper worked there, and two types dropped to one mention:    GradeThreadApp — `@main struct GradeThreadApp: App`. SYSTEM-DISCOVERED: the   Swift runtime finds it through @main and no code can construct it.    SalesStore — SUPERSEDED, and SalesView says so in its own header: it reads   sales from SwiftData "instead of a separate RemoteSale fetch via SalesStore   that could drift from the numbers shown elsewhere". Its only reference   outside its own file is SalesTests calling the static decodeSalesResiliently,   and by this guard's own rule a test is not a caller. 59 lines, and deleting   them needs a machine that can run the iOS suite.  So the guard was right and my stripper was wrong. Both allowlisted with their verdicts; the iOS count goes 4 to 6.  THE SAME LINE WAS WRONG IN check-android-orphans.mjs and is fixed there too, before it hides anything. check-comment-path-refs.mjs uses indexOf rather than a `$`-anchored regex, so it was never affected.  WHAT THIS SAYS ABOUT THE GUARD'S OWN SABOTAGE RUN. Three sabotages passed when I added it, including one asserting that a name in a COMMENT is still reported an orphan. That case passed for the wrong reason — the comment was never stripped, so of course the name still counted. A sabotage can be satisfied by the bug it is meant to exclude. | COMPILATION SETTLED 2026-08-28. This note corrects one stale claim and changes nothing else about the story.

The notes above say some version of 'never been compiled' / 'iOS CI is the gate and it has not seen this' / 'cannot be verified from a Windows box'. That was true when written and is not true now. Every commit carrying this story's iOS code is an ancestor of iOS CI run 33139420556 on main (2026-08-28T03:37Z, head 1c6067106), conclusion SUCCESS - checked with git merge-base --is-ancestor, all commits in, none outside.

The run was checked for substance rather than for a green tick: both jobs succeeded, and the Build + test job's 'Generate Xcode project', 'Build + test' and 'Build app-extension targets' steps all executed. A green run whose build step never ran proves nothing.

ONE DISTINCTION MAKES THIS READABLE, and without it the evidence points the other way: many of these commits' OWN CI runs FAILED. 33 of the last 100 iOS CI runs on main were non-success, in one unbroken stretch from 2026-08-18 to 2026-08-27. iOS reports one error and stops, so a commit is not guilty of the failure it happens to sit on. 'Did its own run pass' has no useful answer; 'is it in a green build' does.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO: it does not close the story. Compilation was never the only thing outstanding here - what remains is whatever the notes above say it is, and it is now the ONLY thing outstanding, which is the point of writing this down. A story parked behind two blockers where one has quietly cleared reads as further away than it is.

THE CHECK IS TWO COMMANDS AND WORKS FROM WINDOWS: gh run list --workflow='iOS CI' --branch main to find the newest green run, then git merge-base --is-ancestor <commit> <that run's head>. Any story blocked on 'iOS CI has not seen this' can be settled the same way once its commits are on main. macOS-only COMPILATION is not macOS-only KNOWLEDGE.

userStories.title: The Terms of Service predate four shipped products
userStories.description: As the business, I want the Terms to cover what we actually sell, so that our terms match our product.
acceptanceCriteria: src/pages/legal/terms.tsx is effective April 1, 2026 and contains zero occurrences of 'buyer plan', 'in-app purchase', 'App Store', 'Google Play', 'extension' or 'consignment'.

Terms cover: buyer subscriptions as a second paid product with its own cancellation; store-billed subscriptions where Apple and Google own refunds and cancellation; the Lister browser extension automating the user's own logged-in marketplace sessions; and consignment, which involves holding third-party goods and paying consignors via Stripe Connect.
The extension section is consistent with the in-product risk disclosure already written at src/pages/flipdesk/marketplaces.tsx:1495-1532.
The AUP is reviewed in the same pass; it carries the same April 1, 2026 date.
This story is legal review, not engineering — it ships when counsel signs off on the copy.

OPERATOR: counsel has to write the extension disclosure section of the Terms (AC5). Nothing here writes legal copy, and terms.tsx and acceptable-use.tsx are deliberately untouched. The drift guard is already in place and is honest in both states - while the section is absent it asserts the absence is tracked as open work, and the moment a section lands it starts checking all four disclosed facts are present, matching on the CLAIM rather than the wording so counsel can rephrase freely.
userStories.notes: BLOCKED ON COUNSEL, not on engineering — AC5 says so explicitly ('it ships when counsel signs off on the copy'), so this stays OPEN. What I did do (2026-08-14, commit below): verified all four gaps against the CODE rather than assuming them, and wrote docs/legal/terms-update-brief-2026-08.md — a brief for counsel with, per gap, what shipped, what the current Terms say, why the two conflict, and DRAFT language marked as draft. Nothing is wired to the live page; terms.tsx is untouched and its April 1 date still stands. The four confirmed gaps: (1) the buyer subscription is a SECOND independent paid product while section 3 describes one subscription in the singular, so a buyer who cancels from the seller Billing page has not cancelled what they think they cancelled; (2) store-billed subscriptions — section 3 says billed through Stripe and cancel in-app, and for an IAP subscriber BOTH sentences are false, with refunds being Apple's or Google's decision rather than ours to grant or refuse; (3) the Lister extension automates the seller's OWN logged-in session on five platforms whose terms restrict automation, which section 8's generic third-party clause does not describe — the draft reuses the four facts the product ALREADY discloses in src/lib/marketplace-disclosure.ts, and I flagged that the AUP's blanket 'scraping' prohibition can be read against our own extension; (4) consignment now involves goods the customer does not own and payouts through Stripe Connect to someone who is not our customer, and the Terms say nothing at all — that clause is the one most in need of a lawyer, so the draft is deliberately narrow. The AUP carries the same April 1 date and is listed for the same pass. Noted for the follow-up commit: a guard test asserting the Terms' extension section carries the same four facts as the in-product disclosure, so the two cannot drift. | FOLLOW-UP SHIPPED, story still OPEN - AC5 blocks it on counsel and nothing here writes legal copy. terms.tsx and acceptable-use.tsx are untouched.  SHIPPED: src/test/legal-extension-disclosure-parity.test.ts, the drift guard the previous note promised. It is written to be honest in BOTH states. While the Terms carry no extension section it asserts that absence is still tracked as open work, so it cannot pass vacuously; the moment a section lands it starts checking that all four disclosed facts are present, matching on the CLAIM rather than the wording so counsel can rephrase freely. It also fails if the Terms and AUP effective dates diverge, which is AC4, and it pins that the four mechanism facts are single-sourced in marketplace-disclosure.ts and come FIRST - a per-platform note (Poshmark's share caps, Grailed's manual delist) is appended and can never displace one of the four.  CORRECTED A FLAG I RAISED IN THE PREVIOUS NOTE. I had written that the AUP's blanket scraping prohibition could be read against our own Lister extension and was worth a carve-out. Re-reading the clause, that is wrong: BOTH the automated-access and the scraping clauses are scoped to the Service - GradeThread - while the extension automates the seller's own signed-in eBay/Poshmark/Mercari session and reads MARKETPLACE pages, and where it does talk to GradeThread it uses our documented API. So there is no self-contradiction and no carve-out is needed. The brief now carries the correction with the reasoning visible rather than the flag deleted, so counsel is not billed for resolving a conflict that does not exist. The guard asserts the scoping, so if either clause is ever broadened past the Service the question comes back on its own.  STILL OPEN and genuinely blocked: the four Terms sections themselves (buyer subscriptions as a second paid product with its own cancellation; store-billed subscriptions where Apple and Google own refunds; the Lister extension; consignment goods and Stripe Connect payouts) plus the AUP pass. Draft language for each is in docs/legal/terms-update-brief-2026-08.md, marked as draft and deliberately not wired to the live page - the guard fails if any of it reaches terms.tsx without sign-off.  Guard: 10 cases, all green on the current tree BY DESIGN. This one pins existing behaviour and arms a future check rather than fixing a defect; the red-before-green shape does not apply and claiming otherwise would be a false report.

userStories.title: iOS shows no unread notification count on the tab bar
userStories.description: As a seller or buyer using the iPhone app, I want an unread count on the tab bar, so that I learn about a new offer or return without opening the app and hunting.
acceptanceCriteria: No badge API is used anywhere in ios/GradeThread — a grep for applicationIconBadge, badgeCount and .badge( over the Swift tree finds only unrelated matches in InventoryFilterSheet and ToolsHubView.

The unread source already exists and needs no new backend: public.notifications (migration 00007) with is_read, RLS-scoped to auth.uid(). Web reads it directly through the authenticated Supabase client in src/components/dashboard/notification-center.tsx; iOS can do the same.
The count badges the relevant tab in ContentView.swift's TabView and clears as rows are marked read, matching the web centre's behaviour.
Set the app icon badge from the same count so it is visible with the app closed, since the transactional-push path (lib/transactional-push.ts) already delivers these events to APNs.
iOS cannot be built or tested from the Windows checkout; the iOS CI lane on macOS runners is the gate. State that in the PR rather than claiming local verification.

OPERATOR: decide where a seller marks a notification read on iOS. AC3 says the badge 'clears as rows are marked read' and nothing on iOS ever marks one - measured 2026-08-22: unreadBadge.reset() has no caller, nothing writes notifications.is_read, and BuyerAlertsView reads the flag without ever setting it. So the badge rises on a push and cannot be dismissed from the phone; it falls only if the same notifications are read on web. A badge that cannot be cleared trains the user to ignore it, and AC4 puts that same number on the app icon. The three candidates behave differently and none is obviously right: clear on opening the alerts view (dismisses things they meant to return to), per row on tap (the count falls one at a time), or an explicit mark-all-read control (matches web, but is a new affordance). Web has a real notification centre to hang this on; iOS has a filtered alerts view and no centre, which is why there is nothing to copy. Everything else in this story is built: the tab badge, the app-icon badge, the shared count, and now UnreadBadgeStoreTests.
userStories.notes:
SLICE SHIPPED 2026-08-14, story STILL OPEN. AC3 and AC4's Swift halves need macOS; the iOS CI lane on macOS runners is the gate and nothing here was built or run against a simulator.  AC1 premise VERIFIED exactly as filed: grepping the Swift tree for applicationIconBadge, badgeCount and .badge( finds only InventoryFilterSheet and ToolsHubView, both unrelated. AC2 verified too - notification-center.tsx reads public.notifications through the authenticated client, so iOS needs no new backend.  But two things the Swift half READS FROM were wrong, and both would have made the iOS work look broken while being correct.  1. NO PUSH HAS EVER CARRIED A BADGE. PushPayload.badge has existed in apns.ts since pushes shipped and buildBody copies it into the aps dictionary - and no caller anywhere has ever set it. So the app-icon number AC4 asks for could not appear no matter what Swift did, because the only thing that can badge a CLOSED app is the payload. New lib/notification-badge.ts counts unread rows and safePush attaches it.  The seam is deliberate in both directions. Not per-helper, because there are a dozen and the next one forgets. Not in sendPushToUser, because that is the transport and it also serves pushes with no notification behind them (cross-listing progress), which would get a number about something else. safePush is the one place every transactional push passes and nothing else does.  THE SHARP EDGE, and the reason this is a named helper rather than one line: in APNs an ABSENT badge key means leave the icon alone and a badge of 0 means CLEAR it. Opposite behaviours, one missing key. So no badge is attached when the count cannot be read (a database hiccup must not wipe a badge showing five unread) or when it is genuinely 0 (pushTokenExpiring and pushSaleCreated have no notification row, and must not clear a badge they know nothing about). The consequence, stated rather than discovered later: the server only ever RAISES the badge. Clearing it is the app's job on the same signal that marks rows read.  2. THE WEB BELL COUNTED A PAGE, NOT THE ROWS. unreadCount was notifications.filter(not is_read).length over a limit-20 fetch, so it stopped counting at 20 - and its own 99+ render branch was unreachable. AC3 says the iOS badge should match the web centre, so matching it would have shipped the cap to the phone, and AC4's server count would have disagreed with the bell on the same account with neither number obviously wrong. Now a head+exact count query, paired with the list on every refresh path.  That fix exposed a THIRD bug underneath it. Mark all read collected ids from the same 20-row page and marked those, so on an account with more unread than that it left the rest unread - invisible while the badge came from the same page (it read 20, you clicked, it read 0) and glaring once the count is real. Now an update by predicate. Chained .eq, never .or: US-1552, prod PostgREST rejects logical operators on a mutation and the local stack accepts them, so CI cannot catch it.  Guards: 8 edge cases in notification-badge_test.ts (every way a 0 reaches a payload) and 7 web cases in src/test/notification-unread-count.test.ts. Verified to BITE, and the first attempt did NOT - two lessons. The break script's replace silently no-op'd because the file is CRLF and my search string was LF, and one assertion only checked that withUnreadBadge appeared in the file, which the IMPORT line satisfies on its own. An import is not a use. Both fixed, then re-verified red.  Also fixed vault drift from the previous commit (49350ff7) that I should have caught in that commit: listings-column-inventory (re-read, unaffected, dated) and subscription-copy-review-register, which earned a real warning - email.ts now holds TWO functions whose names read as cancellation and only one is subscription copy. Anyone grepping during a counsel redline finds both, and mistaking the order notice for reviewed subscription wording is the expensive direction.  STILL OPEN: AC3's TabView badge and AC4's setBadgeCount call, both Swift. Verified here: tsc -b, lint 16 warnings 0 errors baseline, ui:check 0, 1528 web tests, 6727 edge tests 0 failed, vault:lint green. No migration. | 2026-08-17 THE SERVER SIDE OF THE BADGE IS NOW A ROUTE, so the Swift half needs no API this repo has never used.  NEW GET /api/notifications/unread-count -> { unread: n }, behind authMiddleware, reusing unreadNotificationCount - the same function that badges a push payload.  WHY A ROUTE RATHER THAN LETTING iOS QUERY DIRECTLY, which is what AC2 suggested and what web does. The count has to be a head+exact query, and getting that wrong is not a compile error - it is a number that silently stops rising at the page size. That precise bug already shipped once on web (the bell counted a .limit(20) page, so its own 99+ branch was unreachable), and re-implementing the query per platform is how it ships twice. One counter, already tested, behind one route.  AND IT REMOVES THE RISK THAT MATTERS HERE. Swift cannot be compiled on this host, so the dangerous move is writing Swift against an API the repo has no precedent for - supabase-swift head+exact counting appears nowhere in ios/. EdgeAPI.shared.getJSON appears everywhere. The route converts an unverifiable Swift call into a familiar one.  TWO DECISIONS IN THE HANDLER, both of which compile cleanly when wrong and are pinned by tests. (1) THE ID COMES FROM THE SESSION AND THERE IS DELIBERATELY NO PARAMETER: accepting one would turn a self-scoped counter into a cross-tenant oracle - "does this account have unread mail?" - while the rest of the handler looked identical. (2) AN UNREADABLE COUNT IS 503, NOT ZERO. unreadNotificationCount returns null for "could not read", and passing that through as 0 tells the client to CLEAR a badge showing five unread because the database hiccupped. That is the same absent-vs-zero distinction the APNs payload is built around, and the handler refuses to collapse it.  GUARDS: 5 source-scanned cases in notification-unread-route_test.ts (comments stripped) plus 2 tenant-isolation cases - unreachable without a session, and a userId parameter cannot redirect the count at another tenant. SABOTAGE-VERIFIED THREE WAYS: coalescing the null to 0, trusting a query parameter, and removing the auth mount. Each produced a failing run.  ONE HONEST NOTE ABOUT THE HARNESS: my sabotage script mislabelled two of the three as GREEN because its own pass/fail detection was wrong. The summary line it printed for each (4 passed, 1 failed) is the evidence, not the label. Worth recording rather than quietly fixing, because a sabotage harness that reports the wrong verdict is exactly as dangerous as a guard that does not guard.  ALSO CORRECTED: a first draft asserted the auth mount by substring over a comment-stripped copy of main.ts. That file is ~1700 lines and the non-greedy block-comment strip ate a span containing the real line, so a correct mount read as missing. The assertion is line-precise now - find the app.use LINE and require it to be a statement rather than prose mentioning one.  VERIFIED: node scripts/verify.mjs --edge, all 4 checks pass (7157 tests).  STILL OPEN: the Swift half of AC3 and AC4 - badge the Home tab from this route and set the app icon badge, clearing on the same signal that marks rows read. iOS CI on macOS is the gate, exactly as AC5 says. | 2026-08-17 (second pass) THE SWIFT HALF IS WRITTEN. AC3 and AC4 now have code; iOS CI on macOS remains the gate, exactly as AC5 says, and nothing here claims a simulator run.  NEW ios/GradeThread/Notifications/UnreadBadgeStore.swift, modelled on ReconcileBadgeStore deliberately - the same shell-level shape, the same injected fetch so every path is testable without a network, the same best-effort refresh. ContentView gains 13 lines: the store, .badge(unreadBadge.unreadCount) on the Home tab, a refresh at first render and another on foreground.  HOME RATHER THAN A TAB OF ITS OWN, because there is no notifications tab on iPhone - the five-tab limit is already spent - and the notification surface lives on the dashboard, which is what Home renders. SwiftUI renders nothing at 0, so the badge needs no conditional.  THREE DECISIONS THAT ARE CORRECT OR WRONG IN THE SOURCE, which matters because none of them is a compile error: (1) IT READS THE EDGE ROUTE, NOT THE TABLE. AC2 suggested querying notifications directly the way web does, and that is precisely how the web bell ended up counting a 20-row page with an unreachable 99+ branch. One counter, server-side, shared with the push payload. (2) A FAILED REFRESH DOES NOT TOUCH THE ICON. The route answers 503 rather than 0 so this distinction can be held; writing 0 on a failed read clears a badge showing five unread because the network hiccupped. (3) reset() CLEARS BOTH. The server only ever RAISES the badge - a push cannot know a row was read on another device - so bringing it down is the app job, on the same signal that marks rows read.  AND BECAUSE SWIFT CANNOT BE COMPILED HERE, those three are pinned by a source scan that RUNS here: src/test/ios-unread-badge.test.ts, 7 cases, comments stripped. Same arrangement as the ungated-print port beside it - scan the Swift from vitest so the rule is checked on every push rather than only when a macOS runner is free. SABOTAGE-VERIFIED THREE WAYS: writing the icon in the catch block, reverting the store to a direct table query, and deleting the tab badge. Each reddened; each restored.  TWO SMALL THINGS WORTH RECORDING. The Swift tree is CRLF, so the wiring script normalised for matching and restored on write - without that the edit would have rewritten every line ending in a 1400-line file and buried 13 real lines in a whole-file diff. And the new guard tripped eslint no-regex-spaces on consecutive literal spaces in a pattern, the same rule that bit second-opinion_test.ts earlier today; the sabotages were re-run after the fix rather than assumed to still bite.  VERIFIED: npx tsc -b clean, eslint 0 errors, the 6 iOS source guards 6/6, the new scan 7/7.  STILL OPEN: nothing that can be done from a Windows checkout. What remains is a simulator run to confirm the badge renders and the icon updates - iOS CI is the gate, and AC1 premise ("no badge API is used anywhere in ios/") is now deliberately false, which is the story being done rather than a regression. | 2026-08-18 THE SWIFT DID NOT COMPILE, AND iOS CI CAUGHT IT IN THREE AND A HALF MINUTES. This is the value of AC5 being written the way it was, so it is recorded rather than quietly fixed.  THE ERROR, exactly: UnreadBadgeStore.swift:44:29 "property 'unread' is private and cannot be referenced from a default argument value". The response struct was declared INSIDE the default argument of a public init. A type declared there is private to that expression, and Swift refuses to reference its members from a default argument, which is inlined into the caller module.  FIXED by resolving both defaults in the BODY instead: the parameters are optional and nil means "use the real one". The response struct, the fetch and the icon write are now private members of the class, which a body CAN reference. A test passing its own closure is unchanged.  ⚠ WHAT THIS SAYS ABOUT THE GUARD I WROTE, and it is the part worth keeping. src/test/ios-unread-badge.test.ts was 7/7 GREEN over the broken file, and it was right to be: every property it checks - reads the route not the table, does not touch the icon on failure, clears on reset, badges the Home tab - was TRUE of code that could not compile. A source scan checks INTENT. Only a compiler checks compilation. Reporting "7/7 green" as if it meant the Swift was verified would have been the overstatement AC5 exists to prevent, which is why that note said iOS CI is the gate and to state it plainly rather than claim local verification.  ALSO WORTH RECORDING: the previous commit iOS CI run was green (9m32s) and mine failed at 3m30s. A fast failure on that lane is a compile error rather than a test failure, and the run list alone tells you which before you open a log.  ONE HARNESS CORRECTION: after the rewrite, one of the three sabotages SKIPPED because its anchor - the inline EdgeAPI call - had moved into a private static method. Two of three proving is not three of three, so the anchor was updated and all three re-run rather than the skip being accepted.  VERIFIED HERE: the scan 7/7, the six iOS source guards 6/6, three sabotages red and restored. NOT VERIFIED HERE, deliberately stated: that it compiles. iOS CI on the next push is what says so. | 2026-08-18 SECOND COMPILE ERROR, DIFFERENT CLASS: "cannot find 'unreadBadge' in scope" at .badge(unreadBadge.unreadCount).  ContentView.swift holds several view structs. MainShell (562-1004) owns the shell-level state - the reconcile badge, the task, the scenePhase hook - and TabBarShell (1020+) owns the TabView. I put the store in the first and the badge in the second, having assumed one struct because the two lines look adjacent in a grep. They are 400 lines and a type boundary apart.  FIXED by threading the COUNT rather than moving the store: MainShell keeps the refresh (it already owns the other shell-level count and the foreground hook) and passes an Int to TabBarShell, which only renders. The renderer takes no dependency it has no reason to own.  ⚠ AND THE GUARD WAS GREEN OVER THIS TOO, for the second time. It asserted the literal ".badge(unreadBadge.unreadCount)" - which was PRESENT, in a struct where that identifier does not exist. A single-string check cannot see a scope boundary. It now checks the CHAIN: the store is declared, the count is passed to the tab shell, the tab is badged. Three links, each in its own place, so a break anywhere reddens with a message naming which link.  THE PATTERN ACROSS BOTH FAILURES IS THE SAME and worth stating once: a source scan proves a string is in a file. It cannot prove the string means what it appears to mean - not that a type is visible, not that an identifier is in scope, not that it compiles. Both errors were the compiler telling me something the scan is structurally incapable of knowing. | 2026-08-22 AC3 IS HALF UNMET, and it is the half nobody would notice from the code. The criterion reads 'badges the relevant tab ... and clears as rows are marked read'. The badging works. NOTHING ON iOS EVER MARKS A ROW READ.  MEASURED, three greps: `unreadBadge.reset()` has NO caller anywhere in ios/GradeThread. Nothing writes notifications.is_read - the only writes to that table's read flag are absent entirely, and a search for update calls near read/notif turns up AIItemFieldWriter and nothing else. BuyerAlertsView.swift READS is_read (line 49, 56, 273) and never writes it, and it queries public.notifications filtered to type = conditionAlertType, so it is a slice of the centre rather than the centre.  WHAT A SELLER SEES: the badge rises on a push and cannot be cleared from the phone. It falls only when a later refresh returns a lower count - which happens only if they read the same notifications on WEB. Reading them on the device changes nothing. The store's reset() exists for exactly this and is dead code.  That is worse than no badge, because a badge that cannot be dismissed trains the user to ignore it, and the same badge is what US-2557 AC4 puts on the app icon.  NOT FIXED HERE, and the reason is that the fix is a PRODUCT DECISION rather than a wiring gap. Marking read needs a trigger, and the candidates behave differently: on opening the alerts view (clears everything the moment they glance, including things they meant to come back to), per row on tap (leaves a count that only falls one at a time), or an explicit 'mark all read' control (matches the web centre but is a new affordance). Web resolves this by having a real notification centre; iOS has a filtered alerts view and no centre at all, so there is no obvious surface to copy.  Declared as an operator criterion so it reads as a question rather than as unfinished code. | COMPILATION SETTLED 2026-08-28. This note corrects one stale claim and changes nothing else about the story.

The notes above say some version of 'never been compiled' / 'iOS CI is the gate and it has not seen this' / 'cannot be verified from a Windows box'. That was true when written and is not true now. Every commit carrying this story's iOS code is an ancestor of iOS CI run 33139420556 on main (2026-08-28T03:37Z, head 1c6067106), conclusion SUCCESS - checked with git merge-base --is-ancestor, all commits in, none outside.

The run was checked for substance rather than for a green tick: both jobs succeeded, and the Build + test job's 'Generate Xcode project', 'Build + test' and 'Build app-extension targets' steps all executed. A green run whose build step never ran proves nothing.

ONE DISTINCTION MAKES THIS READABLE, and without it the evidence points the other way: many of these commits' OWN CI runs FAILED. 33 of the last 100 iOS CI runs on main were non-success, in one unbroken stretch from 2026-08-18 to 2026-08-27. iOS reports one error and stops, so a commit is not guilty of the failure it happens to sit on. 'Did its own run pass' has no useful answer; 'is it in a green build' does.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO: it does not close the story. Compilation was never the only thing outstanding here - what remains is whatever the notes above say it is, and it is now the ONLY thing outstanding, which is the point of writing this down. A story parked behind two blockers where one has quietly cleared reads as further away than it is.

THE CHECK IS TWO COMMANDS AND WORKS FROM WINDOWS: gh run list --workflow='iOS CI' --branch main to find the newest green run, then git merge-base --is-ancestor <commit> <that run's head>. Any story blocked on 'iOS CI has not seen this' can be settled the same way once its commits are on main. macOS-only COMPILATION is not macOS-only KNOWLEDGE.

userStories.title: [HELP CENTER] Converge support_kb_articles into help_articles so the assistant and the help page cannot disagree
userStories.description: Found while building US-2574: support_kb_articles (00183, US-830) already exists. It is the ONLY corpus the AI Support Assistant may answer from, it has slug/title/body_md/category/audience/is_published/versioned revisions and a weighted FTS column, and it has an admin editor at /admin/support/kb. What it does NOT have is any public web surface: nothing in functions/ or src/ renders it, so it is invisible to Google, to answer engines and to logged-out customers. help_articles (00602) is the superset and owns the web surface. Leaving both is the two-copies-must-agree failure in its worst form: the assistant would quote one wording of an answer while the public page shows another, and nobody would notice until a customer pasted a screenshot.
acceptanceCriteria: Decide and record the direction in a vault note: help_articles becomes the single corpus and support_kb_articles is retired. The assistant reads help_articles.

Migrate every support_kb_articles row into help_articles: category maps onto the 14 help categories, audience public->public and subscriber->members, is_published->status, body_md->body_markdown with body_html rendered from it.

Point the retrieval tool (services/edge-functions/src/lib/support-tools.ts + agent-tools.ts) at help_articles, and give help_articles the weighted tsvector + GIN index support_kb_articles has (US-2577 adds the search column; reuse it rather than adding a second).
The assistant must NEVER quote a members or internal article to an anonymous asker. Its retrieval passes the asker through visibilitiesFor() like every other read.
Retire /admin/support/kb and its route, or redirect it to /admin/content/help. One editor, not two.
Keep support_kb_revisions history: either migrate it alongside or archive it, but say which in the note. Do not drop edit history silently.
A test asserts the assistant cannot return an article the asker could not have read on the public site.

OPERATOR: run the row migration against PRODUCTION, then flip the flag, in that order. AC2 is the migration of support_kb_articles into help_articles - it has been written and re-run against the local stack, but the rows have never landed in prod, and the flag flip is deliberately ordered AFTER they do rather than before. AC5 (retire or redirect /admin/support/kb to /admin/content/help) follows the flip rather than leading it, so it is sequenced behind this, not independently doable. AC6 is a retention decision only you can make: migrate support_kb_revisions alongside, or archive it - the criterion says say which in the note and do not drop edit history silently. ⚠ ONE THING TO KNOW BEFORE THE PROD RUN: the summaries the migration writes are DERIVED from each article's first real paragraph, not authored. deriveSummary skips headings, list items, blockquotes, tables and fenced code, strips link and emphasis markup, prefers a sentence boundary and caps at 200 characters - sized against the 83 hand-written summaries, which run 93-200 and average 133. All 8 migrated articles landed between 80 and 152 characters locally. That removes the duplicate-description problem, and it is still not a substitute for 8 written summaries if these articles matter for search. AC1, AC3, AC4 and AC7 are done.
userStories.notes:
[FOUND DURING US-2574 2026-08-14] Consumers of support_kb_articles today: services/edge-functions/src/lib/agent-tools.ts, lib/support-tools.ts, main.ts, routes/admin-knowledge-base.ts, tests/support-kb-search_test.ts. No consumer in functions/ or src/ - confirmed by grep, which is what proves it has no public surface. This story is deliberately AFTER the help center ships (priority 83, behind US-2592) so the convergence moves content into a finished home rather than a half-built one. Until it lands the two corpora coexist, and the help center is the one customers see. | PARTIAL 2026-08-15 — AC1 and AC6 DECIDED AND WRITTEN, AC2's mechanism BUILT, and the rest is deliberately NOT shipped yet because the order is not symmetric. AC1: vault/20-domain/help-corpus-convergence.md records the direction (help_articles is the single corpus, support_kb_articles retires), the full field mapping, the nine-to-fourteen category map and the ordering constraint. AC6 DECIDED: support_kb_revisions is ARCHIVED IN PLACE - kept, not migrated, not dropped. help_articles has no revision mechanism to migrate INTO, so migrating would mean inventing one to hold history for a corpus that no longer takes edits; dropping is refused because edit history is the record of who changed a customer-facing answer and this repo's rule is that such a record is not the actor's to erase. AC2 MECHANISM: NEW scripts/migrate-support-kb-to-help.mjs, dry-run by default, with the mapping as pure exported functions so it is testable without a database. A SCRIPT RATHER THAN A MIGRATION because help_articles.body_html is NOT NULL and the public reader renders from it - markdown-to-HTML in SQL is not something to invent for a one-off when scripts/seed-help-articles.mjs already has the tested renderer the seeded corpus went through. THREE REFUSALS, WHICH ARE THE ACTUAL ENGINEERING: an unmapped category throws rather than guessing a destination for a customer-facing answer; an unmapped audience throws; and a slug collision STOPS the run by name rather than merging, because the unique index is case-insensitive and a collision means a hand-written help article already owns that URL. THE TEST FOUND A REAL CONTENT DEFECT: markdownToHtml handles ## and ### and NOT #, deliberately (the article title is the page h1, and all 83 seeded files start at h2). Nothing ever held the support KB to that convention, so a body written with # would have migrated into visible hash marks on a public page. demoteTopHeadings fixes it in the MARKDOWN, not just the HTML, so the /.md mirror and the page agree - patching the shared renderer instead would have been the wrong end, since its behaviour is right for the corpus it was written for. WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE: AC3 (repoint retrieval), AC4 (visibility filter), AC5 (retire /admin/support/kb), AC7 (the test that the assistant cannot quote what the asker could not read). Repointing before the data lands leaves the assistant reading an EMPTY corpus, where its designed behaviour is to say it does not know and offer a human - so the failure would be quiet, polite and total. Data first, then retrieval. VERIFIED: 17 cases in src/test/support-kb-to-help-migration.test.ts (17 passed), tsc -b clean, eslint clean, vault:lint strict clean at 178 notes. | PARTIAL 2026-08-15 (second pass) — AC3, AC4 and AC7 SHIPPED, BEHIND A FLAG THAT IS OFF. HELP_CORPUS_UNIFIED (unifiedHelpCorpusEnabled in lib/support-tools.ts) switches searchKnowledgeBase from support_kb_articles to help_articles, and agent-tools.ts fetchKbCatalog moves WITH it - a catalog listing one corpus while search reads the other would offer the operator titles the assistant cannot then quote. Both corpora already carry a weighted GIN-indexed search_tsv (00183 and 00603), so AC3's 'reuse it rather than adding a second' needed no schema work at all. WHY A FLAG AND NOT A SWITCH: the convergence has an ORDER, and the wrong order fails silently. Rows must land in help_articles first; flipping before they do leaves the assistant searching an empty table, and its designed behaviour on an empty result is to say it does not know and offer a human. That is a total outage of the support assistant wearing the face of a polite answer, and nobody files a bug about a polite answer. Default OFF, only 1/true turn it on, and six junk values are pinned as not-on. AC4 IS SHARPER THAN THE AC TEXT AND SHIPPED THAT WAY: the AC says never quote members or internal to an ANONYMOUS asker; the code says NOBODY reaches internal through this tool - not a subscriber, not an admin asking through the assistant. internal did not exist in the old two-value model and holds operator runbooks, and retrieval hands its output to a model that quotes what it is given, so a caller-dependent exception is the one somebody gets wrong later. visibleHelpVisibilities is exported so the guard asserts the mapping itself rather than only its effects. AC7: six new cases in src/tests/support-kb-search_test.ts (13 passed) - off-by-default still answering from the retired corpus, junk flag values, on-reads-help-and-not-the-old-table, anonymous never reaching members, NOBODY reaching internal, and a draft never surfacing. The fake DB's text matcher now spans body_md AND body_markdown, so a case cannot pass by silently reading the other corpus; the help fixture keeps a DIFFERENT row in support_kb_articles for the same reason. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED TWICE: widening visibleHelpVisibilities to include internal reddened the AC4 case alone, and forcing the corpus on reddened the off-by-default case. deno check + deno lint clean. env-reference.md documents the flag with the ordering warning. REMAINING: AC2 (run the migration against prod - operator), AC5 (retire /admin/support/kb, which should follow the flag flip rather than lead it). | 2026-08-16 THE FLAG WAS TURNED ON AGAINST REAL ROWS FOR THE FIRST TIME, and AC4/AC7's property holds. The previous note explains why HELP_CORPUS_UNIFIED is off: the convergence has an ORDER, and flipping before rows land leaves the assistant searching an empty table, which is a total outage of support. The rows now exist on a local stack (the 83-article corpus seeded onto all 609 migrations), so the flipped state could finally be exercised. HELP_CORPUS_UNIFIED=true, searchKnowledgeBase called directly against the local database: visibleHelpVisibilities('public') -> ['public'] visibleHelpVisibilities('subscriber') -> ['public','members'] q='team' public -> 2 [a-tour-of-the-dashboard, connecting-a-marketplace] q='team' subscriber -> 4 [+ inviting-your-team, cancelling] (both members) So the widening works and the narrowing works: a subscriber gains exactly the members rows and an anonymous asker never sees them. ⚠ THE INTERNAL CASE NEEDED A SECOND ATTEMPT, and the first one proved nothing. I first used q='rotation', got zero internal results for both audiences, and nearly recorded that as the proof. It is not: that query returns 5 rows and KB_MAX_RESULTS is 5, so the cap alone explains the absence of ops-key-rotation. Same trap as a fixture that omits the field under test. THE QUERY THAT ACTUALLY PROVES IT is q='runbook'. Checked in SQL first: it matches exactly THREE published articles and all three are internal (ops-the-review-queue, ops-key-rotation, ops-incident-response). Nothing else in the corpus matches, so a top-5 cap cannot be doing the work. Result: q='runbook' public -> 0 q='runbook' subscriber -> 0 Zero for BOTH, which is visibleHelpVisibilities never returning 'internal' to anyone - the rule the function's own comment states, now measured. WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT DE-RISK. The unified path reads through the SERVICE-ROLE client, so RLS is NOT the wall here - the .in('visibility', ...) and .eq('status','published') filters are the whole control. That is worth saying plainly, because the table-level and help_search proofs recorded on US-2572 rest on RLS and do NOT transfer to this path. This is the first evidence for the assistant's own filter with real gated rows behind it. STILL OPEN, unchanged: AC2 (migrate the support_kb_articles rows), AC5 (retire or redirect /admin/support/kb), AC6 (decide what happens to support_kb_revisions), and the flag flip itself - which remains ordered AFTER the rows land in PROD, not local. | 2026-08-16 (same session) THE MIGRATION SCRIPT WAS RUN FOR THE FIRST TIME and it found a collision that is CERTAIN to happen in prod.
