userStories.title: Shadow the footwear category criteria, so the golden set can exist
userStories.description:
US-2222 wrote category criteria for 11 more categories, including sneakers, boots and sandals, and they sit behind GRADING_CATEGORY_CRITERIA_V2, default OFF. That story's blocker is AC4: the golden-set eval gate needs real human-corrected grades on those categories and none exist. A gate with no cases for a category cannot pass or fail it — it would report on the 8 already-covered categories and say nothing about the ones the flag is about.

THAT IS A BOOTSTRAP, AND SHADOW IS THE WAY OUT OF IT. Shadow measures a candidate on live traffic and changes no published grade, so it can run before the eval gate rather than after. The divergences it records on real footwear are the raw material for the golden cases AC4 wants — a reviewer correcting a divergence produces exactly the human-corrected grade that does not exist today.

All three lifecycle legs exist now and this story uses only the first: shadow (US-2443), eval gate (US-2438), canary (US-896). Nothing here flips GRADING_CATEGORY_CRITERIA_V2.

THE PIECES, so this is a runbook and not a research task:
- `ai_prompt_block_versions` (00563) holds the candidate. Relevant columns: version_name, stage='per_image', block_key='category_criteria', garment_scope (the garment_category value — 'sneakers', 'boots', 'sandals'), block_text (EMPTY STRING means 'use the code default text but attribute to this version_name', which is what we want: the V2 text is already in code), is_shadow, shadow_sample_rate, shadow_daily_cap.
- block_key is a CLOSED vocabulary in prompt-blocks.ts PROMPT_BLOCK_KEYS. A row naming a key the code does not know is INERT, never an error — so a typo silently does nothing. Copy the string, do not type it.
- `PER_IMAGE_SHADOW_DAILY_VISION_CAP` is the hard stop and it defaults to OFF: unset reads as 0, and 0 means no shadow runs at all. Setting the rows without setting this env var produces a silent no-op.
- Results land in `grading_shadow_results`, with per_factor_deltas and tier_agreement (00566).

COST IS THE REAL DECISION. Each sampled submission costs a vision call PER PHOTO plus one composite. At 4 photos a submission, a cap of 200 vision calls a day is roughly 40 sampled submissions. This is a spend decision, not a risk decision — no published grade moves either way.
acceptanceCriteria: OPERATOR: choose a daily spend ceiling and set PER_IMAGE_SHADOW_DAILY_VISION_CAP to it. Unset is 0 and 0 is off, so this is the switch that makes everything below actually run.

One ai_prompt_block_versions row per footwear category (sneakers, boots, sandals): stage per_image, block_key category_criteria, garment_scope the category, block_text EMPTY (attribute the code default), is_shadow true, a sample rate, a daily cap.

Verify the rows are live rather than inert: a run appears in grading_shadow_results within the sampling window. A block_key typo is inert by design, so 'nothing happened' has two causes and they must be told apart.
No published grade changes. GRADING_CATEGORY_CRITERIA_V2 stays OFF for the whole of this story, and that is checkable: shadow writes to grading_shadow_results and never to grade_reports.
Review the divergences and promote the corrected ones into grading_eval_cases, tagged per category. That is US-2222 AC4's input and the actual point of running this.
Report what it cost against what it found, so the next sampling window is a decision rather than a repeat.
userStories.notes: 2026-08-23 EVERYTHING THAT IS NOT AN OPERATOR ACTION IS DONE. Commit d1ce9ca94. AC1, AC3, AC5 and AC6 need prod and are unchanged; AC2 is now a script to paste rather than rows to compose, and AC4 is a test rather than a comment.  AC2 IS scripts/shadow-footwear-criteria.sql. Idempotent: an insert with on-conflict-do-nothing plus an explicit update, so re-running sets the rate and cap rather than creating a second candidate per category. block_text is empty on purpose (attribute the code-default V2 text without duplicating it into a row), block_key is copied from PROMPT_BLOCK_KEYS rather than typed, and the update pins is_active and is_canary to false because those two columns are what would turn a shadow candidate into a champion.  ⚠ IT HAD THREE DEFECTS BEFORE IT WAS EVER RUN, which is the CLAUDE.md rule holding again. It selected `candidate_label` and `overall_delta` - the names THIS STORY'S OWN DESCRIPTION implies - where grading_shadow_results actually has `shadow_prompt_version_name` and `score_delta`. And it did not filter on `stage`, which 00566 added when that table started holding both the composite and the per-image shadows. Two of those fail outright on prod after the operator has already pasted; the third silently counts the wrong rows. All three came from trusting the description instead of reading 00115, 00566 and the insert at grading-shadow-per-image.ts:479-503.  DOCKER IS DOWN HERE so the SQL could not be executed against the local stack, which is the check that would have caught those three directly. src/test/shadow-footwear-sql.test.ts substitutes for it and says so in its header: it proves every identifier EXISTS, not that the query means what it says. It extracts every snake_case name the SQL uses, strips aliases and string literals, and requires each to appear in the migration corpus; it reads the garment values out of the SQL and checks them against the garment_category ENUM, because a non-member is `invalid input value for enum` mid-paste rather than an empty result; and it asserts everything after the section-2 marker is read-only.  AC4 IS NOW GUARDED. The shadow module's header has always said 'nothing here reads or writes grade_reports', and that sentence is the whole safety argument for running a candidate on live traffic before the eval gate has cases for it. Three cases in grading-shadow-per-image_test.ts pin it: the module touches only ai_prompt_versions, ai_prompt_block_versions and grading_shadow_results; neither grade_reports nor submissions is named as a string literal; and every write verb is preceded by a .from() naming the results table. A fourth pins that `category_criteria` is still in PROMPT_BLOCK_KEYS, because a key the code does not know is INERT rather than an error - so a typo in the operator rows looks exactly like a quiet week.  THE §3 QUERY IS THE ONE AC3 IS REALLY ASKING FOR, and the story does not name it. 'No shadow rows' has two causes that are indistinguishable from grading_shadow_results - the candidates are inert, or no footwear was graded in the window - and both produce zero rows. So §3 counts the TRAFFIC in public.submissions instead. Real numbers there with nothing in §2 means inert; zero in both means there was nothing to sample and the setup may be perfectly fine.  TWO OF MY OWN GUARDS WERE BLIND ON THE FIRST SABOTAGE RUN AND BOTH WERE THE SAME SHAPE - asserting a fixed list instead of reading the artifact. Changing one of three 'sneakers' sites to a non-enum value stayed green because the other two still matched the hardcoded list; renaming sum(vision_calls) to a column that exists nowhere stayed green because vision_calls appeared elsewhere in the file. Both now extract what the SQL actually uses. Final run: seven mutations, all red, green control either side. A third case caught itself before any sabotage - the read-only split searched for a section marker in the COMMENT-STRIPPED text, found -1, and checked a one-character string, which the length assertion caught.  STILL OPEN, ALL OPERATOR: AC1 (choose the daily spend ceiling and set PER_IMAGE_SHADOW_DAILY_VISION_CAP in Coolify - unset, non-numeric and negative all read as 0, and 0 means nothing runs), AC3 (run §2 after a sampling window, §3 if it is empty), AC5 (review the divergences §4 lists and promote the corrected ones into grading_eval_cases), AC6 (report cost against findings). The SQL's own header carries the run order and the cost arithmetic.

userStories.title: A shoe's size never reaches the grade: the chain breaks in three places
userStories.description:
Traced end to end 2026-08-22 after GRADING_SIZE_VERIFY was turned on and did nothing for footwear. The pieces all exist and none of them connect.

1. GRADING_SIZE_VERIFY CANNOT FIRE ON A SHOE, structurally. grading-pipeline.ts gates it on `sizeVerifyGradingEnabled() && hasMeasurementPhotos`, and isMeasurementPhoto accepts a type starting `measurement` or equal to `flatlay`. The grading image_type enum (00001, grown by 00103) has exactly five measurement values — chest, waist, length, sleeve, inseam — all garment tape measurements, and no `flatlay` at all (that is a flipdesk_photo_type, a different enum). No shoe submission can satisfy the second condition. The call also only receives measurement, front and back photos, and ai-size-estimate.ts contains zero mentions of shoe, footwear or insole.

2. THE STAMP IS READ BY A DIFFERENT FEATURE. ai-tag-ocr.ts fires on `label` and `label_2`, which a grading submission REQUIRES, and its prompt already asks for size "as printed (e.g. M, 32x34, 10, EU 42)" — a shoe size, verbatim. That is the path a shoe's size actually travels, and it is gated on GRADING_TAG_OCR, a different flag.

3. THE NUMBER HAS NO SCALE. Tag OCR yields the digits printed on the stamp and nothing says whether they are US men's, US women's, UK or EU. That is US-2796, and it is what turns a read number into a usable one. The 41 curated footwear sizing charts already record which scale each brand stamps (drmartens UK, birkenstock EU, the rest US) so the answer exists; nothing joins it to the OCR result.

The three are filed together because fixing any one alone changes nothing a seller would notice.
acceptanceCriteria: OPERATOR: set GRADING_TAG_OCR=true on the edge and redeploy. It accepts 1/true/yes/on. This is the switch that makes a shoe's size stamp readable at all, and it is cheap to reverse.
Confirm on a real shoe submission that tag OCR returns the stamped size — the evidence is the OCR result on a graded pair, not the flag being set.

Decide whether GRADING_SIZE_VERIFY should ever cover footwear. Doing so means a shoe-relevant measurement image_type (an insole-length photo) and a size prompt that knows what a shoe is; leaving it garment-only is a legitimate answer and cheaper.
If it stays garment-only, say so where an operator reads it: the env reference should not let the next person conclude, as I did, that this flag reaches footwear.
US-2796 resolves the scale, joining the OCR'd number to the brand's stamped scale from the sizing charts. That story is the one that makes the number mean something.
userStories.notes: 2026-08-22 THE TAG-OCR RECOMMENDATION NEEDS A CAVEAT, and it is the same mistake as the one this story was filed about — traced to a flag and stopped one link short of whether it FITS footwear. GRADING_TAG_OCR is still the right flag: it fires on label / label_2, which a grading submission requires, and the size example in its schema is literally 'EU 42'. What I did not check before recommending it is the PROMPT, and it is written for a garment care label five times over: - SYSTEM: 'You are shown ONLY the brand/size/care label of a single garment.' - tool name read_garment_tag, described as 'printed on the garment's tag/care label' - userInstructions: 'Read the garment tag/label photo(s)' - two of the five requested fields are FIBER CONTENT and an RN NUMBER — a US textile registration that footwear does not carry at all. A shoe's size stamp is moulded or heat-printed on a tongue, insole or outsole. It is not a care label, and the model is being told that is what it is looking at. It may well still read the digits — models are forgiving and the example matches — but 'probably fine' is what I said about GRADING_SIZE_VERIFY. SO AC2 IS THE LOAD-BEARING ONE and should be read strictly: the evidence is an OCR result on a real graded pair, not the flag being set and not this reasoning. Turn it on — cheap, reversible, and correct for the garments already being graded — then look at one shoe before trusting it for footwear. IF IT DOES NOT READ THE STAMP, the fix is a prompt change and therefore goes through shadow then the eval gate, not a silent edit. The same discipline keeping GRADING_CATEGORY_CRITERIA_V2 off applies here, and the shadow path US-2810 sets up is the machinery for it. PATTERN WORTH NAMING, twice in one day: a flag being on is not a feature being reachable. Both times the gate was correct and something one step further in — an enum with no footwear value, then a prompt with no footwear concept — made it inert. Check what the feature READS, not just what turns it on. | 2026-08-23 AC5 IS DONE AND AC4 ALREADY WAS. Checked against the code and the vault rather than against the story text. AC5 pointed at US-2796 for the third link in this chain - the number having a SCALE. US-2796 closed today. lib/shoe-size-scale.ts resolves it two ways: attributes.shoe_size_scale when the seller or the capture pass recorded one, and the brand's curated footwear chart otherwise (drmartens UK, birkenstock EU, the rest US by department). The capture pass now READS the scale off the size stamp as a canonical attribute, which is the same photo tag OCR reads, so link 3 no longer depends on link 2 being turned on. WHERE THE SCALE IS ACTUALLY CONSUMED, since 'resolved' is not the same as 'used': parcel-estimate normalises through shoeSizeToUsMen before the weight exponent, and the eBay path refuses to put a UK or EU number into a US-named aspect on publish, revise and the web composer prefill. So a scale that arrives now changes what ships and what the parcel weighs. AC4 was already satisfied before this story reached me: vault/10-ops/env-reference.md carries a dated warning that GRADING_SIZE_VERIFY is GARMENT-ONLY and structurally inert for footwear, with the enum reasoning. An operator reading the reference cannot now make the inference this story records someone making. Nothing to do. STILL OPEN, ALL THREE OPERATOR OR DECISION: AC1 (set GRADING_TAG_OCR and redeploy), AC2 (confirm on a REAL graded pair that the stamp is read - the story's own caveat is that the tag-OCR prompt says 'garment' five times and asks for fiber content and an RN number, neither of which a shoe carries, so this must be read strictly as evidence rather than reasoning), and AC3 (whether GRADING_SIZE_VERIFY should ever cover footwear at all). NOTE ON ORDERING: with US-2796 done, links 1 and 3 of the three-link chain are settled - link 1 is documented as garment-only, link 3 resolves the scale. Only link 2, the OCR actually reading a shoe stamp, is untested, and it is one flag and one real submission away.

userStories.title: iOS and Android ask a hat for its inseam: the native measurement catalogs never matched the web
userStories.description:
AutoLister/listing dive 2026-08-22, owner-requested. SHOES came out clean; the gaps are in the categories beside them.

MeasurementCatalog.suggestedKeys() on both native clients is a four-branch switch: shoes/footwear, watches/watch, accessories/bags/other, and a default returning the eight-field garment set. The web has ELEVEN groups. The drift, measured:

- shoes: [size_us, insole] both sides. MATCHES.
- watches: 3 fields both sides. MATCHES.
- bags: web has width, height, depth, strap_drop, handle_drop and marks w/h/d REQUIRED (US-2225 AC4: depth is the defining dimension, a 30cm tote and a 30cm clutch are different objects). Native offers length, width.
- accessories: web has length, width, hole_span. Native drops hole_span — the belt's first-to-last-hole span, which US-2224 calls the third number a belt is sold on.
- headwear: THE SHARP ONE. There is no headwear branch, so it falls to `default` and a hat is offered chest, sleeve, inseam, rise and hip. The web has circumference, crown_height, brim_length. This became reachable on 2026-08-22 when US-2797 made `headwear` a producible item_category — before that no item could carry the value, so the missing branch cost nothing.
- clothing: web splits top/bottom/dress/outerwear/suit (4-7 fields each); native returns one flat eight-field list for all of them.

NOTHING GUARDS THIS. MeasurementCatalogTest.kt asserts the catalog's OWN hardcoded list back to itself — self-consistency, not parity — so the native copies can drift from the web without anything going red. measurement-template-parity.test.ts holds web against EDGE and says nothing about Swift or Kotlin.

ALSO FOUND, filed here rather than separately because it is the same audit:
- The aspect registry has category-specific aspects for shoes, bags and accessories ONLY. `headwear` has none, so a hat listing gets no Hat Size or Size Type aspect — same newly-reachable-category cause.
- iOS's BUNDLED photo-profile fallback covers only `clothing` and `other`. The live table is server-driven and correct, so this only bites when the fetch fails — but then a shoe is captured with garment slots instead of Top/Heel/Sole/Size Stamp/Insole.
acceptanceCriteria: The native catalogs cover every group the web does, including headwear, and stop offering an inseam for a hat.
Bags get width/height/depth/strap_drop/handle_drop and accessories get hole_span, matching the web templates that those stories deliberately widened.

A parity guard holds the native catalogs to src/lib/measurement-templates.ts, the way measurement-template-parity.test.ts holds the edge copy. Self-consistency assertions are not parity and did not catch any of this.
The aspect registry gains headwear entries, or records deliberately that a hat uses only generic aspects.
iOS's bundled photo-profile fallback covers the categories a seller can actually photograph offline, or the degraded behaviour is written down where a reader will find it.
VERIFY ON A REAL ITEM, not from the source: add a hat and a belt on iOS and confirm the fields offered. This audit is a read, and reads have been wrong twice this week.

OPERATOR: AC6 is a device check and it is the only thing left. AC1-AC5 are done and guarded — src/test/native-measurement-catalog-parity.test.ts now holds both native catalogs to the web templates key for key, label for label and unit for unit. What no test here can do is look at the screen: open a hat, a bag and a belt on a real iPhone and a real Android and confirm the fields offered are the ones the web asks for. Android is checkable from this box and iOS is not, so a passing Android build is evidence about the shared table, not about what iOS renders.
userStories.notes:
2026-08-22 AC1-AC3 DONE. AC4-AC6 still open and each is its own thing. AC1/AC2. Both native catalogs now branch on bags, accessories and headwear separately: bags get width/height/depth/strap_drop/handle_drop, accessories get length/width/hole_span, headwear gets circumference/crown_height/ brim_length. A hat is no longer offered an inseam. THE GAP WAS BIGGER THAN THE SWITCH STATEMENT. All eight of those keys were absent from both catalogs' Spec lists entirely, not just from suggestedKeys — so even a value arriving from the server rendered with an auto-derived label. Labels are copied VERBATIM from src/lib/measurement-templates.ts rather than derived: "First to last hole (belts)" tells a seller what to measure and "Hole Span" does not. CLOTHING IS DELIBERATELY LEFT FLAT and the guard exempts it explicitly. The web splits clothing five ways by ranking a GARMENT word off the row; suggestedKeys only has the coarse item_category, and `clothing` cannot tell a blazer from jeans. Demanding the web's five groups would be demanding information the caller does not have. The exemption is asserted rather than merely absent, so adding clothing to the map fails and makes the next person read why. AC3. src/test/native-measurement-catalog-parity.test.ts, 5 cases, holds both catalogs to MEASUREMENT_TEMPLATES. SABOTAGE-VERIFIED 6 of 6 with a green control either side: headwear branch removed from iOS, from Android, bags reverted to length+width, accessories losing hole_span, a key offered with no Spec entry, and the Spec parser broken (caught by the vacuity floor). ⚠ TWO SABOTAGES REPORTED 'DID NOT APPLY' ON THE FIRST RUN — the two headwear ones, which are the exact bug. The mutation regexes anchored on a bare \n and these files are CRLF. Reported as proving nothing and re-run CRLF-tolerant. That is the same line-ending trap that made check-ios-orphans green on Windows and red in CI. ANDROID VERIFIED BY RUNNING IT, not by reading: 20 tests, 0 failures, --rerun-tasks so it was a real execution rather than an up-to-date cache. iOS cannot be compiled here; the source guards (orphans) pass and the macOS lane is the gate. AN EXISTING ANDROID TEST CAUGHT A REAL PROBLEM WITH MY OWN CHANGE, which is the best thing that happened here. `every measurement key offers at least one aspect candidate` failed on all eight new keys. Investigating rather than silencing it: the WEB has the same gap — MEASUREMENT_SPECS in src/lib/measurements.ts covers the same sixteen keys the native catalogs used to and none of the eight. They live in MEASUREMENT_TEMPLATES, which is the FORM, not the aspect map. So a bag's depth is collected on the web today and reaches no eBay aspect either. Resolved with a named NO_ASPECT_YET exemption plus a second test asserting the list can only SHRINK, so it cannot become the place unmapped keys go to be forgotten. I did NOT invent aspect names — what eBay calls a hat's inside circumference is a question for real category data, and a guessed name would put an invented aspect on a live listing. STILL OPEN: AC4 (headwear aspect-registry entries), AC5 (iOS bundled photo-profile fallback covers only clothing/other), AC6 (verify on a real device). AC6 matters most — this is still a read, and mapping the eight keys to eBay aspects is now its own piece of work worth its own story. | 2026-08-22 AC4 DONE. A hat listing can now fill eBay's Hat Size aspect. `headwear` had no entry anywhere in ASPECT_REGISTRY, so a hat could only ever fill the generic "Size". The size entry now carries byCategory.headwear = ["Hat Size"], and category candidates are tried BEFORE the defaults (effectiveCandidates spreads extra first), so Hat Size wins when the leaf has it and Size still works when it does not. WHY THIS IS NOT THE GUESS I REFUSED TO MAKE ELSEWHERE, which is worth being precise about since I declined to invent aspect names for the eight measurement keys an hour ago. ownedAspectName resolves every candidate against the REAL aspect list eBay returns for the chosen category — a name that category does not have is never matched. A candidate is a PROPOSAL; only eBay's own vocabulary is ever used. Inventing a measurement-to-aspect mapping is different: that one publishes a value. ONLY "Hat Size", and the omission is the reviewable judgement. "Size Type" was the other obvious candidate and is deliberately absent: on eBay's apparel categories it means Regular/Petite/Plus, so if a hat leaf carries it as FREE TEXT then "7 3/8" would fill it and publish a size where a fit class belongs. A candidate is only safe when its meaning cannot be mistaken — the safety property protects against a name eBay does not have, not against a name that means something else. Registry version bumped 3 -> 4 as the file's own rule requires, and the vendored web copy regenerated with npm run sync:aspects. The drift guard (aspect-registry-drift_test.ts) passes, which is what proves the JSON actually matches rather than my having remembered to run the script. VERIFIED: 43 aspect-registry tests, 8322 edge tests, 6134 web tests, tsc -b exit 0, deno check clean. STILL OPEN: AC5 (iOS bundled photo-profile fallback covers only clothing/other) and AC6 (verify on a real device). Also now worth its own story: mapping the eight new measurement keys to eBay aspects, which needs real category data rather than a guess — the web has that same gap and has had it since US-2224/US-2225. | 2026-08-22 AC5 DONE, and the way it went wrong is the useful part. A shoe captured before the profile fetch answers now gets the shoe slots on all THREE clients — Top/Heel/3-4 Angle/Sole/Size Stamp/Insole instead of the generic Front/Back/Detail. The Sole matters most: it is the first surface a shoe buyer looks at and the old fallback had no slot for it. ⚠ I SAID 'iOS bundled fallback' IN THIS STORY AND THERE ARE THREE. iOS, Android AND src/lib/photo-profiles.ts. I added shoes to two, and the existing US-2769 guard failed on the third — which is the guard doing exactly its job and my audit having been one copy short. ⚠ I ALSO WROTE A DUPLICATE GUARD. src/test/photo-profile-fallback-parity.ts already existed for this, and its header explicitly argues AGAINST the approach mine took: it does not assert client == server because the fallbacks abbreviate the server's hints on purpose, and asserting equality would fail on eight roles and teach the next person to delete the test. Mine asserted exactly that and passed only because I had copied the server verbatim. Deleted it and extended theirs instead. WHAT THE EXTENSION ADDED: Android, which that guard never covered. It compared web against iOS while Android shipped its own copy unguarded the whole time — it could have said anything to an Android seller with nothing going red. SABOTAGE, 2 of 4 red, and the two greens are REAL LIMITS now written into the file rather than left silent. Every parser pools every role literal in a file regardless of profile, so making `front` optional in the shoes fallback alone stays green — the clothing fallback still contributes `front|` to the required set. And nothing sees ROUTING: deleting the line that returns SHOES_FALLBACK leaves the constant defined and every literal still parsed. Both want per-profile parsing and both are recorded. One of the four was my own omission and the sabotage caught it: I put Android in the required-slot check and forgot the label/hint one, so an Android-only hint change stayed green. Fixed. VERIFIED: 1911 Android tests 0 failures (--rerun-tasks, a real run), 6134 web tests, 13 in the parity guard, tsc -b exit 0, eslint clean, both orphan guards OK. An existing Android test also caught the bundled-keys assertion and was updated to expect shoes with the Sole slot asserted by name. STILL OPEN: AC6 only — verify on a real device. Everything above is a source read plus an Android unit run; no iOS build happened and none can here. | 2026-08-22 THE SHOE LISTING PATH IS NOW VERIFIED BY RUNNING IT, not by reading. This story's earlier notes asserted 'a shoe's size reaches the listing' from source. It does — but the way that got confirmed is the point. Ran resolveItemAspects against a realistic eBay shoe leaf. All six shoe aspects fill from a normal item: Brand, US Shoe Size, Color, Upper Material, Department, Shoe Width. A half size (9.5) matches. A shirt gets none of the shoe candidates. And a size the leaf does not offer (13) fills NOTHING, which is the property that matters at publish — eBay rejects an out-of-list value on a SELECTION_ONLY aspect, and silently coercing 13 to 11 would be worse than the rejection because a buyer would receive the wrong shoe. ⚠ THE FIRST RUN OF THAT PROBE REPORTED A PUBLISH-BREAKING BUG THAT DOES NOT EXIST. Size 13 appeared to fill US Shoe Size despite the leaf offering only 8-11. The cause was my harness: the edge's RegistryAspect is FLAT (name/mode/allowedValues) and I had mocked eBay's nested aspectConstraint/aspectValues, so `mode` read undefined, every aspect fell through to free text, and the raw value passed. I was one step from filing it. Verifying by running only helps if the harness is right — the same lesson the CRLF sabotage mutations taught earlier today. Two tests added to the EXISTING aspect-registry_test.ts rather than a new file. The shoe test already there uses FREE_TEXT aspects and a real eBay shoe leaf does not; SELECTION_ONLY is covered generally via Department, so what is genuinely shoe-specific is the DECIMAL half-size token. 44 tests now. SABOTAGE-VERIFIED 3 of 3, green control either side: SELECTION_ONLY validation disabled, an unmatched value falling back to raw, and the shoes byCategory candidates removed. ALSO CHECKED AND CLEAN: photoStandardsPreflight is category-agnostic — pixel size and hero-photo rules only — so nothing there blocks a shoe. VERIFIED: 8324 edge tests 0 failed, deno lint clean. | 2026-08-22 AC1-AC5 RE-VERIFIED GREEN TODAY; AC6 IS THE ONLY THING LEFT AND IT IS A TWO-MINUTE CHECK ON A PHONE. Re-run rather than re-read, because AC6 exists precisely to distrust reads:   - native-measurement-catalog-parity + photo-profile-fallback-parity: 24     tests, all pass. That is AC3 and AC5.   - aspect-registry.ts:91 has headwear: [Hat Size]. That is AC4.   - MeasurementCatalog.kt:147 headwear -> circumference, crown_height,     brim_length. No inseam. AC1.   - MeasurementCatalog.kt:146 accessories -> length, width, hole_span. AC2.  THE EXACT DEVICE SCRIPT, so this does not sit open for want of knowing what to tap. Two items, four fields to read:   1. Add an item, set its category to HEADWEAR (a hat/cap), open Measure.      EXPECT: Circumference, Crown height, Brim length.      FAIL IF: Inseam, Chest, Sleeve or Waist appear - that is the bug this      story is named after, and it means the app is on a build from before this.   2. Add an item, set its category to ACCESSORIES (a belt), open Measure.      EXPECT: Length, Width, Hole span.      FAIL IF: Hole span is missing. Nothing else needs checking by hand - the shoe path was verified by RUNNING the resolver (see the previous segment) rather than by reading it.  ⚠ AC6 SAYS IOS AND IT CANNOT BE CHECKED FROM THIS MACHINE - no Swift toolchain on Windows. ANDROID CAN be built here and its catalog is asserted by the same parity guard against the same web source, so a passing Android build is evidence about the shared TABLE but not about what iOS renders. If a phone is easier to reach than a Mac, checking Android first is still worth something: it would catch a wrong table, just not a wrong iOS screen. | COMPILATION SETTLED 2026-08-28. This note corrects one stale claim and changes nothing else about the story.

The notes above say some version of 'never been compiled' / 'iOS CI is the gate and it has not seen this' / 'cannot be verified from a Windows box'. That was true when written and is not true now. Every commit carrying this story's iOS code is an ancestor of iOS CI run 33139420556 on main (2026-08-28T03:37Z, head 1c6067106), conclusion SUCCESS - checked with git merge-base --is-ancestor, all commits in, none outside.

The run was checked for substance rather than for a green tick: both jobs succeeded, and the Build + test job's 'Generate Xcode project', 'Build + test' and 'Build app-extension targets' steps all executed. A green run whose build step never ran proves nothing.

ONE DISTINCTION MAKES THIS READABLE, and without it the evidence points the other way: many of these commits' OWN CI runs FAILED. 33 of the last 100 iOS CI runs on main were non-success, in one unbroken stretch from 2026-08-18 to 2026-08-27. iOS reports one error and stops, so a commit is not guilty of the failure it happens to sit on. 'Did its own run pass' has no useful answer; 'is it in a green build' does.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO: it does not close the story. Compilation was never the only thing outstanding here - what remains is whatever the notes above say it is, and it is now the ONLY thing outstanding, which is the point of writing this down. A story parked behind two blockers where one has quietly cleared reads as further away than it is.

THE CHECK IS TWO COMMANDS AND WORKS FROM WINDOWS: gh run list --workflow='iOS CI' --branch main to find the newest green run, then git merge-base --is-ancestor <commit> <that run's head>. Any story blocked on 'iOS CI has not seen this' can be settled the same way once its commits are on main. macOS-only COMPILATION is not macOS-only KNOWLEDGE.

userStories.title: Eight measurements are collected and reach no eBay aspect
userStories.description:
MEASUREMENT_SPECS in src/lib/measurements.ts maps a measurement key to the eBay aspect names it can fill. It covers sixteen keys. MEASUREMENT_TEMPLATES in measurement-templates.ts — the FORM — asks for eight more: height, depth, strap_drop, handle_drop, hole_span, circumference, crown_height, brim_length.

So a seller measures a bag's depth, a belt's hole span or a hat's inside circumference, the value is stored on inventory_items.measurements, and resolveMeasurementAspects has nothing to match it to. It never reaches a listing.

Found 2026-08-22 when an Android test — `every measurement key offers at least one aspect candidate` — failed against the eight keys being added to the native catalogs. Investigating rather than silencing it showed the WEB has the same gap and has had it since US-2224 and US-2225 added those fields. The native side now carries a named NO_ASPECT_YET exemption that can only shrink, so this is tracked rather than forgotten.

NOT DONE BY GUESSING, deliberately. What eBay calls a hat's inside circumference, or a tote's depth, is a question for real category data. Unlike an aspect NAME candidate — which is inert if the category does not have it — a wrong mapping here publishes a VALUE under a name that means something else.
acceptanceCriteria: For each of the eight keys, find the real eBay aspect name(s) from the Taxonomy API on the categories that actually use them — bags, belts, hats — rather than from memory.
A key that genuinely has no eBay aspect stays unmapped and is recorded as such, with the reason. Not every measurement a buyer wants is one eBay models.
MEASUREMENT_SPECS gains the mappings, and the native NO_ASPECT_YET list shrinks by exactly what was mapped — its shrink-only test enforces that.
resolveMeasurementAspects fills a CONSTRAINED aspect too, or the limitation is written down: it currently only fills free-text aspects, so a mapping onto a pick-list aspect would still not fill.

OPERATOR: pull the real eBay aspect names for the eight keys from the Taxonomy API, on live bag, belt and hat leaf categories. This is the ONLY thing blocking AC1-AC3 and it cannot be done from this machine: it needs eBay app credentials, which live in Coolify, against live category data. The repo has no cached taxonomy for those categories (checked: the one aspect fixture, src/test/fixtures/required-aspects-cases.json, is the US-2389 required-aspects table and covers none of them). Web search is not a substitute and the story says why: a wrong name here publishes a VALUE under a name that means something else.
userStories.notes:

every platform. Commit 582b27c42. AC4 was already done before this session.

userStories.title: Weekly analytics digest and anomaly alerts: push the finding instead of waiting for a visit
userStories.description: As a reseller, I want a short weekly summary and an alert when one of my numbers moves sharply against my own trailing baseline, so that I find out about a problem in days rather than when I next open a tab.
acceptanceCriteria: A scheduled job composes a weekly per-seller digest containing: the Seller Scorecard biggest gap (US-2822), money left on the table for the week (US-2820), the week's best and worst group by capital velocity (US-2825), and any triggered anomaly.

An anomaly fires when a metric moves more than a configured number of standard deviations from that seller's own trailing 90-day baseline, with the threshold stored in system_settings (00207/00208 registry) so it is tunable without a deploy.
No anomaly fires for a seller below a minimum activity floor, so a seller with three sales never gets an alert about a 100 percent swing.
Delivery reuses the existing alert-channel plumbing rather than adding a new sender, and the digest is a no-op (logged, not sent) when the seller has nothing to report that week.
US-2003 is respected: the job records a delivery outcome per seller per channel, so 'nobody was paged' is provable rather than assumed.
The digest is opt-out from settings, and the opt-out is honored by the job in the same query that selects recipients, not filtered afterwards.
userStories.notes:
2026-08-23 AC2 AND AC3 SHIPPED as pure math. Commit 35c14c9d6. AC1, AC4, AC5 and
AC6 are open, and AC6 needs a migration.

services/edge-functions/src/lib/seller-anomaly.ts - no job, no IO, no DB. Same
split ads-anomaly.ts uses: the detection is unit-tested and the scan that will
call it is separate, so the thresholds are reviewable in one place.

STANDARD DEVIATIONS, NOT PERCENTAGES, and the existing module is the argument.
ads-anomaly.ts compares the latest day to a trailing average BY PERCENT, which
is right for ad spend - a 2x day is a 2x day whoever you are. It is wrong per
seller. Someone selling two or three items most weeks has a hundred-percent
swing constantly and nothing has happened; someone selling forty a week who
drops to thirty has had a real event that a percentage rule ranks BELOW the
first. AC2 already asked for deviations from the seller's own baseline; this
records why that is not interchangeable with the module next door.

THE FLOOR IS ON THE BASELINE, NOT THE LATEST WEEK. AC3 exists because of the
seller with three sales and a 100% swing, and the obvious implementation floors
the LATEST value - at which point a seller whose activity collapses to zero is
silenced BY THE COLLAPSE, losing the one event most worth telling them about.
Flooring the baseline says 'you used to do enough for this to mean something'.
A test drives exactly that case, and it is the one to read if this is ever
revisited.

THREE MORE CHOICES, each with a case: the latest week is excluded from its own
baseline (or a big week inflates the spread it is measured against, and the
detector stops firing precisely when the number gets interesting); a flat
baseline never fires (zero spread makes every non-identical week infinitely
unusual - four items for six weeks then five would page someone); and null means
'nothing to say' rather than a zero-sigma result, so a caller cannot confuse
'not enough history' with 'a normal week'.

DEFAULT 2.5 SIGMA, not 2. At 2, roughly one week in twenty is 'unusual' for a
seller whose numbers are noise, which across a user base is a weekly email to
thousands of people about nothing. The point of an alert is that receiving one
is information.

VERIFIED: 8395 edge tests pass, deno lint + check clean. TEN mutations, green
controls either side, nine red.

THE TENTH FOUND REDUNDANT CODE, which is the useful kind of green: a
`series.length < minBaselineWeeks + 1` early-out was exactly equivalent to the
baseline check below it, so breaking it changed nothing. Removed - one check owns
the rule now and it reddens when broken. Its replacement (an empty-series guard)
is documented as DEFENSIVE and un-reddenable rather than left looking proven.

⚠ TWO OF MY OWN TEST FIXTURES WERE WRONG and the suite caught both. A 'just
under threshold' case was actually 4.65 sigma, and a fractional series ran around
2.0 - below the activity floor - so the detector correctly refused and the test
then dereferenced null. Both recalculated and both now say so in the file. A
fixture chosen by eye is how a threshold test ends up asserting the wrong side of
the line.

STILL OPEN:
  AC1  the scheduled weekly job that composes the digest.
  AC4  delivery through the existing alert-channel plumbing, and the no-op
       (logged, not sent) path when a seller has nothing to report.
  AC5  a recorded delivery outcome per seller per channel, so US-2003's 'nobody

  AC6  opt-out honoured in the SAME query that selects recipients, not filtered

send, the delivery record and the opt-out are still open.

services/edge-functions/src/lib/seller-digest.ts - composeSellerDigest(inputs),

DEFINING what to report was the real work, and the obvious definition breaks the

is - so treating a section s presence as news makes every digest non-empty and
deletes AC4 without anyone editing it. The four sources named in AC1 split into
NEWS (an anomaly, or money left on the table above a floor) and CONTEXT (the

rides along. There is a test named for that rule.

Three smaller decisions with cases: money under $25 is true and not worth
anyone s Monday; both velocity ends or neither, because a best alone reads as
praise and a worst alone as a telling-off; the headline is the first section, so
a reader who stops after one line gets the most actionable one. Every line is

silent one.

AC1/AC4 (seller-digest.ts) are built, pure and tested; 00659 gives AC5 and AC6
their storage and is HELD. What is missing is the read path, and it is missing
for a reason that is now enforced rather than remembered. | 2026-08-23 STATUS CORRECTION, and it is a real incident rather than a wording
fix. prd-lint is RIGHT to flag this note: 00659 IS on origin/main.

would be the hand-edited-marker failure the gate exists to catch. | 2026-08-23. THE NUMBER: TWENTY such functions exist and the edge calls NONE of them today, so the guard holds at zero with no allowlist. They are not bugs - they are correct browser RPCs. flipdesk_source_yield, flipdesk_listing_quality_lift, flipdesk_return_attribution, flipdesk_overview_metrics, finances_dashboard, seller-facing search and the rest. The service-role client bypasses RLS and makes auth.uid() NULL, so calling one from the edge returns NOTHING for every seller, or EVERY TENANT'S ROWS, depending on which the function leans on. Both answer 200. THE EXISTING GUARD DID NOT COVER THIS. rpc-identity-semantics.test.ts asks about functions called from the browser AND the edge; the case that bites here is an edge-ONLY call, where nothing is dual-called, that guard never fires, and the wrong tenant's rows come back anyway. ⚠ VIEWS ARE WHY THE FIRST VERSION SAW NOTHING. The analytics RPCs read items_full, not inventory_items, and a view carries no RLS policy of its own, so a base-table-only rule reads an analytics function as touching nothing tenant-shaped. Six of the twenty are reachable only through a view. Resolved, and pinned by a test naming items_full. ⚠ AND THE FIRST RUN PRINTED A CONFIDENT ZERO for an unrelated reason: the table-matching regex was built from a string literal, where JavaScript reads backslash-b as the BACKSPACE character rather than a word boundary. It could never match. Caught only because a function I had just read the source of - flipdesk_return_attribution, which plainly selects from public.inventory_items - came back clean. Third instance of that escape this week and the first to produce a false PASS instead of a crash. One of the six mutations reintroduces it. Six mutations, each applied, green controls either side. Two real: an edge caller for flipdesk_source_yield (through a view) and for finances_dashboard (base tables) both RED. One GREEN on purpose: an edge call to a DEFINER function taking p_user_id, which is the shape the FIX must produce. FOR AC1 SPECIFICALLY: the digest job would have been the first caller, and the digest is EMAILED - so the RLS-bypass direction of this bug would have posted one seller's figures to another seller. seller-digest.ts stays a pure function with no database access, which is why nothing is wrong today, and the unwired-module allowlist entry for it still stands. | 2026-08-23 I TRIED TO ROUTE AROUND THE BLOCKER AND THE DETOUR IS WORSE. Traced end to end before writing any of the job, and recording it so nobody re-walks it. THE ENCOURAGING PART FIRST: the job needs LESS than AC1 lists. composeSellerDigest sends on `hasNews = anomalies.length > 0 || moneyIsNews` - the scorecard gap and the velocity pair are CONTEXT that never triggers a send, and every DigestInputs field is nullable. So a first version needs only two of AC1's four things. THEN BOTH OF THOSE TWO TURN OUT TO BE BLOCKED BY THE SAME THING. MONEY LEFT (US-2820) is not computed in TypeScript anywhere. flipdesk_price_gap (migration 00652) does the scoring in Postgres; src/lib/price-gap.ts owns only the reading rules and the copy and calls the RPC. That function is SECURITY DEFINER guarded by gt_require_role, and its body scopes by auth.uid() in THREE places (lines 122, 128, 153). Called from the edge with the service-role client, auth.uid() is NULL, so it returns EMPTY for every seller - silently, with a 200. It is the exact failure mode edge-never-calls-caller-scoped-rpc.test.ts describes, in its other direction. ANOMALIES need a weekly series, which means the same aggregates. SO THE THREE WAYS ROUND ARE ALL WORSE:   (a) call the RPCs as they are -> an empty digest for every seller, no error.   (b) reimplement the scoring on the edge -> a THIRD copy of analytics math.       src/lib/price-gap.ts, capital-velocity.ts and seller-scorecard.ts are all       web-only today, and I spent this afternoon fixing the damage from ONE       unnoticed web/edge mirror (US-2796's resolver). Creating another one       deliberately, for money figures that reach a seller's inbox, is the wrong       trade.   (c) read base tables directly -> that IS (b), with the math hidden in a query. CONCLUSION: the DEFINER wrappers taking p_user_id are not one option among several, they are the only one that does not duplicate scoring. The blocker is real and it is not effort. AC1 stays open. WHAT WOULD UNBLOCK IT, in order: (1) Docker Desktop restarted AS ADMINISTRATOR - the engine service is Stopped while the GUI runs, so verify:db has been skipped on every run for two days, and a migration that rewrites five functions gating tenant data is not something to ship with a parse-tree assertion standing in for an execution. (2) then the wrapper migration, which is small once it can be run: each wrapper is SECURITY DEFINER, takes p_user_id, and branches on auth.role() = 'service_role' so a logged-in caller can never pass someone else's id. UNCHANGED: seller-digest.ts and seller-anomaly.ts stay correct and stay allowlisted as PENDING, which is the honest state - built ahead of the caller, with the caller blocked on a decision about a database rather than on code. | 2026-08-23 THE BLOCKER IS GONE. Docker came back, and the migration this story said could not ship without it is written, applied and PROVEN BY EXECUTION: supabase/migrations/00662_flipdesk_price_gap_for_user.sql.  The previous segment traced this end to end and concluded the DEFINER wrappers taking p_user_id were 'not one option among several, they are the only one that does not duplicate scoring', and that what would unblock it, in order, was (1) Docker restarted as administrator, (2) the wrapper migration. Both are now done.  WHAT 00662 DOES. flipdesk_price_gap gains p_user_id uuid default null and a `caller` CTE resolving whose rows to score:   case when auth.role() = 'service_role' then coalesce(p_user_id, auth.uid())        else auth.uid() end The three `= auth.uid()` scoping predicates (00652 lines 122, 128, 153) now read that. Nothing else changed.  PROVEN, not reasoned about, against the local stack with two seeded users:   service_role     + p_user_id=B  -> B's rows      (itemsUnscored 1)   authenticated(A) + p_user_id=B  -> A's rows      (itemsUnscored 0, cannot reach B)   authenticated(B) + p_user_id=A  -> B's OWN rows  (itemsUnscored 1, argument ignored)   service_role     + no p_user_id -> nothing       (itemsUnscored 0, today's behaviour) The third row is the security property. The argument is IGNORED rather than refused for a non-service_role caller, so there is no error to probe and it cannot serve as an oracle either.  THE BODY WAS TRANSFORMED, NEVER RETYPED, and the generator asserts the round trip: undo the three predicate rewrites and the signature and the result is BYTE-IDENTICAL to 00652. That is not fussiness - US-2832 records a hand-typed repair that silently drifted ON DELETE SET NULL to CASCADE, and this is 180 lines of money scoring where one character changes a dollar figure.  TWO THINGS FELL OUT THAT ARE WORTH MORE THAN THE MIGRATION.  1. THE GUARD HAD A HOLE EXACTLY HERE.    src/test/edge-never-calls-caller-scoped-rpc.test.ts skips every SECURITY    DEFINER function, on the reasonable assumption that a DEFINER function    takes its subject as an argument. flipdesk_price_gap disproved that:    DEFINER, no user parameter, scoped by auth.uid(). So the guard whose    message names the p_user_id wrapper as THE fix could never have fired for    the function that needed it. definerRowScoped() now covers that shape, at    zero edge callers, and a case asserts flipdesk_price_gap is NOT in the list    so a revert of 00662 reddens by name. Sabotage 2/2, green control either    side.  2. AND MY FIRST MEASUREMENT OF THE HOLE WAS WRONG, WHICH IS THE MORE USEFUL    HALF. Asking 'DEFINER + reads auth.uid() + no user id' returned 13    functions with FOUR already called from the edge, which reads as a live    breach. It is not. All four use auth.uid() for AUTHORIZATION - reading the    caller's role - and in three of them the matches were inside COMMENTS about    a guard that was fixed months ago. Reading the session is not scoping by    it, and a comment is not code. The real question - a scoping predicate on    an owner column, over the body with comments stripped - answers FIVE, and    ZERO called from the edge. No breach today. That correction is written into    the guard's header so the next person does not re-raise the alarm.  WHAT IS STILL OPEN, and it is now ordinary work rather than a blocked decision:   AC1 - the scheduled job itself. composeSellerDigest sends on         `hasNews = anomalies.length > 0 || moneyIsNews`, so a first version         needs only money-left (now reachable via 00662) and anomalies. The         anomaly half needs a weekly series per seller, and re-reading it, that         does NOT need a wrapper: detectSellerAnomaly takes WeekPoint[], which         is weekly counts and revenue, and those are ordinary tenant-scoped         queries the edge already makes against sales and listings. The earlier         segment's 'anomalies need the same aggregates' is true only of the         SCORED aggregates, which the anomaly rule does not use.   AC6 - opt-out honoured in the recipient query.   seller-digest.ts and seller-anomaly.ts remain correct and remain allowlisted   as PENDING in check-unwired-modules.mjs, which is still the honest state.  ⚠ 00662 IS HELD. Packaged in PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md with the apply order, the NOTIFY pgrst reminder (the SIGNATURE changed, so a stale PostgREST cache will 404 the browser's existing one-argument call), and the reason the two grants are re-issued: dropping a function destroys its grants, measured - CREATE OR REPLACE preserves a prior REVOKE, DROP + CREATE loses it. | 2026-08-25 STALE HELD-MIGRATION CLAIM. Every migration this story's notes
describe as HELD -- 00412, 00451, 00474, 00652, 00654, 00656, 00659, 00662 --
is applied to prod and on origin/main. The owner confirmed the whole backlog
of held migrations is applied, and PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md now carries no
PENDING entry at all.

The segments above stay exactly as written. They were true when written and
they carry the reasoning; what they no longer describe is the state of the
branch. Nothing here freezes a push.

WHAT IS STILL OPEN IS UNCHANGED and is not about migrations: AC1's scheduled
job and AC4's delivery. Both were unblocked once 00662 landed -- the DEFINER
wrapper taking p_user_id is what let the edge read money-left per seller
without a second copy of the scoring. seller-digest.ts and seller-anomaly.ts
remain correct, pure, tested and allowlisted as PENDING in
check-unwired-modules.mjs, which is still the honest state: built ahead of
their caller.

userStories.title: Analytics over the API and CSV parity across every analytics surface
userStories.description: As a reseller with my own spreadsheets, I want every analytics view available as CSV in the UI and over the existing API key, so that my data is mine and not trapped in a chart.
acceptanceCriteria: Every tab on /dashboard/flipdesk/analytics has a working CSV export, including the tabs added by this epic; a test asserts that each registered analytics view has an export handler.
New read-only endpoints under /api/v1/analytics/* expose the same payloads to an API key, authenticated through the existing api_keys path used by /api/v1 routes.
Every endpoint is tenant-scoped to the key's owning user, and a case per endpoint is added to services/edge-functions/src/tests/tenant-isolation_test.ts (US-268).
Cohort figures returned over the API carry the same k-anonymity suppression as the UI; a test proves an API response cannot expose a cohort figure the UI would hide.
Endpoints are rate-limited through the existing limiter rather than a new one, and are documented in the existing API reference surface.
CSV column headers match the UI column labels exactly, so a seller can map them without a guide.
userStories.notes:
2026-08-23 AC1 AND AC6 SHIPPED. Commit a58a77536. AC2-AC5 (the API half) untouched.

THE GAP WAS SIX VIEWS WIDE, measured rather than assumed: the analytics page
mounts twelve lazy modules and three of them offered a CSV. Missing were the
seller scorecard, price-gap (both tables), measurement drift, return attribution
(both tables), listing performance and community insights (both tables).

AC1's 'a test asserts that each registered analytics view has an export handler'
is src/test/analytics-csv-parity.test.ts, and it has NO ALLOWLIST AND NO
REGISTRY. Both would rot - a hand-written allowlist is the easiest thing to
widen when a guard complains, and a hand-listed set of views stops growing the
day someone adds a thirteenth. The rule derives from a split already clean in
the source: a view that calls useQuery fetched rows nobody else has and must let
the seller export them; a chart taking data as props has nothing of its own to
give. Measured first - the report sections have 2-4 useQuery calls each, the
three charts have zero. A new report is covered the moment it is mounted.

THREE CHOICES THAT ARE DECISIONS, NOT DEFAULTS:

1. ONE EXPORT PER TABLE where a view has two. Price-gap labels the same column
   'Asking / Under by' when live and 'Sold for / Short by' when sold. AC6 wants
   headers matching the screen exactly, so a merged file would have to invent
   neutral wording - the decoder AC6 exists to avoid. The seller-facing split is
   real too: the live list is work they can still do, the sold list is a receipt.

2. THE SUPPRESSION TRAVELS WITH THE DATA, and this is AC4's hazard one surface
   early. Measurement drift hides a cohort median below the k-anonymity floor and
   shows 'N of M sellers'. Writing r.cohortMedian into the CSV would hand over
   per row exactly what the screen refused. Nothing about a CSV looks like an
   endpoint, which is what makes it easy to miss. The suppressed cell carries the
   same sentence the table shows. Community Insights follows the same rule, and a
   null stays blank rather than becoming a zero - zero is a claim, blank is an
   absence.

3. LISTING PERFORMANCE RE-QUERIES instead of exporting the rows on screen. That
   table is SERVER-PAGED at 50, so writing pageRows would produce a file that
   looks complete and holds one page of a catalog that may run to hundreds - a
   truncated export is worse than none, because nothing in the file says it is
   partial and the seller reconciles against it. Same search, filter and sort are
   passed so the file matches what they are looking at, and when the 5,000 cap
   bites the toast names both numbers.

VERIFIED: 6449 web tests pass, tsc -b + eslint clean, ui:check 0 blocking. Five
mutations, green controls either side. Four red: a data-owning view losing its
export, a chart starting to fetch, the lazy-import parse breaking on a reformat,
and the owns-data split collapsing so charts are demanded to export. One green ON
PURPOSE: mounting another view that already exports must not fire.

⚠ ONE SELF-INFLICTED SCARE, recorded because the shape recurs. The regex adding
the Download icon to community-insights.tsx was
/^import \{([\s\S]*?)\} from "lucide-react";$/m - and with /m, ^ matches the start
of ANY line, so it began at line 1's React import and lazily consumed everything
up to the lucide block, collapsing four import statements into one. tsc caught it
instantly (ArrowDownRight is not exported by react) and git diff against HEAD
confirmed only the two intended card headers had moved. A multiline lazy match
anchored with /m is not scoped to the statement you meant.

STILL OPEN: AC2, AC3, AC4 and AC5 - the /api/v1/analytics/* endpoints, a
tenant-isolation case per endpoint (US-268), k-anonymity parity between API and
UI, rate limiting through the existing limiter, and the API reference entry.
That is the larger half. AC4 is worth reading against choice 2 above when it is
built: the CSV work already established that the suppression has to travel with
the payload, and the API version of that mistake is the one the criterion names. | 2026-08-23 AC2 CANNOT PROXY THE EXISTING RPCs, and building it the obvious way
leaks other sellers' data. Read from the migrations, not measured (Docker is
wedged on this box, so no local stack to run it against) - but the SQL is not
ambiguous. Nothing shipped for this; the finding IS the deliverable.

THE SETUP. The analytics UI calls these RPCs from the BROWSER via supabase.rpc,
where the caller is the signed-in seller. The edge has only the service-role
client, which bypasses RLS and whose auth.uid() is NULL. So 'expose the same
payloads to an API key' is not a matter of wrapping the same call.

THE EIGHT ANALYTICS RPCs SPLIT INTO TWO FAILURE MODES, and they fail in OPPOSITE
directions:

  SCOPES BY auth.uid()   condition_price_curve (00651), flipdesk_price_gap
  -> RETURNS EMPTY       (00652), flipdesk_defect_cost (00653), seller_scorecard
                         (00654), measurement_drift (00658). Each body carries
                         `where user_id = auth.uid()`. Under service-role that
                         is NULL, so the SELLER'S OWN half comes back empty
                         while the cohort half still computes. A 200 with the
                         seller's own numbers missing and the market numbers
                         present - wrong in a way that looks like a thin
                         account.

  SECURITY INVOKER,      flipdesk_return_attribution (00655),
  NO auth.uid()          flipdesk_source_yield (00656),
  -> RETURNS EVERYONE    flipdesk_listing_quality_lift (00657). These scope
                         PURELY by RLS and take only a date. Service-role
                         bypasses RLS, so they would return EVERY SELLER'S
                         rows. That is a US-268 tenant-isolation breach reached
                         by writing the endpoint the obvious way, and AC3 would
                         not catch it: a per-endpoint tenant-isolation case
                         asserts seller A cannot read seller B's row THROUGH
                         THE ROUTE, and this route would hand A a cohort that
                         silently contains B.

gt_require_role is not the protection here. It ADMITS service_role by design
(00640, and the comment says why: a service-role JWT carries no sub, so a bare
is_admin() would refuse the edge itself). The guard lets the call through and the
BODY is what goes wrong.

WHAT AC2 ACTUALLY NEEDS, and it is a decision rather than a detail:
  (a) New SECURITY DEFINER wrappers taking p_user_id, callable by service_role,
      one per view. Correct, and a MIGRATION - so it lands under the standing
      hold. This is the option I would take.
  (b) A user-scoped PostgREST client in the edge. RULED OUT, checked: the edge
      has no JWT secret (no SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET / JWT_SECRET anywhere in
      services/edge-functions/src) and no existing pattern for minting a user
      token, so it cannot act as a seller.
  (c) Re-implement the aggregates in TypeScript with explicit .eq("user_id").
      Duplicates SQL this repo has repeatedly refused to duplicate, and would
      put the k-anonymity floor in two places - which is AC4's hazard.

NO GUARD SHIPPED, and the reason is worth recording rather than hiding. I tried
three detectors for 'an edge route calling a caller-scoped RPC' and each was
wrong in a way that produced confident false positives:
  1. 'body mentions auth.uid()' - 20 hits, all admin aggregates whose auth.uid()
     sits inside an is_admin() guard, not row scoping.
  2. 'body has <col> = auth.uid()' - 2 hits, both false. admin_audit_log_search
     explicitly branches on `if not v_is_service`, and issue_buyer_reward_credit
     was attributed an RLS POLICY's predicate because my body-slicing runs from
     one CREATE FUNCTION to the next and swallows whatever sits between them.
  3. 'not SECURITY DEFINER' - 8 hits, all fine: they take an explicit id
     (increment_rate_limit, record_campaign_email_open, api_usage_summary and
     so on), so the edge passes the tenant rather than relying on the caller.
The precise rule is 'determines WHOSE rows from the caller', and separating that
from 'takes an explicit id' needs judgement a scan cannot make without an
allowlist. A guard I cannot make precise is not ready, and shipping it would
have added a fourth thing to distrust.

STILL OPEN: AC2, AC3, AC4, AC5. AC1 and AC6 shipped earlier today (a58a77536).
Whoever picks up AC2: read this before writing the first endpoint. The empty-half
mode is annoying; the everyone-else mode is a breach. | 2026-08-23 THE AC2 BLOCKER IS NOW GUARDED, and it turns out to block US-2828 AC1
as well. src/test/rpc-identity-semantics.test.ts, commit 226168b9b.

The rule: a Postgres function called from the BROWSER and from the EDGE must
either take the user as an argument or branch on auth.role() = service_role,
because those two callers mean different things by the same call. Two functions
qualify today (get_or_create_source, admin_audit_log_search) and both are
correct. The analytics RPCs are not dual-called yet - so the guard fires the
moment an endpoint or a job reads one, which is what AC2 will do first.

WHY A GUARD NOW when the earlier note said one was not ready: the earlier attempt
tried to describe every function that COULD be misused, and three detectors in a
row produced confident false positives. Called-from-both describes the MISTAKE
instead of the risk surface. It is narrow, it derives its own justification from
the SQL rather than listing blessed names, and it has no allowlist.

⚠ THREE DEFECTS IN THE GUARD ITSELF, all found by sabotage: the body slicer took
the LONGEST definition rather than the last (both qualifying functions are
redefined later, so breaking the first left a longer one satisfying the check);
the service-role check accepted a MENTION of v_is_service rather than a branch on
it, so deleting the guard left the variable s assignment matching; and a literal
0x08 BACKSPACE sat in the regex, because I edited the file with Python and   in
a non-raw string is a valid escape that converts silently. All three fixed, and
the repo swept for invisible characters afterwards - clean apart from three
deliberate BOM strippers and a binary PDF.

AC2 STILL NEEDS the DEFINER wrappers taking p_user_id. Unchanged. | 2026-08-23 THE BLOCKER IS NOW MEASURED AND ENFORCED, commit 1aea53c2a. src/test/edge-never-calls-caller-scoped-rpc.test.ts fails if any edge production file calls a function whose answer depends on WHO is asking. THE NUMBER: TWENTY such functions exist and the edge calls NONE of them today, so the guard holds at zero with no allowlist. They are not bugs - they are correct browser RPCs. flipdesk_source_yield, flipdesk_listing_quality_lift, flipdesk_return_attribution, flipdesk_overview_metrics, finances_dashboard, seller-facing search and the rest. The service-role client bypasses RLS and makes auth.uid() NULL, so calling one from the edge returns NOTHING for every seller, or EVERY TENANT'S ROWS, depending on which the function leans on. Both answer 200. THE EXISTING GUARD DID NOT COVER THIS. rpc-identity-semantics.test.ts asks about functions called from the browser AND the edge; the case that bites here is an edge-ONLY call, where nothing is dual-called, that guard never fires, and the wrong tenant's rows come back anyway. ⚠ VIEWS ARE WHY THE FIRST VERSION SAW NOTHING. The analytics RPCs read items_full, not inventory_items, and a view carries no RLS policy of its own, so a base-table-only rule reads an analytics function as touching nothing tenant-shaped. Six of the twenty are reachable only through a view. Resolved, and pinned by a test naming items_full. ⚠ AND THE FIRST RUN PRINTED A CONFIDENT ZERO for an unrelated reason: the table-matching regex was built from a string literal, where JavaScript reads backslash-b as the BACKSPACE character rather than a word boundary. It could never match. Caught only because a function I had just read the source of - flipdesk_return_attribution, which plainly selects from public.inventory_items - came back clean. Third instance of that escape this week and the first to produce a false PASS instead of a crash. One of the six mutations reintroduces it. Six mutations, each applied, green controls either side. Two real: an edge caller for flipdesk_source_yield (through a view) and for finances_dashboard (base tables) both RED. One GREEN on purpose: an edge call to a DEFINER function taking p_user_id, which is the shape the FIX must produce. FOR AC2 SPECIFICALLY: the endpoints under /api/v1/analytics/* cannot call these RPCs as written. Each needs a SECURITY DEFINER wrapper taking p_user_id that branches on auth.role() = service_role, so a logged-in caller can never pass someone else's id. That is a migration and therefore owner-gated. AC1 and AC3-AC6 are untouched by this.

userStories.title: The consumer grade flow quotes a price and has no way to pay it, on both phones
userStories.description: Found 2026-08-23 while closing US-2716, by reading the state the flow reaches when the pay step comes back unpaid.  BOTH PHONES SHOW A PRICE AND OFFER NO WAY TO PAY IT. The consumer grade flow ends at needsCredits on iOS (ConsumerGradeProgressView.swift) and Step.NeedsCredits on Android (ConsumerGradeScreen.kt). Each renders a notice reading "You are out of grades" plus "A 10-grade pack covers this one." and nothing else. There is no purchase control, no link out to the paywall, and no way forward at all: the person has uploaded their photos, waited through the upload, and arrives at a dead end quoting them a pack size they cannot buy from that screen.  THE FLOW ALREADY HAS THE OTHER HALF, WHICH IS WHY THIS IS WIRING AND NOT DESIGN. ConsumerGradeFlow carries creditsPurchased() and recheckCredits() on both platforms, plus the AwaitingCredits and CreditsDelayed states with written copy for the gap between a store purchase completing on the device and the grant landing server-side. Every one of those is unreachable today. Android: ConsumerGradeFlow.kt:110 and :117 have no caller outside tests. iOS: ConsumerGradeFlow.swift:145 and :162, same.  THE EXISTING PAYWALL DOES NOT DROP IN, and that is the whole of the work. billing/CreditPackSheet.kt is used by BulkGradeScreen and GradeRequestScreen and takes an itemId plus a GradeTier. CreditTopUpViewModel.kt:205 spends that itemId on grading.validate(id, tier) - the FlipDesk endpoint - to poll whether the balance moved. The consumer path has a submissionId and no item and no tier, so passing one through would call validate on an id it does not own. iOS is the same shape: GradeRequestSheet and BulkGradeSheet wire the paywall, the consumer flow does not.  THE BALANCE SOURCE IS THE DECISION. POST /api/grade/pay/:id already answers with newBalance and suggestedPack, so re-charging is itself a grant check and the consumer flow may not need a balance poll at all - recheckCredits() is exactly that call. Deciding this is what makes the rest mechanical.  NOT INTRODUCED BY THE ANDROID PORT. iOS has had the identical dead end since US-2016 built the consumer flow, and US-2716 reproduced it faithfully. Filed as one story across both phones rather than twice.
acceptanceCriteria: Decide where the consumer flow gets its post-purchase balance from: re-charging through POST /api/grade/pay/:id (which already returns newBalance, and is what recheckCredits does) versus a balance endpoint of its own. The FlipDesk paywall's grading.validate poll is not available here - there is no item id.

A purchase control on the out-of-credits state on BOTH phones, in-flow rather than a link out. US-1338's reason for that still holds: a seller who has to leave the grading flow to buy and then find their way back is a seller who mostly does not come back. They have already uploaded photos at this point.

creditsPurchased() and recheckCredits() get real callers, and AwaitingCredits / CreditsDelayed become reachable. All four exist with written copy and are dead today; if the chosen design does not need one of them, delete it rather than leaving it.

A check-again affordance behind CreditsDelayed, the way GradeRequestSheet.swift:348 and its Android twin already do it. A grant that has not landed inside the poll window is not a failure and the screen already says so, but it offers no way to look again.

An outstanding-purchase redemption on entry, matching CreditTopUpViewModel.redeemOutstanding: a purchase that was paid for but never verified (app killed, network dropped) is otherwise invisible and the buyer is simply out the money. The consumer path has no equivalent today.

A guard that fails if the out-of-credits state has no purchase path, on both phones. This shipped twice on two platforms without anything noticing, which is the argument for asserting it rather than fixing it.

OPERATOR: AC1 is the only real decision and it is small - does the consumer flow re-charge to detect the grant, or ask for a balance? Everything else follows from it. Worth knowing before you answer: nobody can currently spend money at this screen, so whatever the consumer conversion rate looks like today, it was measured with the buy button missing.
userStories.notes:
2026-08-23 AC1 IS ANSWERED BY THE CODE, and the answer is RE-CHARGE. No new endpoint, no balance API. This does not close the story - nothing was built - but AC1 was written as an open question and it is not one.  POST /api/grade/pay/:id IS ALREADY IDEMPOTENT PER SUBMISSION. It passes `grade_pay:${submissionId}` as the debit's idempotency key (routes/grade.ts:1441), added by US-2298 after exactly the failure this matters for: the paid-check is a read and the debit is a separate write, so two concurrent calls could both see `unpaid` and both charge, and each time it fired a customer paid twice. The route's own comment is worth reading before anyone 'simplifies' it - it explains why the FOR UPDATE row lock inside debit_grade_credits is NOT the same protection, because the lock serialises the arithmetic and does not deduplicate the DECISION to charge.  SO RE-CALLING PAY AFTER A PURCHASE CANNOT DOUBLE-CHARGE, which is the only thing that made 'ask for a balance instead' worth considering. And the route already returns everything the client needs either way: if the submission is no longer unpaid it returns early with paid:true and the method; if the debit succeeds it returns paid:true plus newBalance or newIncludedUsed; if it cannot it returns paid:false, checkoutRequired:true, the tier price and the suggestedPack.  recheckCredits() ON BOTH PHONES ALREADY CALLS EXACTLY THIS. It is not a stub to design - it is a written function with no caller, which is the whole finding of this story.  AND THE STORY IS SMALLER THAN ITS DESCRIPTION IMPLIES. The description says the existing paywall 'does not drop in' because CreditPackSheet takes an itemId and spends it on the FlipDesk grading.validate poll. True of the WRAPPER, and not true of the machinery underneath, which I checked rather than assumed:   - Android BillingRepository - creditPackOffers() and redeemOutstanding() take no item id and no GradeTier.   - iOS StoreKitService.purchase(productId:appAccountToken:) - same. The FlipDesk coupling lives only in CreditTopUpViewModel, which holds the itemId to poll grading.validate for the new balance. Replace that poll with a re-call of pay and the rest of the purchase stack is reusable as it stands.  WHICH MAKES AC5 CHEAP TOO. The outstanding-purchase redemption it asks for is BillingRepository.redeemOutstanding, already written and already generic - a purchase that was paid for but never verified is otherwise invisible and the buyer is simply out the money.  STILL UNBUILT, AND STILL YOURS: AC2's in-flow purchase control on both phones is a UI decision about where the sheet lives inside ConsumerGradeScreen / ConsumerGradeView, and AC6 asks it as an operator question. What this note removes is the technical uncertainty underneath it, not the design. | 2026-08-23 BUILT ON BOTH PHONES. Commit a5eb3c61c (android + ios + the AC6 guard). NOT CLOSING IT: the iOS half has never been compiled, and iOS CI has not seen it because nothing is pushed. Android is verified end to end.  AC1 was answered from the code rather than decided - see the previous segment. Re-charge. POST /api/grade/pay/:id is idempotent per submission, so asking again after a purchase is safe and is the only thing that settles it. Neither client concludes a submission is paid.  AC2 IS DONE ON BOTH, and the two halves cost very different amounts. ANDROID needed a new view model: CreditTopUpViewModel is the FlipDesk paywall and polls grading.validate(itemId, tier) to watch the balance move, which the consumer path has no item id for. It does not need the poll at all. Everything below the purchase is BillingRepository unchanged - it takes no item id and no tier, which is what made this a mount rather than a refactor. IOS needed almost nothing: CreditPackSheet(userId:onPurchased:) was already generic. It lives on ConsumerGradeProgressView rather than ConsumerGradeView because that view already spends its one sheet slot on the camera-or-library picker, and two .sheet modifiers on a view compete.  AC3 AND AC4 ARE DONE ON BOTH. creditsPurchased, recheckCredits, awaitingCredits and creditsDelayed all have real callers for the first time since US-2016 wrote them. Nothing was deleted - every one of the four turned out to be wanted.  AC5 IS COVERED DIFFERENTLY ON EACH PLATFORM and the asymmetry is deliberate rather than an oversight. Android settles an unverified purchase automatically when the sheet opens (BillingRepository.redeemOutstanding). iOS offers 'Restore purchases', which is Apple's convention and was already in CreditPackSheet. Either way a purchase paid for but never verified stops being invisible.  AC6 IS src/test/consumer-credits-reachable.test.ts, six cases. Every assertion is SCOPED TO ITS BRANCH rather than the file, because a file-wide search passes on the import line or the neighbouring state's handler - the mistake this repo has made five times this month. It also pins the property that matters most: neither client may set a terminal step from a purchase. A client that flipped itself to grading on a successful buy would show a grade in progress that nobody is paying for.  VERIFIED: 8 Android unit tests against a fake Play Store, and 5 mutations each applied and each RED with a green control either side - including the two that cost real money, handing back after a CANCELLED purchase (a re-charge that must fail) and after a FAILED verification (money gone, no grant). AC6's guard: 5 mutations, all red. The full Android lane passes all 16 checks including R8, the release bundle and the ABI size budget. tsc -b, eslint and 2759 web tests clean.  ⚠ SWIFT IS NOT COMPILED ON THIS MACHINE. Every symbol was checked against its declaration: the AuthStore read copied from GradeRequestSheet, both flow functions and their baseline: label, CreditPackSheet's init, the trailing-closure form of SessionExpiredView, and the parameter order of the view extended. AuthStore is injected at ContentView.swift:62 and reaches ConsumerGradeView (ContentView.swift:2013) through the same subtree its siblings use. All six iOS source guards pass, including check-chained-sheets.  ONE JUDGEMENT CALL WORTH CHALLENGING: both clients pass baseline 0 to the grant wait. A seller reaches this state because their balance was too low, so zero is right in the normal case. If they held one credit and needed two, the wait ends early, the re-charge fails and they land back on the same screen - annoying, not harmful, because the route stays the authority. A real balance would need a read the consumer flow does not currently make.  TO CLOSE: push, let iOS CI compile it, and put a real purchase through on each phone. Nothing here has been exercised against a live store. | COMPILATION SETTLED 2026-08-28. This note corrects one stale claim and changes nothing else about the story.

The notes above say some version of 'never been compiled' / 'iOS CI is the gate and it has not seen this' / 'cannot be verified from a Windows box'. That was true when written and is not true now. Every commit carrying this story's iOS code is an ancestor of iOS CI run 33139420556 on main (2026-08-28T03:37Z, head 1c6067106), conclusion SUCCESS - checked with git merge-base --is-ancestor, all commits in, none outside.

The run was checked for substance rather than for a green tick: both jobs succeeded, and the Build + test job's 'Generate Xcode project', 'Build + test' and 'Build app-extension targets' steps all executed. A green run whose build step never ran proves nothing.

ONE DISTINCTION MAKES THIS READABLE, and without it the evidence points the other way: many of these commits' OWN CI runs FAILED. 33 of the last 100 iOS CI runs on main were non-success, in one unbroken stretch from 2026-08-18 to 2026-08-27. iOS reports one error and stops, so a commit is not guilty of the failure it happens to sit on. 'Did its own run pass' has no useful answer; 'is it in a green build' does.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO: it does not close the story. Compilation was never the only thing outstanding here - what remains is whatever the notes above say it is, and it is now the ONLY thing outstanding, which is the point of writing this down. A story parked behind two blockers where one has quietly cleared reads as further away than it is.

THE CHECK IS TWO COMMANDS AND WORKS FROM WINDOWS: gh run list --workflow='iOS CI' --branch main to find the newest green run, then git merge-base --is-ancestor <commit> <that run's head>. Any story blocked on 'iOS CI has not seen this' can be settled the same way once its commits are on main. macOS-only COMPILATION is not macOS-only KNOWLEDGE.

userStories.title: Live Capture earns one badge for three different strengths of evidence
userStories.description: Filed 2026-08-23 by US-2802 AC5, and the timing is the point: US-2802's own note said this should be decided BEFORE the native halves landed rather than after, and they have now landed (Android 97797cd63, iOS dcb2a1e8f).  ONE BADGE, THREE DIFFERENT STRENGTHS OF EVIDENCE. verified-capture.ts has a single IN_APP_CAPTURE_SOURCE value and evaluateLiveCapture grants one live_verified badge. A browser sends it, an iPhone sends it, an Android phone sends it, and the certificate says the same thing about all three.  THEY ARE NOT THE SAME CLAIM. A browser cannot attest: getUserMedia has no Secure Enclave and no Play Integrity signature, and a virtual camera device can feed it. That was a RECORDED DECISION on US-1283 - web should not offer Live Capture because a browser cannot truly attest - and the on-page copy carrying it was removed when the web half shipped. The native clients could do better than the browser and currently do not: neither sends a DeviceCheck/App Attest assertion nor a Play Integrity verdict.
