All three are app-OBSERVED capture, which is stronger than an unconstrained upload and weaker than what the badge's own description implies.  US-1283 AC1 ASKED FOR device-attested AND timestamped and neither exists. Nothing sends the moment of capture; the server has only the request time, which a slow upload moves by minutes.  NOT AN ARGUMENT THAT THE CURRENT BADGE IS WRONG, which matters for scoping. App-observed capture is a real improvement over an unconstrained upload and the tier is honestly earned today. The question is whether a certificate should distinguish the three, and that is a server-side policy call - a second capture-source value, or a tier on the badge - not a per-client change.
acceptanceCriteria: Decide whether the certificate distinguishes app-observed capture from device-attested capture at all. Doing nothing is a legitimate answer and should be recorded as one: the badge is honestly earned today, and a second tier is a promise every future client has to keep.

If they are distinguished: the shape is a server-side policy change in verified-capture.ts - a second capture-source value, or a tier on the badge. Clients already send a source string per image, so the wire format needs nothing new.

If native clients are to attest: iOS App Attest / DeviceCheck and Android Play Integrity, verified SERVER-side. A client-asserted attestation result is worth nothing, which is precisely the failure mode this whole tier exists to prevent.
A capture TIMESTAMP, which US-1283 AC1 asked for and no client sends.
Whatever is decided, the public wording matches it. certificate.tsx calls live_verified the strongest provenance tier; if that is app-observed capture, it should say what was actually checked.

OPERATOR: AC1 is the decision and it is a product one, not a technical one. The honest summary: today a photo taken in the GradeThread browser tab and a photo taken in the iPhone app earn the same badge, and the iPhone one could prove more than it currently claims. Deciding nothing is fine and leaves a working, honestly-earned tier in place; deciding to split it is a promise every future client has to keep.

userStories.title: The listings.draft_id prod repair exists only in a markdown file, so no audit can prove it was applied
userStories.description: Filed 2026-08-23 from a gap PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md flags about itself at line 906: 'The 00134 repair leaves no durable record. It is SQL in a markdown file, so scripts/apply-prod-migrations.sh will never run it and no applied_migrations row will ever mark it done. A future audit cannot tell a repaired production from one that still has the gap.'  WHAT HAPPENED. US-2726 found production had no listings.draft_id, so every extension cross-listing writeback failed with PGRST204. The column comes from 00134, which is pre-footer-era, so the boot guard never checked it - applied_migrations only records 00254 and up. 00134 could not simply be re-run because its CREATE TRIGGER and three CREATE POLICY statements have no guards; the 42710 it raises is itself the proof that the rest of 00134 DID apply and only the column was missing. So the missing half was applied by hand as two statements pasted from a markdown file.  THE STATE IS NOW UNKNOWABLE FROM THE DATABASE. Production has the column, and nothing in the schema records why or when. Re-running apply-prod-migrations.sh on a fresh environment does not produce it. A second environment - a staging stack, a restored backup, a new region - would silently lack it again, and the only symptom is that every writeback fails.  THE FIX IS SMALL AND ITS COST IS ZERO ON A REPAIRED PROD: a numbered idempotent 'ensure' migration carrying exactly the two statements already applied by hand, plus the US-1108 triple. ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS and CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS are both no-ops where the column already exists, so applying it to production changes nothing and leaves an applied_migrations row behind. That row is the whole point.  NOT DONE WHEN FOUND, and the reason is worth recording rather than repeating. A concurrent agent had migrations 00651 and 00652 uncommitted in the working tree with EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION already bumped to 00652 and the manifest regenerated. The US-1108 triple requires the version bump in the SAME commit as the migration, so writing 00653 would have meant editing another agent's uncommitted line and sweeping their work into this commit. The numbering hazard is real and recorded on US-2670 too, where a migration written as 00619 on a stale main had to be renumbered to 00624 before pushing.  THE BIGGER QUESTION THIS IS A CORNER OF, already flagged in PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md and not answered: how a pre-00254 migration came to be half-applied, and whether anything else below 00254 is missing from production. scripts/prod-schema-audit.sql exists for exactly that and reports every missing table, column, index and function in one read-only pass.
acceptanceCriteria: A numbered migration carries the two statements from PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md verbatim: ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS listings.draft_id uuid REFERENCES public.listings(id) ON DELETE SET NULL, and CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_listings_draft_id ON public.listings (draft_id) WHERE draft_id IS NOT NULL.
It carries the US-1108 triple: idempotent SQL, EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION bumped in the same commit, self-record footer, and node scripts/gen-migration-manifest.mjs re-run.

Take the number LAST, immediately before writing the file, and check the working tree for uncommitted migrations from a concurrent agent as well as the committed ones. This story was deferred once for exactly that reason.
The 00134 repair section in PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md is rewritten to point at the migration instead of carrying loose SQL, so the next reader is not handed a paste-this block that leaves no trace.

A test asserts the migration is a no-op against a schema that already has the column - it is applied twice against the local stack and the second run succeeds. This is what makes it safe to apply to a production that was already repaired by hand.

OPERATOR: apply it to prod. It changes nothing there - the column exists - and the point is the applied_migrations row, so that a future audit, a restored backup or a staging stack can tell a repaired database from a broken one. Then NOTIFY pgrst, 'reload schema'.

OPERATOR, SEPARATE AND BIGGER: run scripts/prod-schema-audit.sql against prod. 00134 was half-applied and nothing noticed for months; that script reports every missing table, column, index and function in one read-only pass, and it is the only way to know whether anything else below 00254 is missing too.
userStories.notes: 2026-08-23 AC1-AC5 SHIPPED, commit 66c96919e. 00660_ensure_listings_draft_id.sql carries the two statements from 00134 verbatim and nothing else, plus the US-1108 triple: EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION 00660 in the same commit, self-record footer, manifest regenerated (403 footer-era entries). AC3 DONE AS WRITTEN: the number was taken last. Checked the committed set AND git status on supabase/migrations for a concurrent agent's uncommitted file; 00659 was the max and there were none in flight. AC5 COULD NOT BE DONE AS WRITTEN AND THE SUBSTITUTE IS NAMED AS ONE. The criterion asks for two applies against the local stack. Docker Desktop's engine is running but WEDGED (docker info does not answer in 20s), so verify:db could not run. src/test/migration-00660-idempotent.test.ts parses the file with libpg_query - PostgreSQL's own C parser as WASM - and asserts idempotency as three flags in the syntax tree rather than as a spelling: AT_AddColumn missing_ok, IndexStmt if_not_exists, ONCONFLICT_NOTHING on the footer. The words 'if not exists' in a comment or a string literal satisfy none of them. It also diffs the column and index against 00134's OWN parse trees with source offsets stripped, so a re-invented definition fails even when it reads correctly - that is AC1's 'verbatim' made checkable. What it cannot prove is that the SQL succeeds against a real catalog: the parser has no schema. SEVEN MUTATIONS, each confirmed applied, each RED, green controls either side: both IF NOT EXISTS clauses dropped, ON CONFLICT dropped, column type drifted to text, the partial index losing its WHERE, ON DELETE SET NULL drifted to CASCADE, and a CREATE TRIGGER copied in from 00134. Re-run after the file was retyped. AC4 DONE: PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md no longer carries the paste-this block, and the paragraph that called this work 'worth promoting before launch' no longer says it is undone. Both now point at 00660. PROD STATE CONFIRMED, not assumed: listings.draft_id is present in the live PostGREST schema document, so 00660 is a genuine no-op there and the applied_migrations row is the only thing it adds. MY OWN MISTAKE, RECORDED: the first cut typed the parse tree as Record<string, any> in seven places and I wrote 'eslint clean' in the commit message before checking, because I read an exit code that belonged to tail rather than to eslint. Retyped with named interfaces so a mistyped field is a compile error instead of an undefined that passes, and the message was amended. STILL OPEN: AC6 (OPERATOR - apply 00660 to prod; it is HELD and the held-migration gate blocks the push, verified) and AC7 (OPERATOR - the bigger one: run scripts/prod-schema-audit.sql, because 00134 was half-applied for months and nothing noticed, and nothing has yet checked whether anything else below 00254 is missing). | 2026-08-23 STATUS CORRECTION: 00660 AND 00661 ARE APPLIED AND PUSHED. Earlier segments call them HELD, which was true when written and is an instruction to stop - a stale one tells the next reader the branch is frozen when it is not, and that has cost real sessions here (US-2286 records one). Recording it rather than rewording the originals, because notes are append-only and a correction should be findable rather than merely present. CONFIRMED FROM PRODUCTION, not from the fact of the push: /health/ready reports schema {expected: 00661, applied: 00661, status: match} with no missing key, the DB Migrations CI lane is green on origin, and PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md now records both as APPLIED with the evidence. FOR THIS STORY: AC6 is DONE. listings.draft_id is still present in the live PostgREST schema, which is exactly right - 00660 is a no-op wherever the column already exists, and its whole deliverable is the applied_migrations row. A restored backup or a staging stack can now tell a repaired database from one that still has the gap. AC7 remains OPERATOR and is the bigger half: run scripts/prod-schema-audit.sql, because 00134 was half-applied for months and nothing has yet checked whether anything else below 00254 is missing. | 2026-08-23 AC5 IS NOW AN EXECUTION RATHER THAN A PARSE TREE. The story shipped with src/test/migration-00660-idempotent.test.ts asserting missing_ok / if_not_exists / ONCONFLICT_NOTHING on libpg_query's AST, because Docker was wedged and the substitution was named as a substitution in both the test header and these notes. Docker is back, so AC5 was done as written: applied 00660 a SECOND time against a local stack that already had the column, and it is a clean no-op.    NOTICE:  column "draft_id" of relation "listings" already exists, skipping   ALTER TABLE   NOTICE:  relation "idx_listings_draft_id" already exists, skipping   CREATE INDEX   INSERT 0 0   EXIT=0  The INSERT 0 0 is the footer's ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING working, and applied_migrations already carried both 00660 and 00661 from the reset. The AST test stays - it is cheap, it runs with no Docker, and it pins the SHAPE against a future edit - but it is no longer the only evidence.  A SEPARATE FINDING CAME OUT OF TESTING THIS, and it bears directly on why 00134 sat half-applied for months. I re-applied all 658 migration files against an already-migrated schema to check the 'safe to re-run the whole directory' claim. 31 failed. THIRTY OF THOSE ARE ARTIFACTS OF MY TEST, not defects: a CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW rewound against a view a later migration widened ('cannot drop columns from view'), and brand-knowledge seeds hitting a CHECK constraint a later migration added. Replaying out of order is not the contract.  BUT THE PREMISE OF THE TEST WAS WRONG IN A WAY WORTH RECORDING. scripts/apply-prod-migrations.sh does NOT re-run the whole directory. It reads the highest recorded version and skips everything at or below it (`[[ "$prefix" > "$current" ]] || continue`). That skip is by MAXIMUM, not by membership - which is precisely the mechanism that let 00134 be missing while every version above it was recorded, and precisely what this story's description says. The .claude/skills/migrations body tells agents the opposite: 'safe to re-run the whole directory (scripts/apply-prod-migrations.sh does exactly that)'. It does not, and believing it is how the gap stays invisible.  ONE GENUINE NON-IDEMPOTENT MIGRATION FELL OUT: 00609. See US-2837.  AC7 REMAINS OPERATOR and is still the bigger half: run scripts/prod-schema-audit.sql against prod. Nothing here answers whether anything else below 00254 is missing.

userStories.title: EPIC: condition-priced comps - grade the market, not only our own items
userStories.description: As the GradeThread team, we want the grading engine pointed at comp listings from other sellers so that every price we quote comes from a measured price-vs-grade slope rather than an eBay condition label a stranger picked, so that sourcing ceilings, listing prices and the public index rest on condition we measured instead of condition someone claimed.
acceptanceCriteria: Umbrella only: children are US-2842..US-2851; this story closes when every child passes
Standing constraint: a comp read is never called a grade in any UI string, API field name or public page, and is never published against a named listing, seller or URL

At close, valueAtGrade in services/edge-functions/src/lib/condition-value.ts derives its range from a measured curve for cells that have one, and all six existing callers (routes/grade.ts, routes/public-grading.ts twice, routes/flipdesk-scout.ts, routes/flipdesk-pricing.ts, lib/grade-band-pricing.ts) get it with no per-caller change
Not US-2708: that epic aggregates buyer claimed-vs-actual reads into a public gap report, this one fits price against measured condition for pricing. Neither story may write tables owned by the other
No cell is published whose held-out prediction error fails to beat the plain comp median it would replace (gate enforced by US-2846)

userStories.title: Calibration spike: prove a comp read is close enough to price with, and measure what one costs
userStories.description: As the founder, I want measured answers on comp-read accuracy, repeatability and cost before any of this is built, because the whole approach rests on a few-photo read being close enough to a certified grade, and a wrong slope costs a seller money on every buy.
acceptanceCriteria: Runs the existing POST /grade-from-url path (services/edge-functions/src/routes/public-grading.ts) against the listing photos of our own certified garments and reports mean signed error and mean absolute error against grade_reports.overall_score, with the sample size stated
Test-retest: the same listing photo set read twice reports the score delta as a number, not a claim
Cost: 100 reads executed, actual spend read from the ai_budget_status RPC (migration 00219) for the comp_read feature, reported as dollars per read
Written GO or NO-GO decision recorded in the story notes, stating the accuracy bar the decision used
No new tables, no new routes, no UI. Findings only

OPERATOR: cannot run from the Windows dev box and is not a coding task. services/edge-functions/.env points SUPABASE_URL at prod but carries a 21-char SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY and a 22-char ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, both placeholders, and EBAY_ENV is sandbox, which has no real comp inventory. Needs a run with real prod service-role, real Anthropic and EBAY_ENV=production credentials, plus the ~100 reads of real AI spend.
userStories.notes: 2026-08-24 BLOCKED, measured not assumed. Checked local credentials before starting: SUPABASE_URL is https://api.gradethread.com but SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY is 21 characters and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is 22 characters, so both are placeholders rather than keys, and EBAY_ENV=sandbox returns no real comp listings to read. No Docker containers are running either, so there is no local stack to substitute. This story is an operator run, not a build. Everything downstream depends on it only for the GO/NO-GO decision, not for code: US-2843 (stock-photo detector) and US-2844 (comp_condition_reads table) are pure local work whose value does not change with the spike outcome, while US-2845 spends real money and genuinely must wait for GO. | HARNESS BUILT 2026-08-25, SPIKE NOT RUN. The story stays open: it ends in a written GO or NO-GO and that is the founder to write, from real data. What exists now is everything except the data. services/edge-functions/scripts/comp-read-calibration.ts runs POST /grade-from-url against our own certified garments listing photos and reports mean signed error, mean absolute error, median, within-0.5 and within-1.0 shares, worst case, per-grade-band splits, test-retest delta, and dollars per read from the ai_budget_status delta. Every judgement it makes lives in src/lib/comp-read-calibration.ts and is unit tested by src/tests/comp-read-calibration_test.ts (21 tests): the three-way join from certified grade_reports through flipdesk_grading_submissions to item_photos, the http(s) photo filter, the photo and limit caps, PostgREST numerics arriving as strings, signed-versus-absolute error, band boundaries, test-retest pairing, and the cost caveats. HOW TO RUN IT: vault/10-ops/comp-read-calibration-spike.md. Needs SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY and CALIBRATION_EDGE_BASE_URL (the EDGE host, functions.gradethread.com, not api.gradethread.com). Start with --dry-run, which makes zero AI calls. THE RATE LIMIT DECIDES THE SCHEDULE: /grade-from-url allows 20 grades per IP per hour, and the script paces UNDER that rather than around it, so 20 garments is about an hour and --retest doubles it. Do not raise the limit to go faster; lower --limit. THREE REFUSALS ARE DELIBERATE. It will not spend without --confirm. It requires --owner or --all-tenants with no default, because reading your own garments and reading every seller is not the same act. It computes no verdict. TWO THINGS THAT WILL SAVE TIME: failed reads are counted rather than dropped, because a reader that answers on the easy half and refuses the rest posts a beautiful mean and is useless; and an empty result names WHICH of the three requirements failed, because "no candidates" reads as "we have no graded garments" and is almost never what happened. COST NEEDS A BUDGET ROW: dollars per read is the ai_budget_status delta for feature=grading period=day, so that budget must exist or there is no counter to difference. NOT VERIFIED: the harness has never touched production. Its CLI guards were executed here (missing owner, missing Supabase env, missing edge URL all exit with the right message) and its arithmetic is tested, but loadCandidates has never run against real rows.

userStories.title: Notification delivery cadence: instant, daily digest, or off
userStories.description: notification_preferences is per-category and per-channel but only on/off. A seller who wants offers instantly and selling activity once a day has no way to say so, so the only lever is a total mute. Add a per-category cadence (instant | daily | weekly | off) plus quiet hours, honored by the notify path.
acceptanceCriteria: Each notification category carries a cadence alongside its channel flags, defaulting to instant so existing rows are unchanged
The notify path batches a non-instant category into a digest instead of dropping it
Quiet hours defer a push/email into the next allowed window rather than discarding it
Categories whose copy promises immediacy (returns, disputes, billing) cannot be set to weekly
Settings UI exposes cadence per category without turning the notifications tab into a spreadsheet
userStories.notes: Partially done 2026-08-24 — quiet hours shipped, cadence/digest did NOT and stays open under a follow-up. Read the split before assuming this story is closed work.  SHIPPED: migration 00669 adds users.notification_quiet_hours jsonb ({enabled,start_hour,end_hour,tz}) and a CHECK on the hour range. Owner applied it to prod before the push. Gate: services/edge-functions/src/lib/quiet-hours.ts, wired at BOTH push seams — safePush() in transactional-push.ts (iOS/Android) and deliverPush() via notifyUser() in notify.ts (web). notifyUser now reads users once for both preference columns instead of skipping the read for always-on types: an unmutable category is still not a reason to buzz someone at 3am.  It MUTES, it does not DEFER. Push only; the in-app row is still inserted and email still sends, so the notification is in the bell when the window closes. Deferral needs a queue, a drain job, and an answer to what a six-hour-old offer-received push means once the offer has expired. Muting's failure mode is you read it in the morning; deferral's is being paged about something that is no longer true. Additive later if wanted.  Two rules that look like edge cases and are not, both pinned by tests: start_hour === end_hour is NO window rather than a 24-hour mute (an all-day mute is what turning push off is for), and a stored window with no enabled flag reads as ON (written by a client predating the flag; the window is what the user expressed). Everything fails OPEN — a malformed blob, an unknown IANA zone or a DB error all answer send it, because silence the user did not ask for is the worse failure on a fire-and-forget path.  The parser is duplicated across Deno and Vite, so src/test/quiet-hours-parity.test.ts guards the drift both behaviourally and textually — a card showing a window the server never applies is the worst failure for a do-not-disturb control, because nobody can notice it.  Verified: 8 deno tests green, 15 web tests green, tsc -b and deno check clean, eslint and deno lint clean, ui:check 0 blocking.  STILL OPEN — this story stays open for it: per-category cadence (instant | daily | weekly | off), the digest queue and drain that batching needs, and the rule that immediacy-promising categories (returns, disputes, billing) cannot be set to weekly. Quiet hours is the delivery-TIMING half; cadence is the delivery-FREQUENCY half, and they share only the preferences column.

userStories.title: Seller defaults for shipping, returns and handling on new listings
userStories.description: Listing format and Best Offer now have seller defaults (US-2852) but the rest of the listing terms do not: business policy trio, handling time, and whether a listing is private. These are per-listing today with eBay's account default as the only fallback, which is a different account's setting rather than the seller's stated preference.
acceptanceCriteria: Seller-level default shipping, payment and return policy ids, seeded into a new draft and overridable per listing
A default policy id that no longer exists on the connected eBay account falls back to the account default and tells the seller once
Defaults are per marketplace connection, not global, since policy ids are account-scoped
userStories.notes:
2026-08-29 SCOPED FROM THE CODE BEFORE BUILDING ANYTHING, and two of the three
criteria are further along than the description says while the third is a real
and currently-live gap. No code changed.

THE DESCRIPTION SAYS the business policy trio has no seller default and is
'per-listing today with eBay's account default as the only fallback'. That is
not what the code does.

AC1 IS LARGELY DONE AT PUBLISH TIME. `PUT /api/flipdesk/ebay/policies/default`
(flipdesk-ebay.ts:1983) already sets a seller-level default for all three,
validating each id against the workspace's cached policies first so a stale or
foreign id cannot be stored. `assemblePublishContext` reads it through
`resolveCachedDefaults(userId)` and then lets a per-listing override win
(US-555, flipdesk-ebay.ts:14054-14068) - each id falls back independently, so a
partial override still publishes.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY MISSING FROM AC1 is the word SEEDED. The default is applied
invisibly at publish; nothing puts it on the draft where the seller can see it
and change it before pressing publish. That is the same distinction US-2852
drew for format and Best Offer, where the default seeds the composer and the
listing row then owns the value.

AC2 IS HALF DONE AND THE MISSING HALF IS THE TONE. A default that no longer
exists on eBay disappears when `syncBusinessPolicies` refreshes the cache, and
`resolveCachedDefaults` then returns `missing`, which becomes a publish BLOCKER
('Configure eBay business policies on your seller account: ...'). So the seller
is told - at the worst moment, as a refusal to publish, rather than 'we fell
back to your account default' once.

⚠ AC3 IS A REAL GAP AND IT IS LIVE. Read from the schema, not inferred:
  marketplace_connections  UNIQUE (user_id, marketplace, account_handle)  00008
  business_policies        UNIQUE (user_id, marketplace, policy_id)       00052
The connection table is keyed per ACCOUNT; the policy table is not. So a seller
with two eBay accounts connected has both accounts' policies in one bucket, and
`is_default` picks one of them irrespective of which account is publishing.
eBay policy ids are account-scoped, so the wrong one is not a wrong preference,
it is an id the receiving account does not own.

Multiple eBay accounts are supported rather than theoretical: account_handle is
in the uniqueness constraint precisely so a second one can exist, and the
Android strings carry marketplaces_ebay_accounts (plural).

WHY I DID NOT BUILD IT IN THIS PASS, stated rather than left as silence. The
AC3 fix is a schema change to a live table on the PUBLISH path - adding a
connection scope to business_policies, backfilling existing rows to the right
connection, and threading that scope through every call site that resolves a
policy. A migration cannot be pushed from this host under the held-migration
rule, and getting it half right on the path that moves money is worse than
leaving it recorded. It wants its own pass with the two ordering questions
answered first: what a backfill does for a seller who already has two accounts
connected, and whether the composer's seed reads the connection or the listing
reads it at publish.

SUGGESTED ORDER FOR WHOEVER TAKES IT: AC1's seeding half first (no migration -
the defaults already exist and the composer already has a seed mechanism from
US-2852), then AC2's fallback-and-notice, then AC3 on its own.

Handling time and the private-listing flag, which the description also names,
were not traced in this pass.

userStories.title: iOS cannot open a web-only surface without asking the user to log in again
userStories.description: US-2879 decided that Rewards, MeasureCard and Developers stay web-only and that the iOS Tools hub should link them out. It could not build those rows, for one reason: NOTHING IN THIS PRODUCT TAKES AN iOS SESSION AND PRODUCES A WEB SESSION. ASWebAuthenticationSession appears in Marketplaces/EbayConnectionService.swift, but that is eBay's OAuth flow; WKWebView appears in Auth/TurnstileView.swift, for a CAPTCHA widget. Neither signs a seller into gradethread.com. So a Tools-hub row today can only open a cold Safari tab that asks for a login, which is exactly what US-2879 AC2 forbids. This story builds the handoff, and only then the rows. Decision and constraint: vault/60-decisions/adr-web-only-surfaces.md section 4.
acceptanceCriteria: An edge endpoint mints a single-use, short-lived handoff token from an authenticated iOS session, and a web route redeems it into a normal web session and then lands on a requested path.
The token is single-use and expires in minutes, not hours; redeeming it twice fails, and a redeemed or expired token is indistinguishable from a wrong one in the response.
The token is never written to a log, never put in a page the browser caches, and the redeem route strips it from the URL before the SPA mounts.

The iOS Tools hub carries a row for each surface the registry marks web-only (read from the generated ProductSurfaces mirror, not a hand-written list), stating in one line what it does and opening it already signed in.
A tenant-isolation test case covers the mint and redeem routes, per US-268 -- an id from the request body never resolves a session on its own.
If the handoff cannot be built safely, the fallback is recorded rather than silently shipped: the row says the surface is on the web and does NOT pretend the tab will be signed in.
userStories.notes: Split out of US-2879 on 2026-08-25 rather than left as an unmet AC. It carries a migration (the token table) and session-minting logic, so it is a security-shaped story, not a UI one -- load the tenant-isolation and migrations skills before starting. The three surfaces it links out are pinned by src/test/web-only-surfaces.test.ts, so read that list rather than retyping it.

userStories.title: A cold launch on a dark-mode phone flashes a white window
userStories.description: res/values/themes.xml is three lines: Theme.GradeThread extends android:Theme.Material.Light.NoActionBar. There is no values-night. So the window background is white on every device, in every system theme, from the moment the launcher starts the activity until Compose draws its first frame.  On a phone in dark mode that is a full-screen white flash before a dark app appears. It is the first thing anyone sees, it is the single most common 'this app feels cheap' tell on Android, and it is entirely a resource file.  IT COMPOUNDS WITH THE AUTH GATE. MainActivity renders `AuthRepository.Phase.Loading -> Unit`, deliberately, so a sign-in form does not flash and vanish on every cold start. The comment defending that is right about the flash and leaves a hole: for however long the session takes to restore from encrypted storage, the app shows an empty white window with nothing on it. The correct shape for both problems is the same one - the platform SplashScreen API, held on screen with keepOnScreenCondition until the auth phase leaves Loading, so the launch icon stays up instead of a blank rectangle, and it is themed for the system's dark mode.  Neither androidx.core:core-splashscreen nor any splash theme exists in the project today; grepping libs.versions.toml for splashscreen returns nothing.
acceptanceCriteria: res/values-night/themes.xml exists and the window background matches the app's dark surface, so a cold start in dark mode never shows a light frame.
The platform splash screen (androidx.core:core-splashscreen for the pre-31 backport) is wired, with the brand icon and a background that follows the system theme.
keepOnScreenCondition holds the splash until AuthRepository.phase leaves Loading, replacing the blank window the Loading branch currently renders.
The splash does not outstay a slow restore - a bound is set past which the shell or the sign-in screen renders anyway, so a broken session cannot leave the seller staring at a logo.
Cold, warm and hot starts are each checked on a device in both light and dark mode, and the flash is confirmed gone rather than assumed.
The app-lock path is checked in the same pass: a launch that starts locked goes splash -> lock screen with no flash of the shell behind it.
userStories.notes:
2026-08-26 AC1-AC4 and AC6 DONE (a0f22dc54). STORY STAYS OPEN ON AC5 ALONE, and the reason is more specific than 'no device' - see the last three paragraphs.

AC1 res/values-night/themes.xml exists. THE BACKGROUND ALONE DID NOT NEED IT: window_background is a @color, so it already resolves per configuration from values-night/colors.xml. The PARENT did. The light style extends android:Theme.Material.Light.NoActionBar, and a Light platform theme in dark mode is not only a white window - it sets light defaults for every surface Compose does not draw: platform dialogs, the text-selection handles and toolbar, autofill and share sheets, and windowLightStatusBar. Those would render dark-on-dark while the app around them is correct. So values-night overrides the parent, and restates the background only because a style in a qualified folder replaces the whole style rather than merging.

AC2 androidx.core:core-splashscreen 1.0.1 in the catalog and the app deps; Theme.GradeThread.Splash extends Theme.SplashScreen with postSplashScreenTheme back to Theme.GradeThread, so it is a launch-time wrapper and not a second app theme. THE ICON IS @mipmap/ic_launcher, NOT drawable/ic_launcher_foreground, and that is the one design call here: the foreground layer is a WHITE mark and would be invisible on the light splash background (#F5F5F5). The adaptive icon carries its own navy circle, so one reference is legible under both palettes with no second copy of the artwork to maintain.

AC3 installSplashScreen() before super.onCreate (the library swaps the window theme there and it must precede the content view); setKeepOnScreenCondition after it, because that is where Hilt has filled authRepository.

AC4 THE BOUND IS NOT ENOUGH ON ITS OWN, which is the trap in this criterion. Letting the splash go while Phase.Loading still rendered Unit would trade a logo for a blank window - the exact defect the story is about. So the Loading branch changed too: past SPLASH_MAX_HOLD_MS it renders AuthScreen(). The shell cannot draw without a session, so sign-in is the only surface with an action on it, and a restore that has not finished in five seconds has failed. Cost of being wrong is the US-2369 form-flash, on the failure path only. Both escapes are driven by ONE launchedAt clock (elapsedRealtime, so a clock change during launch cannot extend or end the hold) and a test asserts they share it - two independently-started timers would drift apart and nothing would fail.

AC6 A LOCKED LAUNCH LETS THE SPLASH GO IMMEDIATELY. AppLock.initialize already ran blocking in Application.onCreate, so the locked flag is settled before the first composition; holding for the session restore would delay the lock screen behind up to five seconds of logo for nothing, since the lock is what the seller must answer either way. The shell still cannot flash behind it - the locked branch is checked before the auth phase, and a test pins that order.

NEW TEST LaunchWindowThemeTest.kt, 11 cases, 0 failures. Source-scanning in the DeleteReconcilerWiringTest / CameraCaptureProcessedTest idiom, with comments stripped so a header describing a deleted call cannot pass. The case worth keeping is the one asserting the window background matches the Compose scheme in both modes: it pins #F5F5F5/#1A1A2E against LightColors.background, DarkColors.background AND the two BrandPalette constants. If those drift nothing fails and nothing looks broken in a screenshot - the first Compose frame just changes colour under the seller, which reads as a flicker rather than as a mismatched constant.

GREEN: testDebugUnitTest 11/11 on the new class; spotlessApply (no churn), detekt, lintDebug all BUILD SUCCESSFUL, lint 'found no new issues'.

AC5 IS OPEN, AND THIS HOST HAS AN EMULATOR AFTER ALL - the blocker is not the one previous Android stories assumed. There IS a working AVD here (Pixel_7_API_35, google_apis_playstore x86_64, the only image installed) and it boots in ~40s. It was not tried before. What it proved and what it did not:

PROVED: at 3.2s into a cold dark-mode launch the screen is the navy adaptive icon with the white hang-tag mark, centred - the splash theme rendering correctly - and no capture in any burst showed a white frame. NOT PROVED: the shell sections under the status and navigation bars, because THE APP CRASHES IMMEDIATELY AFTER THE SPLASH on this emulator: java.lang.ClassNotFoundException com.gradethread.app.GradeThreadApp. That is NOT a defect in the APK and not caused by this change - the class IS defined (not merely referenced) in classes5.dex, verified by parsing the dex class_defs table rather than grepping for the string; all three ABIs are present; the dex is normally deflated; /data has 4.5 GB free; a full uninstall and clean reinstall reproduces it with a new install path. The emulator runs on WHPX with 15.6 GB of host RAM (about 2.7 GB free), which is the likeliest cause. Somebody should try a real handset before spending more on this.

THREE MEASUREMENT TRAPS HIT ON THE WAY, all of which produced confident wrong numbers. (1) The first burst ran while Gradle held the CPU and the emulator's System UI was ANR'd - every frame was the launcher wallpaper, so the app was never on screen and the reading was of nothing. (2)  could not overwrite its output file and printed 'ERROR: couldn't remove existing file' to a stream that was being discarded; the pull then returned the PREVIOUS run's video, so two different runs gave byte-identical results with no error visible. (3) Git Bash rewrites /sdcard/... into a Windows path, so screenrecord's output argument vanished and it reported 'Must specify output file'; MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 fixes it. The general shape is worth more than the three bugs: every one of them returned a plausible-looking measurement rather than an error. | 2026-08-29 ⚠ CORRECTION TO THIS STORY'S AC5 NOTE, from a measurement rather
than a re-reading. No code changed.

That note says the shell walk could not be finished because 'THE APP CRASHES
IMMEDIATELY AFTER THE SPLASH on this emulator: java.lang.ClassNotFoundException
com.gradethread.app.GradeThreadApp', having checked the dex class_defs table,
all three ABIs, the deflate mode and the free disk, and concluding WHPX with
2.7 GB free host RAM was the likeliest cause.

MEASURED ON THE EMULATOR 2026-08-29, with the CI-BUILT APK. Not inferred.

METHOD, because the choice of artefact is the whole point: the app-debug-apk
artifact from Android CI run 33238496128 was downloaded (gh run download),
installed on the local gt_api36 AVD, and launched with `am start -W`. Using
CI's binary rather than a local build is what separates 'the APK is broken'
from 'this machine builds it wrong'.

RESULT 1 - THE APP IS NOT BROKEN. It installs, launches with no FATAL and no
AndroidRuntime entry in logcat, holds focus (mCurrentFocus = MainActivity), and
reaches the SIGN-IN FORM: Email, Password, Continue with Apple, a disabled Sign
in, and 'Need an account? Sign up'. Screenshot taken to confirm rather than
reading the window dump alone.

⚠ SO US-2899's CONCLUSION IS WRONG AND SHOULD NOT BE RELIED ON. That story
recorded 'THE APP CRASHES IMMEDIATELY AFTER THE SPLASH on this emulator:
java.lang.ClassNotFoundException com.gradethread.app.GradeThreadApp', ruled out
the dex, the ABIs and the disk, and settled on WHPX plus low host RAM. On the
same host, with a different AVD and CI's APK, there is no crash at all. The
install even had to be forced through INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE from a
previously installed locally-built package, so a stale or differently-signed
local install is the likelier explanation than the hypervisor.

RESULT 2 - COLD LAUNCH IS 5.4 TO 8.6 SECONDS. `am start -W`, LaunchState COLD,
four runs: 8576 ms (first, includes dexopt), then 6509, 5364, 6000. Every one
of them is at or above MainActivity.SPLASH_MAX_HOLD_MS (5000), which is the
clock the splash and the Loading branch both hang off.

That is the confirmation the AppLaunchTest change was written on an inference
about: a test that asserts on the sign-in form the instant hilt.inject()
returns is asking a question the app cannot answer for another five to eight
seconds. The 15s waitUntil is comfortably past the worst observed launch, and
past the app's own give-up clock, which is what makes a red run after it worth
reading.

WHAT THAT MEANS FOR AC5. The blocker recorded here is not real as stated, so
the shell walk this story wanted is worth retrying: boot gt_api36, install the
app-debug-apk artifact from any recent Android CI run, and look. The part that
genuinely still needs a human is unchanged - publish needs an item, an item
needs a signed-in account, and no session is available on a throwaway emulator.
The sign-in form, the splash and the lock cover are all reachable without one.

AND THE DARK-MODE CLAIM THIS STORY MADE STANDS INDEPENDENTLY: the launch I
captured is the light theme and shows no white flash before it, which is what
AC1-AC4 shipped. This corrects only the reason AC5 was parked. | 2026-08-29 AC5 PARTLY MEASURED, on gt_api36 with the debug APK installed -
which the previous segment correctly said was reachable.

  cold, DARK   -> launcher, then the DARK splash (navy, brand icon). No white
                  frame between them.
  cold, LIGHT  -> the LIGHT splash (SoftGray, navy icon). Not raw white.
  warm, LIGHT  -> the same light splash. No flash.

So the claim this story was filed on is confirmed on a device rather than
inferred: there is no white flash in either theme on a cold start.

METHOD, because catching a flash is the hard part: am start, then a
DEVICE-SIDE loop of screencap with no sleep, which lands several frames inside
the launch window. Frame 1 is the launcher still showing; frame 2 is the app's
first drawn frame. Screencap from the host is far too slow - eight host-side
captures all returned the same settled image.

NOT DONE: hot start, and warm in dark. AC6's app-lock path is still out of
reach here - AppLock.locked needs the lock enabled, which needs a signed-in
account, and no session is available on a throwaway emulator.

⚠ AND THE CHECK FOUND A DIFFERENT BUG, filed and fixed as US-3003: the sign-in
HEADLINE was invisible in dark mode - black text on the navy window, because
setContent had no Surface and LocalContentColor defaulted to black. This story
is about the window background before the first frame; that one is about the
first frame itself. Looking at the launch in dark mode is what surfaced it,
which is the argument for AC5 being a device check rather than a code review.

userStories.title: Two blocking disk reads on the main thread before the first frame, and no baseline profile
userStories.description: GradeThreadApp.onCreate starts twelve subsystems and two of them block. Telemetry.bootstrap does `runBlocking { context.telemetryDataStore.data.first()[OPT_OUT_KEY] ?: false }`. AppLock.initialize does `runBlocking { Mode.fromStorage(context.appLockDataStore.data.first()[MODE_KEY]) }`. Both comments call it 'one small disk read'. Both are on the main thread, in Application.onCreate, before any activity exists - and each one is a DataStore first collection, which means creating the DataStore, opening the file, and parsing it, on the critical path of every cold start. Under storage contention this is the textbook ANR shape, and StrictMode would flag both.  AppLock's is the harder one to just move, and that is the interesting part: the lock state has to be known before the first frame or the shell renders unlocked for a moment. Which is the same constraint the splash-screen story solves for auth, with the same mechanism - hold the splash, resolve asynchronously, then render. Telemetry's has no such constraint at all; PostHog can start a few hundred milliseconds late and lose nothing.  AND THERE IS NO BASELINE PROFILE. No androidx.baselineprofile plugin, no profileinstaller, no macrobenchmark module - grepping libs.versions.toml returns nothing for any of them. A Compose app of this size without a baseline profile pays JIT cost on every screen the first time it is opened, and the whole shell is Compose. Play's Android vitals will show it, and so will the first reviewer on a mid-range phone.  Nobody has measured the number. That is the first acceptance criterion, because a startup story with no before-figure cannot be finished.
acceptanceCriteria: Cold, warm and hot start are measured on a real mid-range device before any change, and the numbers are written into the story, so the after-figures mean something.
Telemetry.bootstrap no longer blocks: the opt-out is resolved asynchronously and PostHog starts when it resolves.
AppLock.initialize no longer blocks the main thread, and the first frame still cannot render unlocked - resolved by holding the splash rather than by blocking, alongside the splash-screen story.
No runBlocking remains anywhere on the Application.onCreate path; a guard or a test pins that, since this is a pattern that returns.
A baseline profile is generated from a macrobenchmark that walks the real critical path - launch, shell, inventory list, item detail, capture - and is committed and packaged.
The twelve subsystem starts in onCreate are triaged into 'must be before the first frame' and 'can be deferred', and the deferred ones are moved off it.
The measured improvement is recorded in the story, and Android vitals is named as where it will be watched after release.
userStories.notes:
Partial 2026-08-28, shipped in b72fa4552. AC2, AC3 and AC4 DONE and verified on this host. AC1, AC5, AC6 and AC7 OUTSTANDING - see the last two paragraphs.

AC2 WAS ALREADY DONE BEFORE THIS STORY WAS PICKED UP, by US-2897. Telemetry.bootstrap no longer does runBlocking { telemetryDataStore.data.first() }; it takes the app scope and resolves asynchronously, because the consent regime needs a network round trip and cannot happen on the main thread. The story's premise was true when filed and half of it had since been fixed by a story about something else.

AC3 AppLock.initialize(context, scope) reads the stored mode on Dispatchers.IO, and AppLock exposes a `resolved` StateFlow. MainActivity's splash now holds on that flag, bounded by the same SPLASH_MAX_HOLD_MS clock as the auth escape. THE GUARANTEE IS KEPT BY WAITING RATHER THAN BY BLOCKING - which is exactly what the AC asked for, and the same mechanism US-2899 uses for the session restore. It costs nothing that was not already being spent, because the splash was on screen anyway.

WHY THE BLOCKING READ EXISTED, because it was not carelessness: the lock state has to be known before the first frame or the shell renders unlocked for a moment, and blocking is the shortest way to guarantee that from a non-suspending onCreate. MainActivity's own splash-hold comment depended on it in writing - 'AppLock.initialize has already run (blocking, in Application.onCreate), so `locked` is settled before the first composition'. Removing the runBlocking without moving that clause would have reintroduced the unlocked-flash the block was preventing.

IT FAILS TO OFF, deliberately. A failed read means no stored preference could be loaded, and an app that locked itself on a storage error would be unopenable with no way for the seller to fix it. The lock guards financial screens behind a shell that still requires a session, so failing open here is not a bypass.

AC4 android/app/src/test/.../StartupBlockingTest.kt, 4 cases. A source scan over the FIVE files Application.onCreate touches - a named list, not a transitive walk, because a walk would pull in most of the app and turn this into a repo-wide ban on runBlocking, which is a different and much harder rule. It strips comments first: both original offenders are now DESCRIBED in comments (Telemetry.kt literally says 'It used to do runBlocking { dataStore.first() }'), and a raw scan would fire on the note explaining the fix - mode 7 of this repo's guards-that-do-not-guard list. A case proves the stripper did not disarm the scan, which is a failure recorded here before.

SABOTAGE-TESTED, AND THE FIRST ATTEMPT WAS NOT A RESULT. Reintroducing runBlocking without its import made the module fail to COMPILE, so the test never ran - a red build is not a passing guard, and reading it as one is how a guard gets trusted for the wrong reason. With a version that compiles, the guard fails and names the file: 'runBlocking is back on the startup path in [platform/applock/AppLock.kt]'.

OUTSTANDING, and none of it is answerable from a Windows box with no phone:
  AC1 cold / warm / hot start measured on a real mid-range device BEFORE the change. The story is right that a startup story with no before-figure cannot be finished, and it is now partly un-measurable: the AppLock read is already gone. Measure what remains and treat that as the new baseline rather than pretending to a before.
  AC5 a baseline profile from a macrobenchmark walking launch / shell / inventory / item detail / capture. There is still no androidx.baselineprofile plugin, no profileinstaller and no macrobenchmark module. An emulator can run one but the numbers are not trustworthy, which is Google's own guidance.
  AC6 the twelve subsystem starts in onCreate are NOT yet triaged into must-be-before-first-frame and can-be-deferred. Worth doing with the measurement rather than before it, since the triage is only interesting if a deferred start shows up in the number.
  AC7 the after-figures and the Android-vitals watch.

WHAT SHIPPED IS CORRECT REGARDLESS OF THE NUMBER: removing a main-thread file read from Application.onCreate does not need a benchmark to justify it, only to size it. The guard is what stops it coming back while the measurement waits for hardware.

VERIFIED 2026-08-28 on JDK 21 / compileSdk 36: spotlessCheck, detekt, lintDebug ('found no new issues') and testDebugUnitTest all green - 190 result files, 2088 tests, 0 failures, 0 skipped. | 2026-08-29 A COLD-LAUNCH NUMBER, which this story did not have. Measured, not modelled.

The app-debug-apk artifact from Android CI run 33238496128 was installed on the
local gt_api36 AVD and launched four times with `am start -W`, force-stopped
between each. LaunchState COLD every time. TotalTime: 8576 ms (first run,
includes dexopt), then 6509, 5364, 6000.

That is an emulator with swiftshader, so it is not a handset number and must
not be quoted as one. It is a usable BEFORE for the same device: whatever the
blocking main-thread reads and the missing baseline profile are worth, they are
worth it against 5.4-6.5 seconds here.

Worth knowing alongside it: MainActivity.SPLASH_MAX_HOLD_MS is 5000, and every
one of these launches took LONGER than that. So on this device the splash is
not masking the wait - it lets go and the seller watches the rest of it.

Nothing here changes AC status. AC5 still needs the androidx.baselineprofile
plugin and a macrobenchmark; this is the number to beat. | 2026-08-29 A SECOND MEASUREMENT ON THE SAME EMULATOR, AND IT SAYS THE METHOD
IS NOT GOOD ENOUGH RATHER THAN THAT ANYTHING GOT FASTER.

  earlier today (recorded above): 8576 (dexopt), 6509, 5364, 6000 ms
  now, same gt_api36, am start -W, force-stopped between, LaunchState COLD
  every time:                     5071, 3495, 3337, 3881 ms

⚠ DO NOT READ THAT AS A 40% WIN. I nearly did. The two blocking DataStore
reads were already gone when the FIRST set was taken: b72fa4552 landed
2026-08-28 20:21, the day before. Nothing between the two runs touches
GradeThreadApp.kt at all - `git log b72fa4552..HEAD -- GradeThreadApp.kt` is
empty - and today's commits are screen goldens, a root Surface and a grade
colour, none of which is on the startup path.

WHAT ACTUALLY DIFFERS is the host: the earlier runs were taken while a full
npm run verify plus Gradle builds were competing for CPU and the page cache
was cold; these were taken on a quiet machine with the emulator warm and the
app already installed and dexopted.

SO THE USEFUL FINDING IS ABOUT AC1 AND AC7, not about startup: the
between-session spread on this emulator is 3.3 to 6.5 seconds for the SAME
code, which is larger than any effect a baseline profile or a deferred
subsystem is going to produce. A before/after built from `am start -W` on this
host cannot carry the weight AC7 wants to put on it.

THAT IS AN ARGUMENT FOR AC5 RATHER THAN A DETOUR AROUND IT. A macrobenchmark
controls exactly this - repeated iterations, explicit CompilationMode, a
warm-up, and a median with a distribution rather than four hand-run numbers -
which is why the story asks for one. Until it exists, the honest status of
AC1/AC7 is 'measured, on a device too noisy to compare against itself'.

AC2, AC3 and AC4 ARE DONE and were already done before this pass: both
runBlocking calls are gone (the comments in AppLock.kt and Telemetry.kt record
the change), and StartupBlockingTest pins the named startup files against the
pattern returning. Confirmed by reading them, not assumed.

STILL OPEN: AC5 (baselineprofile plugin + macrobenchmark), AC6 (triage the
twelve subsystem starts), AC7 (a comparison worth quoting, which needs AC5). | 2026-08-29 AC6: THE TRIAGE, AND ONE THING MOVED.

Application.onCreate makes fourteen calls. Classified by the only question
that matters - can the first frame be correct without it?

MUST STAY, and why:
  AppConfig.validateAtStartup   the fail-fast contract from US-1301. Reads
                                BuildConfig; a bad base URL must die here with
                                a name, not inside the first request.
  Telemetry.bootstrap           Sentry starts INLINE on purpose. Deferring it
                                means a crash during startup - the window most
                                worth reporting - is not reported. PostHog is
                                already async inside it.
  WorkspaceScope.initialize     backs every X-Workspace-Owner header, so it
                                must precede any request the first screen makes.
  AppLock.initialize            the splash holds on it. The first frame must
                                not render unlocked; already off-thread inside.
  authRepository.start          phase decides what MainActivity renders at all.
  syncTrigger.observeForeground the FIRST foreground event fires during this
                                launch. Register late and the cold-start sync
                                is silently skipped - a correctness change
                                dressed as a performance one.
  syncTrigger.observeSignIn     same argument against a sign-in during startup.

MOVED to Looper.myQueue().addIdleHandler, which runs when the main looper has
drained - i.e. after the first frame:
  PushNotifier.createChannels   a channel matters when a notification is
                                posted; that needs a push, which needs the
                                registration below.
  PushConfig.initialize         FirebaseApp.initializeApp - class loading and
                                a disk-backed init, ON THE MAIN THREAD. The
                                heaviest single call in the method, and
                                PushConfig's own comment already says push "is
                                a convenience; the app has to open without it".
  pushRegistration.register     unchanged, still in appScope; it just starts
                                from the idle handler now.

LEFT ALONE, deliberately, with the reason recorded so nobody re-opens it as an
oversight: subscriptions.observe, realtimeCoordinator.start,
intakeDrainer.observeForeground, syncTrigger.observeConnectivity and the
BackgroundRefreshWorker launch are all ALREADY off the main thread or are pure
listener registrations whose cost is a callback registration rather than work.
Moving them would add ordering risk - the connectivity monitor and the intake
drainer both react to events that can arrive during startup - for a saving
this device cannot measure. See the previous note: the between-session spread
here is 3.3 to 6.5 seconds for identical code.

WHY addIdleHandler AND NOT appScope.launch: launch moves work off the main
thread but starts it immediately, competing with startup for CPU on a device
that has little to spare. Idle means the first frame is up. Returning false
runs it exactly once.

VERIFIED: installed on gt_api36, cold launch reaches the sign-in screen, no
FATAL EXCEPTION in logcat. spotlessCheck, detekt, lintDebug and
testDebugUnitTest green.

⚠ NOT CLAIMED: a speed-up. The launch after this change measured 9086 ms, but
that run included a fresh install and dexopt, and the previous note explains
why am start -W on this host cannot support a before/after at all. AC6 is a
structural criterion and is met on structure; the number belongs to AC7, which
needs AC5's macrobenchmark.

STILL OPEN: AC5 and AC7.

userStories.title: Play Billing is a major version behind and never shows Play's own recovery message
userStories.description: libs.versions.toml pins billing = 7.1.1. Play Billing Library 8 has been out for over a year, and Google enforces a minimum PBL version on an annual clock the same way it enforces target API - an app on the version below the floor cannot upload. 7.1.1 is one step from that edge and the app has not shipped yet, which means the first update after launch is likely to be the one that gets blocked.  THE MISSING PIECE IS MORE INTERESTING THAN THE VERSION. RealPlayBilling wires launchBillingFlow, queryPurchasesAsync, consume, acknowledge, pending purchases and the response codes - it is a complete and careful implementation. What it does not call anywhere is BillingClient.showInAppMessages. That is Play's own in-app surface for a subscriber whose payment method has declined, and it is the mechanism that turns a grace period into a recovered subscription instead of a lapsed one.  PLAY_STORE_SUBMISSION.md section 5.1 turns the grace period ON, deliberately, with the reasoning that 'a failed card should not drop a paying seller's inventory limits mid-week'. That decision buys three days. Nothing in the app uses them: the seller is never told, and the only thing that happens is the plan quietly lapses when the grace period ends and the sweep catches it. The server-side handling (RTDN, the 72-hour sweep) is built. The one client-side call that lets the seller actually fix it is not there.
acceptanceCriteria: The current Play minimum Billing Library version is read from the official page and recorded with the date, the same way the target-API floor is.

The Billing Library is upgraded to 8.x, every deprecated call it removes is migrated, and the six subscriptions plus four credit packs are re-tested end to end against license testers using the five-step round trip in PLAY_STORE_SUBMISSION.md section 5.5.
BillingClient.showInAppMessages is called on a foreground where the seller's plan is in grace or on account hold, so a declined card is recoverable inside the app.
The paywall and any plan-gated screen tell the seller their subscription is in grace, rather than behaving normally until it lapses.
SubscriptionCatalog and services/edge-functions/src/lib/google-play/products.ts stay pinned to each other by the existing test through the upgrade.
PlayPurchaseRules' settlement logic is re-verified against the 8.x purchase model, since consume-vs-acknowledge is where a billing migration goes wrong silently.
userStories.notes:
PREMISE CORRECTION 2026-08-28, from US-2906 AC1 (npm run android:updates, run on this host).

This story says Play Billing is "a major version behind" and AC2 asks for an upgrade to 8.x. The dependency report says com.android.billingclient:billing-ktx 7.1.1 -> 9.1.0. TWO majors behind, and 9.x is current.

Upgrading to 8.x as written would land on a version that is itself already superseded, and the whole migration - deprecated-call sweep, the six subscriptions and four credit packs re-tested against license testers, the consume-vs-acknowledge re-verification in AC6 - would need doing again. AC1 here already says to read the current minimum from the official page and record it with the date; do that BEFORE touching the pin, and expect the target to be 9.x rather than 8.x.

Everything else about this story stands. AC2 still needs a device: license testers and the five-step round trip in PLAY_STORE_SUBMISSION.md 5.5 cannot be exercised from a Windows checkout.

userStories.title: Android has no in-app help, and no buyer surface at all
userStories.description: Two whole modules exist on iOS and have no Android counterpart. This is not a naming difference - the directories and every file in them are absent.  HELP. ios/GradeThread/Help holds HelpSheet.swift, HelpSlugs.swift and ProductTerms.swift: contextual help articles reachable from the screen the seller is stuck on, and a glossary of the product's own vocabulary. Android has support/ - SupportScreen, SupportThreadScreen, SupportService - which is TICKETING. Those are different things: one answers the question now, the other files it with a human. A seller on Android who does not understand what 'comped' means, or why an aspect is required, has no answer inside the app and one route out of the confusion, which is to open a ticket. That is a worse product and it is also more support load.  BUYER. ios/GradeThread/Buyer holds seven files: BuyerAlertsView, BuyerEntitlements, BuyerEntitlementsStore, BuyerGuaranteeView, BuyerPortfolioView, BuyerToolsSection, BuyerTrustScoreView. Android has none of it. The buyer economy (US-1816/1817 and the six buyer epics) is built server-side, on the web, and on iOS. An Android user who buys a graded garment has no alerts, no portfolio, no trust score and no view of the guarantee they are covered by.  NEITHER BLOCKS SUBMISSION and that is why they are one story at this priority rather than two urgent ones. The app is a seller tool first and it is complete as one. But 'production ready' against the product as it exists on the other two clients means naming these, and the buyer half in particular is a feature customers have been sold on a certificate page that an Android phone cannot open into the app.
acceptanceCriteria: The iOS Help sheet's article set and slugs are mirrored on Android, reachable from the same screens, reading from the same help-article source rather than a second copy of the text.
ProductTerms - the in-app glossary - is available on Android wherever iOS offers it.
The buyer surface is scoped explicitly: which of the seven iOS views Android needs for parity, and which are deliberately not being built, each with a reason.
Whatever is in scope from that list is built, including buyer entitlement resolution, so a buyer's Android app knows what they are entitled to.
A certificate deep link opens the Android app for a buyer, rather than dropping them on the website - which is the moment the missing surface is actually felt.
The parity table (or vault note) recording which client has which surface is updated, so the next person asking this question reads an answer instead of two directory listings.
userStories.notes:
2026-08-30 THE PREMISE IS TRUE ABOUT THE FILES AND MISLEADING ABOUT THE
PRODUCT. Read this before building anything, because the obvious next move -
mirror the iOS Help module onto Android - would ship dead code on a second
platform.

WHAT I WENT TO DO. AC1 and AC2, the help sheet and the glossary. The plan was
sound on paper: scripts/generate-swift-mirrors.mjs already turns
src/lib/help-slugs.ts and src/lib/product-terms.ts into Swift, its --check runs
in verify and CI, and generalising it to emit Kotlin is a small change. I made
that change and then reverted it, because of what the check below found.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE ON iOS:
  HelpButton is a KNOWN ORPHAN, already listed in check-ios-orphans.mjs with a
  frank reason: "The button that opens HelpSheet is written and placed on ZERO
  screens ... placement is a follow-on for somebody on a Mac."
  ProductTerm is read by NO FILE but its own. It is not in that allowlist, and
  the check cannot see it - its rule is "declared and never mentioned ANYWHERE,
  not even in its own file", chosen deliberately because the looser rule cries
  wolf on every inline sheet. A GENERATED table is mentioned by its own
  generated entries, so it clears that bar while being just as dead.

So iOS does not have in-app help either. It has the FILES for it. A seller on
iOS who does not know what "comped" means has the same one route out of the
confusion that this story says an Android seller has. The story's own sentence
- "Two whole modules exist on iOS and have no Android counterpart" - is
literally true and reads as a parity gap when it is a gap on both.

AND IT IS WORSE THAN TWO FILES. Checked all four mirrors the generator writes:
  ProductSurface    read by no other file  (US-2865, the Tools screen)
  ProductTerm       read by no other file  (US-2864 AC6, the glossary)
  ActivationEvent   read by no other file  (US-2884, the funnel event names)
  HelpSlug          read by HelpSheet - which HelpButton opens, and HelpButton
                    is unreachable
Three of four are generated from TypeScript, parity-checked on every push in
verify AND in CI, and read by nothing. The activation-event one is the sharpest:
Telemetry.event takes a raw String on iOS and every call site still passes one,
which is the exact typo risk the mirror was built to remove, still live.

SHIPPED THIS PASS: src/test/native-mirrors-are-read.test.ts (commit 292759a31).
It pins each mirror to a reader, lists the three without one with the reason and
the story, and is shrink-only - an entry that stops matching fails, so a stale
reason cannot outlive the fix. It also asserts it covers every id the generator
declares, so a fifth mirror cannot arrive without someone answering "who reads
this". Sabotage-verified both ways. The file states plainly that a pass is not
reachability.

WHAT THIS STORY SHOULD DO NOW, and the ordering matters:
  1. AC1/AC2 are NOT "mirror iOS to Android". They are "make in-app help
     reachable", and the cheapest honest version is Android-first: Android CAN
     be built and screenshot-tested on this machine (npm run verify:android,
     46 screens with Roborazzi goldens as of US-2902), and iOS cannot. An
     Android help sheet would be the first REACHABLE in-app help on any client
     but the web, and it would be verifiable by a golden rather than by hope.
  2. THE GLOSSARY HAS A TRANSLATION PROBLEM THE OTHER CLIENTS DO NOT.
     src/lib/product-terms.ts is English-only. Android ships en + es and
     check-string-formats.py requires EVERY values/strings.xml name to exist in
     values-es (check_translations, line 96: "missing"). So a generated Kotlin
     glossary either goes in strings.xml and needs 26 Spanish definitions that
     do not exist, or goes in a plain Kotlin object and trips
     no-unlocalized-copy.py, which exists precisely to stop English copy
     shipping where it cannot translate. Neither is a blocker; both are a
     DECISION that has to be made before code, and it does not exist on iOS
     because iOS ships English only.
  3. AC3's scoping question (which of the seven buyer views Android needs) is
     untouched and is still the owner's call.

Nothing about AC3-AC6 changed. No Android code was written.

userStories.title: On a tablet the app is a phone layout with a rail down the side
userStories.description: MainActivity computes a WindowSizeClass and reduces it to one boolean, isCompactWidth. Sections.navKindForWidth turns that boolean into NavigationBar or NavigationRail. That is the entire adaptive story: on a 10-inch tablet the seller gets the same single stretched column of inventory with the navigation moved to the left edge.  PLAY_STORE_SUBMISSION.md section 2 says 'the app is Compose with material3-window-size-class wired in, so it adapts; take the shots.' The library is wired in. The app does not adapt beyond the navigation chrome, and a screenshot of a 1200dp-wide list of single-line rows is an argument against installing this on a tablet, not for it.  WHAT PLAY DOES WITH THAT. Omitting the tablet screenshot sets puts a 'not designed for tablets' notice on the listing for tablet and ChromeOS users. Supplying screenshots of a stretched phone layout is worse - it is the same notice, delivered by the images. Play also surfaces large-screen quality in its own app-quality checks, and a list-detail surface with no detail pane is the specific thing those checks look for.  THE APP HAS THE SHAPE FOR IT ALREADY. Inventory is a list of items that open a detail screen. Money is a list of sales that open a sale. Marketplaces is a list of listings. Every one of those is a list-detail pair that becomes two panes on a wide screen with no new concepts, and Compose has a supporting library for exactly this pattern.
acceptanceCriteria: Inventory renders as list-detail on Medium and Expanded widths: the list stays, the item opens beside it, and nothing about the compact layout changes.
The same treatment is applied to at least Money/Sales and Marketplaces, or those are explicitly deferred with a reason.
Rotation and window resize (split screen, a foldable unfolding, a ChromeOS window drag) preserve the selected item and the scroll position rather than resetting.
Text measure stays readable on a wide screen - a 65-75ch bound rather than a line of body text running the full width of a tablet.
Screenshot goldens cover the expanded layout, so the two-pane arrangement is a thing a regression can break visibly.
The tablet screenshot sets in the listing are taken from the new layout, and PLAY_STORE_SUBMISSION.md's 'so it adapts' claim is rewritten to say what actually adapts.
userStories.notes:
2026-08-29 THE PREMISE IS NOW A PICTURE, and it is worse than the sentence.

NEW: android/app/src/test/.../TabletLayoutScreenshotTest.kt, one capture at
sw800dp-w1280dp-h800dp-land-xhdpi (Expanded width, the shape the Play listing
wants shots of): screen-inventory-tablet-light.png.

It confirms 'the same single stretched column', and shows a specific harm the
story's wording does not carry:

  THE ROW'S TWO ENDS ARE ABOUT 1900px APART. Title, brand and price sit at the
  far left; the grade badge and the Grade action sit at the far RIGHT edge,
  alone in empty space. On a phone those are one glanceable row. At 1280dp the
  eye cannot associate '8.5 Excellent' with 'Levi's 501 Straight Jean' without
  tracking across the whole screen, so the row stops working as a unit.

  THE LIST OCCUPIES THE TOP QUARTER. Three items fill roughly 400 of 1600px
  and the rest is white. That is the space AC1's detail pane would use.

So AC4's 65-75ch bound is not a polish item here - it is the fix for a row
that has come apart, and it is independent of the list-detail work in AC1.

⚠ WHAT THE CAPTURE DOES NOT SHOW, stated so nobody reads more into it: the
navigation RAIL. InventoryListContent is the content; the rail lives in
AppShell, which is still ViewModel-bound and not extracted. This is the half
of the complaint AC1 and AC4 are about, not the whole sentence.

This is the BEFORE for AC5. The two-pane layout now has something to be
compared against, and the claim in the description is evidence rather than
assertion.

VERIFIED: spotlessCheck, detekt, lintDebug and verifyRoborazziDebug green. | 2026-08-29 AC4 PARTLY DONE for inventory, and the golden earned its keep
three times over.

InventoryListContent's root Column now carries widthIn(max = 840.dp).

⚠ IT TOOK THREE ATTEMPTS AND THE CAPTURE CAUGHT ALL THREE. Worth recording,
because each failure was invisible in the source:

  1. `.fillMaxSize().widthIn(max = 840.dp)` — A NO-OP. fillMaxSize sets the
     MINIMUM width as well as the maximum, so the later bound cannot shrink
     anything. The tablet golden came back BYTE-IDENTICAL, which is the only
     reason I noticed; the code reads as if it works.

  2. Correct order, but applied to the Column INSIDE PullToRefreshBox — which
     is the list only. The search field, counts row, stage tabs and sort chips
     all sit ABOVE that box. Result: a centred list under full-width chrome,
     WORSE than the stretched version, because the screen stopped reading as
     one column at all.

  3. The root Column. Chrome and rows bounded together, aligned as a unit.

PHONES ARE PROVABLY UNTOUCHED. verifyRoborazzi passes with only the tablet
golden modified — every phone capture in the repo is byte-identical. That is
why widthIn rather than a size-class branch: below the bound nothing changes,
so the existing goldens ARE the regression test and no new phone case was
needed to prove it.

⚠ WHAT THIS IS NOT. It is not AC1. A bounded single column is a narrower
stretched column, not list-detail, and the row's two ends are still about
740dp apart inside the bound — better than 1900px and not yet good. It is also
not AC4's 65-75ch prose measure, which is tighter and belongs on the
text-heavy screens rather than on a scannable list.

It is worth having on its own because it is independent of AC1 and ships
today, and because the story now has a before AND an after.

STILL OPEN: AC1 (list-detail), AC2, AC3 (rotation/resize state), AC5 for the
expanded two-pane layout once it exists, AC6. | 2026-08-29 AC2 PARTLY DONE: Money carries the same bound, and the token is now
shared rather than copied.

ui/theme/Dimens.kt gains ContentMaxWidth (840dp, Material large-pane). Both
inventory and Money use it. It carries the trap in its own doc comment: APPLY
IT BEFORE fillMaxSize, never after, because fillMaxSize sets the minimum width
too and a later widthIn is a silent no-op.

MONEY IS THE SHARPER CASE than inventory, which is why AC2 names it. It is a
DASHBOARD: at 1280dp a chart puts a bar label at one end of the screen and its
value at the other, and the KPI row grows until three figures stop reading as a
set. NEW capture: screen-money-tablet-light.png.

PHONES PROVABLY UNTOUCHED AGAIN. verifyRoborazzi passes with only the new
tablet golden added - no existing capture moved. That is the property that
makes this safe to apply screen by screen without a size-class branch each
time.

SEEN IN THE CAPTURE, not fixed here: with two aging buckets the bars are each
about 350px wide, because the chart fills whatever width it is given rather
than capping a bar. Bounded it is merely wide instead of absurd, so it is a
separate and much smaller problem than the one this AC is about.

STILL OPEN on AC2: Sales and Marketplaces. Neither is extracted yet, so each
needs the US-2902 AC3 treatment first or its own bound at the screen root.

userStories.title: The Android dependency set is a year stale and lint is told not to mention it
userStories.description: gradle/libs.versions.toml pins AGP 8.13.2, Kotlin 2.1.20, Compose BOM 2025.04.00, Room 2.7.0, core-ktx 1.15.0, Hilt 2.56, Sentry 7.22.0, PostHog 3.11.2, Firebase BOM 33.7.0, Play Billing 7.1.1, ML Kit barcode 17.3.0 and text recognition 16.0.1. That set was current in the first half of 2025.  The lint block disables GradleDependency, AndroidGradlePluginVersion and NewerVersionAvailable, with a comment that is right about why: 'a newer version exists' is a real thing to know and a terrible thing to fail a build on, since it turns red the day an unrelated library ships. The comment also names the intended replacement - ./gradlew dependencyUpdates reports it on purpose - and npm run android:updates exists to run it. Nothing schedules it, so nobody runs it, and the version set has drifted for a year with the one check that would have said so switched off by design.  THREE OF THESE ARE NOT COSMETIC. Play SDK Index findings, which lint DOES report and which checkDependencies = true was turned on to catch, will block an upload outright when a dependency version is flagged as known-vulnerable - and old versions accumulate those. ML Kit is where the 16 KB page-size answer lives. Play Billing 7.1.1 is one step from the enforced floor. Those three have their own stories; this one is the other twenty and the process that let them drift.  A pre-submission upgrade is also the cheapest time to do it. After launch every dependency bump is a change to an app people have installed.
acceptanceCriteria: npm run android:updates is run and its full report is attached to the story, so the gap is a list rather than an impression.
Every dependency is either upgraded or has a written reason for staying, and the reasons are in libs.versions.toml next to the pin, in the idiom that file already uses.
lintRelease is run with checkDependencies = true and every Play SDK Index finding is resolved - a known-vulnerable dependency version is an upload rejection, not a warning.
The full suite, the screenshot lane and a real-device smoke pass on the upgraded set before it is committed; a Compose BOM jump in particular is a visual change.
A recurring check is scheduled (a monthly workflow, or the vault deploy runbook) so this cannot silently drift for another year with the lint checks still disabled for the same good reason.

The Data safety form is re-checked after the upgrade, as PLAY_STORE_SUBMISSION.md section 3.6 requires: an SDK that starts collecting an advertising id makes the form false with no change to our code.
userStories.notes:
Partial 2026-08-28. AC1 DONE and AC3 ANSWERED, both by running things on this host rather than reasoning about them. AC2, AC4, AC5, AC6 outstanding. TWO OF THIS STORY'S OWN PREMISES ARE WRONG - see below.

AC1 npm run android:updates was run (JDK 21, 3m). THE GAP AS A LIST: 14 dependencies at their latest milestone, 87 behind, and 17 of those are MAJOR-version jumps. Report at android/build/dependencyUpdates/report.txt; it is a build artefact, so regenerate rather than trusting this summary once the set moves.

The seventeen majors, which are the ones with real work behind them: compose-bom 2025.04.00 -> 2026.08.00; Android Gradle Plugin 8.13.2 -> 9.3.2; billing-ktx 7.1.1 -> 9.1.0; okhttp and mockwebserver 4.12.0 -> 5.5.0; sentry-android 7.22.0 -> 8.54.0; firebase-bom 33.7.0 -> 34.18.0; spotless 7.2.1 -> 8.10.1; the eight android-test-plugin-host-* artefacts 31.13.2 -> 32.3.2; and Gradle itself 8.13 -> 9.7.1. Kotlin is 2.1.20 -> 2.4.10, which is a minor by their numbering and a compiler change in practice.

⚠ PREMISE CORRECTION 1, AND IT BELONGS TO US-2901. That story says Play Billing is 'a major version behind' and its AC2 asks for an upgrade to 8.x. The report says billing-ktx 7.1.1 -> 9.1.0: TWO majors behind, and 9.x is current. Upgrading to 8.x as written would land on a version that is itself already superseded, and would need doing again. Whoever picks up US-2901 should re-read Play's minimum-version page (its own AC1) before touching the pin.

⚠ PREMISE CORRECTION 2, AND IT IS THIS STORY'S OWN TITLE. 'lint is told not to mention it' is half true. checkDependencies = true is ALREADY set (android/app/build.gradle.kts:293), with a comment saying why: Studio inspects library code and the CLI default does not, and the Play SDK Index findings live almost entirely in dependencies. What IS disabled is three version-NAG checks - GradleDependency, AndroidGradlePluginVersion, NewerVersionAvailable - each with a written reason already in the idiom AC2 asks for: 'a real thing to know and a terrible thing to fail a build on, it turns red the day an unrelated library ships'. The Play SDK Index checks (RiskyLibrary, OutdatedLibrary, DeprecatedLibrary) are NOT disabled.

AC3 ANSWERED, and the answer is clean. ./gradlew :app:lintRelease run here in 10m 8s - the lane CLAUDE.md calls CI-only, which turns out to mean 'not in verify' rather than 'not runnable'. Result: 'Lint found no new issues (and 246 errors and 3 hints filtered by baseline)', and parsing lint-results-release.xml for Play SDK Index ids returns ZERO RiskyLibrary, ZERO OutdatedLibrary, ZERO DeprecatedLibrary. So the upload-rejection risk this AC was written to find does not currently exist. That is worth knowing BEFORE the upgrade rather than after, because it means the upgrade is a maintenance decision and not a blocker.

OUTSTANDING, and deliberately not started:
  AC2 upgrade-or-justify each of the 87, with reasons pinned next to the version in libs.versions.toml.
